explanation.tip: Flash = quick; back = to the past.

items.stem: Which words signal that the story is moving back in time?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Had been” and the younger age show that we are hearing about an earlier time.
explanation.tip: Words like “had,” “remembered” and earlier ages signal a flashback.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is the present action of the story.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is dialogue in the present.

options.label: C
options.rationale: “Now” brings the story back to the present.

items.stem: Why does the author include the flashback?

explanation.whyCorrect: The memory contrasts her old fear of the waves with her new fear of the months without her father.
explanation.tip: Ask what the flashback helps you understand about a character now.

options.label: A
options.text: To show that Noura once feared the sea but now fears missing her father.

options.label: B
options.text: To describe the market in the town.
options.rationale: The market is not in the flashback.

options.label: C
options.text: To explain how pearls are made.
options.rationale: The flashback is about Noura’s feelings, not pearls.

options.label: D
options.text: To show that her father is a good swimmer.
options.rationale: The memory is about her fear, not his swimming.

items.stem: What brings the story back to the present after the flashback?

explanation.whyCorrect: The word “Now” and her present age (ten) return the reader to the day of the story.
explanation.tip: Look for words like “now” and “today” after a flashback.

options.label: A
options.text: “From up there, the sea had looked like a sheet of blue glass.”
options.rationale: This is still part of the memory.

options.label: B
options.text: “Now Noura was ten, and she was not afraid of the sea.”

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is still in the past.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is still part of the memory.

items.stem: Put these events in the order they really happened in Noura’s life (not the order in which they are told).

explanation.whyCorrect: The flashback events happened five years before the day the father sails.
explanation.tip: A flashback is told later but happened earlier. Arrange events by time, not by page.

sequence: Noura cries at the waves when she is five.
Her father lifts her onto his shoulders.
Ten-year-old Noura walks to the shore.
Her father sails away on the dhow.

items.stem: How does Noura feel about her father leaving?

explanation.whyCorrect: She is “afraid of the empty months without him” and promises to count stars until he returns.
explanation.tip: A character’s perspective is how that character thinks and feels about events.

options.label: A
options.text: Angry because he forgot her dates
options.rationale: She packed the dates for him.

options.label: B
options.text: Excited because she wants to go pearling
options.rationale: She is not going; she will wait at home.

options.label: C
options.text: Sad and worried about the months without him

options.label: D
options.text: Afraid of the waves on the shore
options.rationale: She was afraid as a five-year-old, not now.

items.stem: How is Maya’s point of view different from Omar’s right after the bridge breaks?

explanation.whyCorrect: Maya says, “It’s ruined.” Omar says, “Maybe we just need stronger shapes.”
explanation.tip: Compare what two characters say about the same event.

options.label: A
options.text: Maya thinks it can be fixed; Omar wants to quit.
options.rationale: It is the other way around.

options.label: B
options.text: Both think the contest is not important.

options.label: C
options.text: Both think the bridge is ruined.
options.rationale: Omar offers a solution, so he does not think that.

options.label: D
options.text: Maya thinks the bridge is ruined; Omar thinks it can be fixed.

items.stem: In “The Stick Bridge,” Maya and Omar react the same way when the bridge breaks.

explanation.whyCorrect: Maya is upset and wants to give up, while Omar calmly suggests a solution.
explanation.tip: Read each character’s words carefully to find their point of view.

items.stem: How does Noura’s father seem to feel about leaving?

explanation.whyCorrect: He kneels, takes her hand, smiles and gives her a shell so she will feel close to him.
explanation.tip: Actions can show a character’s feelings even when the character does not name them.

options.label: A
options.text: Calm and caring, wanting to comfort Noura

options.label: B
options.text: Angry that Noura came to the shore
options.rationale: He kneels and holds her hand, which is caring.

options.label: C
options.rationale: He gives her a special shell.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Nothing shows he is afraid; he smiles.

items.stem: Read: “Everyone cheered when the rain began, but Faisal stared at the soggy football field and sighed.” What is Faisal’s perspective?

explanation.whyCorrect: While others cheer, Faisal stares at the field and sighs, showing a different feeling.
explanation.tip: When a character reacts differently from others, the author is showing a different point of view.

options.label: A
options.text: He is excited to play in the mud.

options.label: B
options.text: He is disappointed because the rain may stop his game.

options.label: D
options.text: He is happy about the rain like everyone else.

items.stem: The story is told from the outside (third person). How would the ending change if Omar told it?

explanation.whyCorrect: A first-person narrator shares his own thoughts and feelings, so we would know how Omar felt.
explanation.tip: Point of view decides whose thoughts the reader can hear.

options.label: A
options.text: Maya would no longer be in the story.
options.rationale: She would still be in the story; only the narrator changes.

options.label: B
options.text: The bridge would break at the contest.
options.rationale: Changing the narrator does not change the events.

options.label: C
options.text: We would hear Omar’s own thoughts about helping his sister.

options.label: D
options.text: We would learn the name of Maya’s teacher.
options.rationale: The narrator choice does not add new facts like this.

items.stem: Which words help you picture the bridge breaking?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sound of a snap and the image of the middle sagging help you see and hear the break.
explanation.tip: To visualize, look for words that appeal to your senses.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This describes the materials, not the break.

options.label: C
options.rationale: These words do not create a picture.

options.label: D
options.text: “a sharp snap” and “sagged down to the table”

items.stem: In the flashback, the sea “looked like a sheet of blue glass.” What should you picture?

explanation.whyCorrect: A sheet of glass is flat and shiny, so the sea looked calm and smooth.
explanation.tip: Comparisons help you build a picture in your mind.

options.label: B
options.text: A sea full of big crashing waves

options.label: D
options.rationale: The sea is compared to glass; nothing is broken.

items.stem: At the end, the boat becomes “only a speck on the bright water.” What does this help you see?

explanation.whyCorrect: A speck is a tiny dot, so the boat has sailed so far that it looks tiny.
explanation.tip: Think about how things look smaller when they are far away.

options.label: A
options.rationale: A speck is tiny, so the boat looks small.

options.label: B
options.text: The boat is very far away.

options.label: C
options.text: The water is dark and dirty.

options.label: D
options.rationale: A speck shows distance, not sinking.

items.stem: In “Rain on the Roof,” the words “splashing puddles on the grass” help you picture the rain.

explanation.whyCorrect: You can see and hear the water splashing into puddles.
explanation.tip: Words that show action and sound help you visualize.

items.stem: Which line from “Rain on the Roof” helps you HEAR the rain?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tapping on tin makes a sound, so this line helps you hear the rain.
explanation.tip: Visualizing uses all your senses: sight, sound, touch, smell and taste.

options.label: A
options.text: “Slow and low, the gray clouds go”
options.rationale: This helps you see the clouds.

options.label: D
options.text: “Then the sun slides out to say”
options.rationale: This shows the sun coming out.

items.stem: What picture do the last two lines of the poem create?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sun “slides out” and tells the showers to “slip away,” so the rain ends.
explanation.tip: Picture what the words describe, not their literal meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: Silver coins fall from the sky.

options.label: B
options.text: The night sky fills with stars.
options.rationale: The sun is out, so it is daytime.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The sun is coming out, not a storm.

options.label: D
options.text: The rain stops and the sunshine returns.

items.stem: How is most of “How Honeybees Share Directions” organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article gives details about what the waggle dance and round dance are and what they show.
explanation.tip: A description structure gives details and features about one topic.

options.label: A
options.text: It describes how bees use dances to share information.

options.label: B
options.text: It tells events in time order from one bee’s life.
options.rationale: It does not follow one bee from birth to death.

options.label: D
options.text: It explains a problem and its solution.
options.rationale: There is no problem being solved.

items.stem: Which detail describes the waggle dance?

explanation.whyCorrect: The second paragraph tells exactly what the dance looks like.
explanation.tip: Descriptive details tell what something looks like or how it works.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is not a description of the dance.

options.label: B
options.text: The bee walks in a straight line while shaking her body.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is about bees in general, not the dance.

options.label: D
options.text: Scientists watched hives with glass walls.
options.rationale: This tells how people learned about the dance.

items.stem: A text with a description structure gives many details about one topic.

explanation.whyCorrect: Description gives features, characteristics and examples of a topic.
explanation.tip: Signal words for description include “for example,” “such as” and “looks like.”

items.stem: What does the round dance tell other bees?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article says the round dance is used when flowers “are very close to the hive.”
explanation.tip: Find the paragraph that describes the round dance.

options.label: B
options.text: The food is very far away.
options.rationale: A long waggle shows food is far; the round dance shows it is near.

options.label: C
options.text: The food is very close to the hive.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The article does not mention danger.

items.stem: Match each bee movement with what it tells other bees.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article describes what each part of the dances means.
explanation.tip: In a description, each detail explains one feature of the topic.

pairs.right: How far away the food is

items.stem: Why did the author describe the dances in so much detail?

explanation.whyCorrect: The details explain how direction and distance are shared through movement.
explanation.tip: Authors use description to help readers picture and understand a topic.

options.label: A
options.text: To explain how to build a beehive.

options.label: B
options.text: To convince readers to buy honey.
options.rationale: The article informs; it does not sell anything.

options.label: C
options.text: To tell a story about one famous bee.
options.rationale: No single bee is the main character.

options.label: D
options.text: To help readers understand how bees communicate without words.

items.stem: Which is the BEST summary of “The Dripping Taps”?

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary tells the most important ideas from beginning to end in a few words.
explanation.tip: Include the main problem, the key actions and the result. Leave out small details.

options.label: A
options.text: Students found that taps wasted water, got them fixed, and helped the school save water.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is not the main point and is not stated.

options.label: C
options.text: A cup was placed under a tap for one hour.
options.rationale: This is one detail, not a summary of the whole text.

options.label: D
options.text: Mrs. Hassan is the principal of Al-Noor Elementary.

items.stem: Which detail is LEAST important to include in a summary of “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The cushion is a small detail; the main steps are mixing, rising, heating, shaping and baking.
explanation.tip: Summaries keep main ideas and drop small details.

options.label: A
options.text: The bread is baked on the hot wall of the oven.
options.rationale: This is the main baking step.

options.label: B
options.text: The baker uses a padded cushion.

options.label: C
options.text: The oven is heated with a fire.

options.label: D
options.text: The dough must rise before baking.

items.stem: A good summary includes your own opinion about the text.

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary retells the important ideas in your own words, without adding opinions.
explanation.tip: Summaries are short, accurate and objective.

items.stem: Which sentence BEST summarizes “The Stick Bridge”?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence includes the problem, the solution and the result.
explanation.tip: A story summary includes the main character, the problem and how it is solved.

options.label: A
options.text: Maya has forty craft sticks and a dictionary.
options.rationale: These are details from the beginning only.

options.label: B
options.text: Omar likes math books with pictures.
options.rationale: This is not stated and is not the main idea.

options.label: C
options.text: When Maya’s bridge breaks, she and Omar fix it with triangles, and it holds at the contest.

options.label: D
options.text: The bridge contest happens every year.
options.rationale: The story does not say this.

items.stem: Put these sentences in order to make a summary of “How Honeybees Share Directions.”

explanation.whyCorrect: These sentences follow the article from finding food to how scientists learned about the dances.
explanation.tip: A summary follows the order of the main ideas in the text.

sequence: Bees that find food return to the hive.
They dance to show other bees where the food is.
A waggle dance shows direction and distance; a round dance shows food is close.
Scientists learned this by watching hives with glass walls.

items.stem: A student wrote: “The fourth graders measured, wrote, fixed, signed, checked and saved.” What is wrong with this summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: A useful summary explains the main problem (wasted water) and the result (saving water), not just a list of verbs.
explanation.tip: Check that a summary would make sense to someone who has not read the text.

options.label: A
options.rationale: It is very short; the problem is missing information.

options.label: B
options.text: It uses words from the text.
options.rationale: Using some key words is fine.

options.label: C
options.rationale: There is no opinion in it.

options.label: D
options.text: It lists actions but does not explain the problem or why it mattered.

items.stem: Which question is answered in the third paragraph of “How Honeybees Share Directions”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The third paragraph says the length of the waggle shows how far away the flowers are.
explanation.tip: Match the question to the paragraph that gives the answer.

options.label: A
options.text: How do bees show how far away the food is?

options.label: C
options.rationale: That is in a different article.

options.label: D
options.text: Why do bees live in colonies?
options.rationale: The text says they live in colonies but does not explain why.

items.stem: Which question can you answer using “The Dripping Taps”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says, “First, the students wrote a letter to the principal.”
explanation.tip: Good readers ask questions the text can answer, and find the evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: What is the principal’s favorite subject?
options.rationale: This is not in the text.

options.label: B
options.text: What did the class do first to solve the problem?

options.label: C
options.text: How much did the plumber charge?

options.label: D
options.text: How many students go to Al-Noor Elementary?

items.stem: “The Dripping Taps” tells how full the cup was after one hour.

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says that “By the end of the hour, the cup was almost full.”
explanation.tip: Find the exact sentence that answers the question.

items.stem: A reader asks, “How did scientists learn about the bee dances?” Which sentence answers this question?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence directly names how scientists studied the bees.
explanation.tip: Use key words from the question (scientists, learn) to find the answer.

options.label: A
options.text: A longer waggle means the food is farther away.
options.rationale: This explains the dance, not how it was discovered.

options.label: C
options.text: Scientists learned about these dances by watching bees in hives with glass walls.

options.label: D
options.text: Honeybees live and work together in large groups called colonies.

items.stem: Which question would be the MOST useful to ask before reading “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The title tells you the article explains a process, so asking about the steps guides your reading.
explanation.tip: Use the title and headings to ask questions that guide your reading.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This does not help you understand the process.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This detail is too small to guide your reading.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Your opinion will not help you understand the text.

options.label: D
options.text: What steps are needed to bake bread in a clay oven?

items.stem: Which question CANNOT be answered from “Keeping Bees in the Mountains”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article never gives the number of beekeepers.
explanation.tip: Some questions need another source. Check whether the text really gives the answer.

options.label: A
options.text: How many beekeepers live in the mountains?

options.label: B
options.rationale: The text says it is sold at local markets.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The text says the smoke calms the bees.

options.label: D
options.text: Why do beekeepers move their hives?
options.rationale: The text says they move them closer to blooming flowers.

items.stem: You are not sure what the round dance means. What should you do?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading the part that explains the round dance will clear up the confusion.
explanation.tip: When something is confusing, go back and reread that part slowly.

options.label: A
options.text: Skip to the end of the article.
options.rationale: The end does not explain the round dance.

options.label: B
options.text: Reread the paragraph about the round dance.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Rereading gives you real evidence instead of a guess.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The title does not explain the dance.

items.stem: Rereading can help you find details you missed the first time.

explanation.whyCorrect: Good readers reread to check their understanding and find evidence.
explanation.tip: Rereading is a fix-up strategy, not a sign of a weak reader.

items.stem: After reading “The Dripping Taps,” you are not sure why the bill was lower. Which part should you reread?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph about checking a month later explains the fixed taps and the lower bill.
explanation.tip: Reread the part of the text that matches your question.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The letter came before the results.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The title does not explain the bill.

options.label: C
options.text: The paragraph about what happened a month later

options.label: D
options.rationale: The first sentence introduces the problem.

items.stem: Rereading the second paragraph of “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven” helps you answer which question?

explanation.whyCorrect: The second paragraph says the dough rests “for about an hour.”
explanation.tip: Know which paragraph covers which idea before you reread.

options.label: A
options.rationale: That is in the last paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: What is the oven made of?
options.rationale: That is in the title and first paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: How is the bread taken off the wall?
options.rationale: That is in the last paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: How long does the dough rest?

items.stem: Why might a reader reread the sentence “The length of time she waggles tells them how far away the flowers are”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence explains a key idea (distance), so rereading helps you understand it.
explanation.tip: Reread sentences that hold important or difficult ideas.

options.label: A
options.text: To understand how the dance shows distance

options.label: B
options.text: To find out what honey tastes like

options.label: C
options.rationale: Bees in the article are not named.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Counting paragraphs does not help understanding.

items.stem: Which TWO are good reasons to reread a text?

explanation.whyCorrect: Readers reread to check understanding and to find evidence.
explanation.tip: Rereading is a tool for understanding.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Rereading takes extra time; it is for understanding.

options.label: B
options.text: To find evidence for an answer

options.label: C
options.text: To clear up a confusing part

options.label: D
options.rationale: Rereading helps with hard words; it does not skip them.

items.stem: Put the bread-making steps in order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article describes mixing, rising, baking and removing, in that order.
explanation.tip: Signal words like “early,” “next” and “finally” show the order of steps.

sequence: Mix flour, water, salt and yeast.
Let the dough rise under a cloth.
Press the dough onto the hot oven wall.
Take the bread off with a long hook.

items.stem: What does the baker do WHILE the dough is rising?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article says, “While the dough rises, the baker lights a fire inside the oven.”
explanation.tip: “While” means two things happen at the same time.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This happens after the dough has risen.

options.label: B
options.text: Lights a fire inside the oven

options.label: C
options.text: Takes the bread out of the oven
options.rationale: This happens at the very end.

items.stem: Which word in “The Dripping Taps” signals the second step the class took?

explanation.whyCorrect: First they wrote a letter; next the plumber fixed the taps; then they made signs.
explanation.tip: Sequence words: first, next, then, after that, finally.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This word is not used for the steps.

items.stem: Put the events of “The Dripping Taps” in time order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article tells the events in the order they happened.
explanation.tip: Follow time words and the order of paragraphs.

sequence: Students notice dripping taps.
They measure water with a cup.
They write to the principal.
A plumber fixes the taps.
They check again a month later.

items.stem: Why is a sequence structure a good choice for “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each step depends on the one before it, so time order helps readers follow the process.
explanation.tip: Authors choose sequence for processes, instructions and events over time.

options.label: A
options.text: It compares two kinds of bread.
options.rationale: The article explains one process; it does not compare.

options.label: B
options.text: It argues that bread is healthy.
options.rationale: The article does not give an opinion.

options.label: C
options.text: It tells a story with characters.

options.label: D
options.text: Making bread is a process that must be done in a certain order.

items.stem: What would MOST likely happen if the baker skipped heating the oven?

explanation.whyCorrect: The bread bakes on the “hot inner wall,” so a cool oven would not cook it.
explanation.tip: In a process, each step has a reason. Think about why a step is needed.

options.label: A
options.text: The bread would not bake properly on the cool walls.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Heating the oven does not affect rising.

options.label: C
options.text: The bread would turn golden more quickly.
options.rationale: Without heat, it cannot turn golden.

options.label: D
options.text: The bread would not need to be shaped.

items.stem: What problem did the fourth graders find?

explanation.whyCorrect: Taps dripped all day and some students left the water running.
explanation.tip: In a problem-and-solution text, the problem usually comes first.

options.label: A
options.text: The principal was not at school.
options.rationale: The students wrote to her; she was there.

options.label: B
options.text: Water was being wasted at the school sinks.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The cup was used to measure the problem.

options.label: D
options.rationale: There were sinks with dripping taps.

items.stem: Which was one solution to the problem?

explanation.whyCorrect: Fixing the taps stopped the dripping, which solved part of the problem.
explanation.tip: A solution is an action that fixes the problem.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This shows how big the problem was.

options.label: C
options.text: A plumber fixed the leaking taps.

options.label: D
options.text: The students measured water in a cup.
options.rationale: Measuring showed the problem; it did not solve it.

items.stem: In “The Dripping Taps,” making signs was part of the solution.

explanation.whyCorrect: The signs reminded students to turn off the tap while soaping.
explanation.tip: Some problems need more than one solution.

items.stem: How do you know the solutions worked?

explanation.whyCorrect: The results a month later show the problem had been solved.
explanation.tip: Look for results or evidence after the solution.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Bright signs do not prove they worked.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Writing a letter was an action, not proof that it worked.

options.label: D
options.text: The taps stopped dripping and the water bill was lower.

items.stem: Match each problem with the solution the class used.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each action answers a different part of the problem.
explanation.tip: Match each solution to the part of the problem it fixes.

pairs.right: Signs reminded them to turn off the tap

items.stem: Why did the author include the detail about the cup of water?

explanation.whyCorrect: The nearly full cup gave the class proof they could share with the principal.
explanation.tip: Evidence in a problem-and-solution text shows how serious the problem is.

options.label: A
options.text: To show that the problem was real and could be measured

options.label: B
options.rationale: The taps were in the bathrooms.

options.label: C
options.text: To explain how to drink more water

options.label: D
options.text: To show that cups are useful
options.rationale: The cup is evidence, not the topic.

items.stem: Which group of words from “Rain on the Roof” shows alliteration?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Tapping,” “tin” and “tiny” all begin with the same t sound.
explanation.tip: Alliteration is the repetition of the same beginning sound in nearby words.

options.label: A
options.rationale: These words begin with different sounds (w, g, d).

options.label: C
options.rationale: These words begin with different sounds (k, g, l).

options.label: D
options.rationale: These words begin with different sounds (s, p, g).

items.stem: Which line repeats the long o sound (assonance)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Slow,” “low” and “go” share the long o vowel sound.
explanation.tip: Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words.

options.label: A
options.text: “Drip and drop on the window glass,”
options.rationale: This repeats consonants, not the long o.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This repeats p and t sounds.

options.label: C
options.text: “Slow and low, the gray clouds go,”

options.label: D
options.rationale: There is no repeated long o sound.

items.stem: In “Silver showers, slip away,” the s sound is repeated.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Silver,” “showers” and “slip” begin with s sounds, which is alliteration.
explanation.tip: Say the words aloud to hear repeated sounds.

items.stem: Match each sound device with its example from the poem.

explanation.whyCorrect: Repeated beginning sounds, repeated vowel sounds, and words that imitate sounds.
explanation.tip: Say each line aloud and listen for which sounds repeat.

pairs.right: tapping tin roofs with tiny pins
Slow and low, the gray clouds go

items.stem: Why does the poet repeat sounds in “Drip and drop”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The short, repeated d sounds feel like drops hitting the glass.
explanation.tip: Poets use sound devices to help readers hear and feel what is described.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Sound devices are chosen for effect, not length.

options.label: B
options.text: To explain where rain comes from

options.label: C
options.text: To show that the rain is dangerous
options.rationale: Nothing in the poem suggests danger.

options.label: D
options.text: To imitate the sound of rain falling

items.stem: Which sentence uses consonance (a repeated consonant sound inside or at the end of words)?

explanation.whyCorrect: The t sound repeats at the end of “cat,” “sat” and “mat,” and the k sound in “black” and “back.”
explanation.tip: Consonance repeats consonant sounds that are not only at the beginning of words.

options.label: A
options.text: The black cat sat back on the mat.

items.stem: What topic do “How Honeybees Share Directions” and “Keeping Bees in the Mountains” have in common?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both texts give information about honeybees.
explanation.tip: First find what two texts share, then look for differences.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Clay ovens are in a different article.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Pearl diving is in a story, not these articles.

items.stem: How is the focus of the two bee texts different?

explanation.whyCorrect: “How Honeybees Share Directions” is about dances; “Keeping Bees in the Mountains” is about beekeepers.
explanation.tip: Compare the main idea of each text.

options.label: A
options.text: Both tell a story about one beekeeper.

options.label: B
options.text: Both explain only how honey tastes.

options.label: C
options.text: One explains bee dances; the other explains how people keep bees.

options.label: D
options.text: One is about ants and one is about bees.

items.stem: Both bee texts say that bees need flowers to find food.

explanation.whyCorrect: One describes bees dancing to show where flowers are; the other says bees near many flowers fly less far.
explanation.tip: Look for a key idea that appears in both texts.

items.stem: Using BOTH texts, why might beekeepers move hives near blooming flowers?

explanation.whyCorrect: Text 2 explains that nearby flowers mean shorter flights; Text 1 shows that bees share where nearby food is.
explanation.tip: Combine information from both texts to answer a bigger question.

options.label: A
options.text: Because flowers keep bees warm at night.

options.label: B
options.text: Because honey is sold near flowers.
options.rationale: Honey is sold at markets, not near flowers.

options.label: C
options.text: Because bees cannot dance near flowers.
options.rationale: The first text says bees dance about the flowers they find.

options.label: D
options.text: So bees do not need to fly far, and dancing bees can lead others to food nearby.

items.stem: Which TWO details come ONLY from “Keeping Bees in the Mountains”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The smoke and the markets are only described in the mountain beekeeping text.
explanation.tip: Keep track of which text each detail comes from.

options.label: A
options.text: Beekeepers use gentle smoke to calm bees.

options.label: B
options.text: Scientists watched hives with glass walls.
options.rationale: This is from the bee dance article.

options.label: C
options.text: A longer waggle means the food is farther away.
options.rationale: This is from the bee dance article.

options.label: D
options.text: Honey from the mountains is sold at local markets.

items.stem: A student wants to write a report on how bees and people work together. Which text is MORE useful, and why?

explanation.whyCorrect: The mountain text describes what beekeepers do: moving hives, calming bees, and leaving honey.
explanation.tip: Choose the source that best matches the research question.

options.label: A
options.text: “Keeping Bees in the Mountains,” because it explains how beekeepers care for bees and collect honey.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither text, because both are only about flowers.
options.rationale: Both are about bees, not only flowers.

options.label: C
options.text: “The Dripping Taps,” because it is about saving water.
options.rationale: That article is not about bees.

options.label: D
options.text: “How Honeybees Share Directions,” because it explains bee dances.
options.rationale: The dance article is about bees, not about people working with bees.

items.stem: What is the complete subject? “The tall giraffe ate leaves from the tree.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The complete subject tells who or what the sentence is about: the tall giraffe.
explanation.tip: Ask: Who or what is the sentence about?

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is the complete predicate: what the giraffe did.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is part of the predicate.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is part of the predicate.

items.stem: What is the simple subject? “My older cousin from Jeddah visited us on Friday.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The simple subject is the main noun in the complete subject: cousin.
explanation.tip: Remove the describing words; the main noun that is left is the simple subject.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This tells where the cousin is from.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the verb, part of the predicate.

items.stem: What is the simple predicate? “The students in Room 4 planted seeds in the garden.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The simple predicate is the main verb that tells what the subject did.
explanation.tip: Find the main action word in the predicate.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is a noun, not the main verb.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This phrase tells where; the main verb is “planted.”

items.stem: In “Lina and Sara painted a mural,” the sentence has a compound subject.

explanation.whyCorrect: Two subjects, Lina and Sara, share the same predicate, joined by “and.”
explanation.tip: A compound subject is two or more subjects with the same predicate.

items.stem: Which sentence has a compound predicate?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Washed the dishes” and “dried them” are two predicates for the same subject.
explanation.tip: A compound predicate has two or more verbs for one subject, usually joined by and or or.

options.label: A
options.text: Ahmed washed the dishes and dried them.

options.label: B
options.text: The clean dishes were on the shelf.

options.label: C
options.rationale: There is only one predicate verb.

options.label: D
options.text: Ahmed and Ali washed the dishes.
options.rationale: This has a compound subject, not a compound predicate.

items.stem: Add a predicate to make a complete sentence: “The noisy crowd ____ when the team scored.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A predicate tells what the subject did, such as “cheered.”
explanation.tip: Every complete sentence needs a subject and a predicate.

items.stem: Which group of words is an independent clause?

explanation.whyCorrect: An independent clause has a subject and a verb and can stand alone as a sentence.
explanation.tip: Read it alone. If it makes a complete thought, it is independent.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This has no verb, so it is not a clause.

items.stem: Which word begins the dependent clause? “We stayed inside because it was very windy.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Because it was very windy” is a dependent clause that begins with the subordinating conjunction “because.”
explanation.tip: Dependent clauses often begin with because, when, before, after, if or although.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This word is part of the main clause.

options.label: B
options.rationale: “We” is the subject of the main clause.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the last word, not the beginning of the clause.

items.stem: “When the bell rings” can stand alone as a complete sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: It is a dependent clause; it leaves the reader asking, “What happens when the bell rings?”
explanation.tip: A dependent clause cannot stand alone as a sentence.

items.stem: Which sentence is a complex sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: A complex sentence has an independent clause and at least one dependent clause (“After we ate lunch”).
explanation.tip: Look for a subordinating conjunction such as after, when or because.

options.label: A
options.text: We ate lunch, and we played football.
options.rationale: This is a compound sentence (two independent clauses).

options.label: B
options.text: We ate lunch and played football.
options.rationale: This is a simple sentence with a compound predicate.

options.label: D
options.text: After we ate lunch, we played football.

items.stem: Choose the best subordinating conjunction: “____ it rained all morning, the picnic went ahead in the afternoon.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Although” shows a contrast: rain in the morning, but the picnic still happened.
explanation.tip: Choose the conjunction that shows the right relationship between ideas.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This does not make sense with the second clause.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The picnic happened despite the rain, not because of it.

options.label: D
options.rationale: “And” is a coordinating conjunction, not a subordinating one.

items.stem: Match each dependent clause with the main clause that completes it best.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each dependent clause needs a main clause that completes the thought logically.
explanation.tip: Read each pair as one sentence to check that it makes sense.

items.stem: Which sentence is a compound sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: It has two independent clauses joined by a comma and “but.”
explanation.tip: A compound sentence joins two complete sentences with a coordinating conjunction.

options.label: A
options.text: I wanted to swim, but the pool was closed.

options.label: B
options.text: The pool and the gym were closed.
options.rationale: This is a simple sentence with a compound subject.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the pool was closed, I went home.

options.label: D
options.text: I wanted to swim in the pool.

items.stem: Where does the comma belong? “Huda read a book and her sister drew a picture.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Use a comma before the coordinating conjunction when it joins two independent clauses.
explanation.tip: Put the comma just before and, but or or when each part could be its own sentence.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Two independent clauses joined by “and” need a comma before “and.”

options.label: C
options.rationale: That would split the second subject from its verb.

options.label: D
options.rationale: A comma there would split the subject from its verb.

items.stem: Choose the conjunction: “Do you want rice ____ do you want bread?”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Or” shows a choice between two options.
explanation.tip: and = adds, but = contrasts, or = gives a choice, so = shows a result.

items.stem: Choose the conjunction: “The road was icy, ____ the drivers went slowly.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The drivers went slowly as a result of the icy road, so “so” fits.
explanation.tip: Ask how the two ideas are related: result, contrast, choice or addition.

options.label: B
options.rationale: “But” shows a contrast; the second clause is a result.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma is needed before “and” because it joins two independent clauses.
explanation.tip: Check whether both parts could stand alone as sentences.

items.stem: Which is the best way to combine these sentences? “Nasser likes math. He does not like spelling.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The ideas contrast, so a comma and “but” join them correctly.
explanation.tip: Choose the conjunction that matches the relationship between the ideas.

options.label: A
options.text: Nasser likes math, and he does not like spelling.
options.rationale: “And” does not show the contrast between the ideas.

options.label: B
options.text: Nasser likes math he does not like spelling.
options.rationale: This is a run-on sentence with no comma or conjunction.

options.label: C
options.text: Nasser likes math, but he does not like spelling.

options.label: D
options.text: Nasser likes math, so he does not like spelling.
options.rationale: “So” suggests one causes the other, which is not true.

items.stem: Combine the sentences: “Jamal washes the dishes. Teri washes the dishes.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Join the two subjects with “and,” remove repeated words, and make the verb agree: wash.
explanation.tip: When you combine subjects, check that the verb agrees with the new plural subject.

options.label: A
options.text: Jamal washes and Teri washes the dishes.
options.rationale: This repeats the verb and sounds awkward.

options.label: B
options.text: Jamal and Teri washes the dishes.
options.rationale: The verb must be “wash” with a compound subject.

options.label: D
options.text: Jamal and Teri wash the dishes.

items.stem: Combine the sentences: “Our team won the game. Our team won the trophy.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Join the two objects with “and” and leave out the repeated words “Our team won.”
explanation.tip: Leave out words that repeat when you combine sentences.

options.label: A
options.text: Our team won the game and the trophy.

options.label: B
options.text: The game and the trophy won our team.

options.label: C
options.text: Our team won and our team won.
options.rationale: This repeats words and leaves out what was won.

options.label: D
options.text: Our team won the game our team won the trophy.

items.stem: “Mona sings. Mona dances.” can be combined as “Mona sings and dances.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The two predicates share one subject, so they can be joined with “and.”
explanation.tip: If two sentences have the same subject, you can join their predicates.

items.stem: Combine the sentences using an appositive: “Mr. Salem teaches science. Mr. Salem is our neighbor.”

explanation.whyCorrect: An appositive renames a noun and is set off with commas: “our neighbor.”
explanation.tip: Place the appositive right after the noun it renames, with commas around it.

options.label: A
options.text: Our neighbor teaches Mr. Salem science.

options.label: B
options.text: Mr. Salem, our neighbor, teaches science.

options.label: C
options.text: Mr. Salem our neighbor teaches science.
options.rationale: The appositive needs commas around it.

options.label: D
options.text: Mr. Salem teaches science our neighbor.
options.rationale: The appositive is in the wrong place.

items.stem: Which is the BEST combined sentence? “The kite was red. The kite was huge. The kite flew over the park.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Move the describing words before the noun and keep one predicate.
explanation.tip: Adjectives from short sentences can often move in front of the noun.

options.label: A
options.text: Over the park the red the huge kite flew.

options.label: B
options.text: The kite was red, huge, flew over the park.
options.rationale: The verbs do not fit together correctly.

options.label: C
options.text: The huge red kite flew over the park.

options.label: D
options.text: The kite was red and the kite was huge and the kite flew over the park.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A compound subject joined by “and” is plural, so the verb must be “play.”
explanation.tip: After combining subjects, check subject-verb agreement.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “The ____ tail was long and fluffy.”

explanation.whyCorrect: One cat owns the tail, so add an apostrophe and s: cat’s.
explanation.tip: Singular possessive: add ’s.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The noun needs an apostrophe and s to show ownership.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This shows more than one cat.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “The two ____ bikes were in the garage.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Plural nouns that end in s take only an apostrophe: boys’.
explanation.tip: Plural possessive ending in s: add only ’.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This shows one boy, but the sentence says “two.”

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “The ____ coats hung by the door.”

explanation.whyCorrect: For plural nouns that do not end in s, add an apostrophe and s: children’s.
explanation.tip: Irregular plurals (men, women, children, people) take ’s.

options.label: A
options.rationale: “Children” does not end in s, so add ’s, not s’.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The plural of child is children.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The noun needs to show ownership.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a possessive noun correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: One teacher owns the desk, so “teacher’s” is correct.
explanation.tip: Ask: Does the word show ownership? Is the owner singular or plural?

options.label: A
options.text: The teacher’s were busy all day.
options.rationale: This needs a plural (teachers), not a possessive.

options.label: B
options.text: The teachers’s desk was covered with papers.

options.label: C
options.text: The teachers desk was covered with papers.
options.rationale: It needs an apostrophe to show ownership.

options.label: D
options.text: The teacher’s desk was covered with papers.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The trophy belongs to the school, so “school’s” needs an apostrophe and s.
explanation.tip: Check every noun that comes right before something it owns.

items.stem: Match each phrase with its correct possessive form.

explanation.whyCorrect: One dog: ’s. Two dogs: s’. Women (plural without s): ’s.
explanation.tip: Decide singular or plural first, then whether the plural ends in s.

items.stem: Choose the contraction for “do not”: “I ____ like cold soup.”

explanation.whyCorrect: An apostrophe replaces the missing o: do not → don’t.
explanation.tip: In a contraction, the apostrophe takes the place of missing letters.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The apostrophe goes where the letter o is missing.

items.stem: Write the contraction for “it is”: “____ time to go home.”

explanation.whyCorrect: It is → it’s. The apostrophe replaces the i in “is.”
explanation.tip: Say both words quickly to hear the contraction.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “The bird fed ____ babies.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Its” is a possessive pronoun, and possessive pronouns do not have apostrophes.
explanation.tip: Try “it is.” If it does not make sense, use “its.”

options.label: B
options.rationale: “It’s” means “it is,” which does not make sense here.

options.label: C
options.rationale: “The bird fed it is babies” does not make sense.

items.stem: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: “They’re” is the contraction of “they are,” which fits the sentence.
explanation.tip: Expand the contraction to check if it makes sense.

options.label: A
options.text: They’re going to the museum today.

options.label: B
options.text: Their going to the museum today.
options.rationale: “Their” shows ownership; the sentence needs “they are.”

options.label: D
options.rationale: Possessive pronouns like “yours” have no apostrophe.

items.stem: Match each contraction with the words it stands for.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each apostrophe replaces the missing letters in the second word.
explanation.tip: Say the two words slowly, then quickly, to match the contraction.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The first word should be “It’s,” meaning “It is.” The second “its” is correct because it shows ownership.
explanation.tip: “It’s” = it is. “Its” = belonging to it. “Its’” is never correct.

items.stem: Which is the correct abbreviation for “Doctor”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The title Doctor is abbreviated “Dr.” with a capital D and a period.
explanation.tip: Titles before names (Mr., Mrs., Dr.) begin with a capital and end with a period.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Only the first letter is capitalized, and a period is needed.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Titles are capitalized and end with a period.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is not the standard abbreviation.

items.stem: Which title of a story is written correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Story titles go in quotation marks, and the first word and important words are capitalized.
explanation.tip: Use quotation marks for stories, poems, songs and articles.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The first word of a title is always capitalized.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Important words in a title need capital letters.

options.label: D
options.rationale: “Lost” is an important word and needs a capital.

items.stem: The title of a book should be underlined or written in italics.

explanation.whyCorrect: Long works such as books, movies and magazines are underlined or italicized.
explanation.tip: Short works go in quotation marks; long works are italicized or underlined.

items.stem: Nadia recited a poem called desert moon at the assembly. How should the poem’s title be written?

explanation.whyCorrect: Poem titles go in quotation marks, with the first word and important words capitalized.
explanation.tip: Short works (poems, songs, stories, articles) take quotation marks.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The title of a poem needs quotation marks.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Use double quotation marks for a poem title.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The first word and important words of a title need capitals.

items.stem: Which is the correct greeting for a friendly letter?

explanation.whyCorrect: Capitalize the first word and the name, and end the greeting with a comma.
explanation.tip: Friendly letter: greeting with a comma; closing such as “Your friend,” with a comma.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A name and a title used as a name are capitalized.

options.label: C
options.rationale: A friendly letter greeting ends with a comma.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The first word of a greeting is capitalized.

items.stem: Put the parts of a friendly letter in order.

explanation.whyCorrect: A friendly letter has five parts in this order.
explanation.tip: Remember: date, greeting, body, closing, signature.

sequence: Date
Greeting (Dear Huda,)
Body
Closing (Your friend,)
Signature

items.stem: Which word has the most positive connotation?

explanation.whyCorrect: All four words mean “not heavy,” but “slender” suggests something graceful and pleasant.
explanation.tip: Connotation is the feeling a word gives, beyond its dictionary meaning.

options.label: A
options.rationale: “Thin” is neutral, neither positive nor negative.

items.stem: Which word gives a more negative feeling? “The old house was ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Creepy” suggests fear, which is a negative feeling.
explanation.tip: Think about how the word makes you feel.

items.stem: “Home” and “house” have the same denotation but different connotations.

explanation.whyCorrect: Both name a building where people live, but “home” suggests warmth and family.
explanation.tip: Denotation = dictionary meaning. Connotation = feeling.

items.stem: A writer wants readers to admire a boy who asks many questions. Which word should describe him?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Curious” shows a positive love of learning, while the others sound negative.
explanation.tip: Writers choose words with connotations that match the feeling they want.

options.label: B
options.rationale: “Nosy” suggests poking into others’ business, which is negative.

items.stem: Match each neutral word with a word that has a more positive connotation.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each pair has a similar meaning, but the second word sounds more pleasant.
explanation.tip: Ask which word you would rather hear about yourself or your things.

items.stem: In a poem, the moon “crept” over the hills instead of “rose.” What feeling does “crept” add?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Crept” suggests slow, quiet movement, which adds mystery to the scene.
explanation.tip: Compare the feeling of the author’s word with a plain word.

options.label: A
options.text: A slow, quiet, slightly mysterious feeling

options.label: B
options.text: No feeling; it means exactly the same as “rose”
options.rationale: The dictionary meaning is similar, but the feeling is different.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The word suggests mystery, not cheerfulness.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “We ate dinner at ____ house.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Their” shows ownership: the house belongs to them.
explanation.tip: their = belongs to them; there = a place; they’re = they are.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “I can ____ the birds singing.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Hear” is what you do with your ears.
explanation.tip: Hear has the word ear inside it.

items.stem: Which pair of words are homophones?

explanation.whyCorrect: Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings.
explanation.tip: Homo = same, phone = sound.

options.label: D
options.rationale: These are spelled the same (homographs), not homophones.

items.stem: In which sentence does “bow” mean to bend forward?

explanation.whyCorrect: Actors bend forward to thank the audience, so “bow” means to bend.
explanation.tip: Homographs are spelled the same but have different meanings. Use context clues.

options.label: A
options.text: He shot an arrow with a bow.

options.label: B
options.text: The bow of the ship cut through the waves.
options.rationale: Here “bow” is the front of a ship.

options.label: C
options.text: The actors bow at the end of the play.

options.label: D
options.text: She tied a bow in her hair.

items.stem: Read: “The wind was too strong, so we had to wind the kite string back in.” How are the two words pronounced?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first “wind” rhymes with “pinned”; the second rhymes with “find.” They are homographs.
explanation.tip: Some homographs change pronunciation as well as meaning.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Only the first one rhymes with “pinned.”

options.label: B
options.rationale: They are spelled the same but pronounced differently.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Only the second one rhymes with “find.”

options.label: D
options.text: Differently: wind (moving air) and wind (to turn)

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Through” means in one side and out the other. “Threw” is the past tense of “throw.”
explanation.tip: Homophones sound the same, so check the meaning of each spelling.

items.stem: Where would you look to find a synonym for “happy”?

explanation.whyCorrect: A thesaurus lists synonyms and antonyms.
explanation.tip: Thesaurus = words with similar meanings.

options.label: D
options.rationale: A glossary defines words from one book.

items.stem: What does a glossary contain?

explanation.whyCorrect: A glossary is a small dictionary at the back of a book for words used in that book.
explanation.tip: Glossaries are in the back of nonfiction books and textbooks.

options.label: A
options.text: A list of chapters and page numbers
options.rationale: That is a table of contents.

options.label: B
options.text: Meanings of important words used in that book

options.label: D
options.text: Synonyms for every word in English

items.stem: A dictionary can show how to pronounce a word.

explanation.whyCorrect: Dictionary entries give pronunciation, syllables, meanings and parts of speech.
explanation.tip: Look for the respelling in parentheses after the entry word.

items.stem: Guide words at the top of a dictionary page are “mango” and “market.” Which word would be on that page?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Map” comes after “mango” (n before p) and before “market” (p before r).
explanation.tip: Guide words show the first and last words on the page. Use ABC order.

items.stem: A dictionary entry says: “bat (noun) 1. a club used to hit a ball 2. a flying animal.” Which meaning fits “The bat hung upside down in the cave”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Animals hang upside down in caves, so the second meaning fits.
explanation.tip: Read each meaning and test it in the sentence.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A club does not hang upside down in a cave.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Only one meaning fits this sentence.

items.stem: Put these words in the order they would appear in a dictionary.

explanation.whyCorrect: Compare letters one by one: cam-e-l, cam-e-r, cam-p, can-a, can-d.
explanation.tip: When the first letters match, compare the next letter.

sequence: camel
camera
camp
canal
candle

items.stem: What is the main conflict in “The Last Repair”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Khalid faces a deadline (sunset) and a sudden problem (the missing spring).
explanation.tip: The conflict is the main problem that creates tension in a story.

options.label: A
options.text: Khalid must fix the captain’s watch before the ship sails, but he loses the spring.

options.label: B
options.text: Khalid and his uncle argue about the shop.
options.rationale: They never argue; the uncle is ill.

options.label: C
options.text: Khalid wants to become a sailor.
options.rationale: Nothing in the story suggests this.

options.label: D
options.text: The captain refuses to pay for the repair.
options.rationale: The captain smiles at the end.

items.stem: What kind of conflict does Khalid face when his hands shake and the spring flies away?

explanation.whyCorrect: His shaking hands and pounding heart show that the struggle is inside him.
explanation.tip: Conflicts can be with another character, nature, society or oneself.

options.label: A
options.rationale: No storm or natural force causes the problem.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The village or rules are not the problem.

options.label: D
options.rationale: No one is working against him.

items.stem: How does Khalid resolve the conflict?

explanation.whyCorrect: He counts to ten, uses the magnifying glass, and finds the spring caught in his apron.
explanation.tip: Look at what the character does differently to solve the problem.

options.label: A
options.text: He waits for Uncle Faris to get well.
options.rationale: He solves it himself that afternoon.

options.label: B
options.text: He gives the captain a different watch.
options.rationale: He repairs the captain’s own watch.

options.label: C
options.text: He calms himself, searches slowly, and finds the spring in his apron.

options.label: D
options.text: He buys a new spring from another shop.

items.stem: In “The Two Wells,” the conflict begins when Hamdan builds a wall around the well.

explanation.whyCorrect: Charging for water makes the poorest families go thirsty, which creates the problem.
explanation.tip: The conflict usually begins with an event that changes everyday life.

items.stem: How does the resolution of “The Two Wells” change Hamdan?

explanation.whyCorrect: When no one buys his water, he unlocks the gate and says shared water is worth more.
explanation.tip: A strong resolution often shows how a character has changed.

options.label: A
options.rationale: He stays and admits his mistake.

options.label: B
options.text: He makes the children pay for their well.
options.rationale: The Children’s Well is shared freely.

options.label: C
options.text: He builds a second wall around the new well.

options.label: D
options.text: He realizes sharing is more valuable than selling and opens the gate.

items.stem: Which detail BEST shows that the conflict in “The Two Wells” affects the whole village, not just Salma?

explanation.whyCorrect: Many families suffer when water is sold, so the conflict reaches the whole community.
explanation.tip: Look for details that show who is affected by a problem.

options.label: A
options.text: “The poorest families began to go thirsty.”

options.label: B
options.text: “Hamdan laughed at them from his gate.”

options.label: C
options.text: “Salma watched the palm trees outside the village.”

options.label: D
options.rationale: This shows the children’s effort, not the wider effect.

items.stem: Put the main events of “The Last Repair” in order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The events follow the afternoon from the captain’s visit to the ship’s departure.
explanation.tip: Plot events build toward a climax and then a resolution.

sequence: The captain leaves his watch at the shop.
Khalid cleans every gear.
The spring flies away.
Khalid finds the spring in his apron.
The watch ticks as the ship’s horn sounds.

items.stem: What is the climax of “The Last Repair”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The moment of greatest tension is solved when the watch starts ticking just in time.
explanation.tip: The climax is the turning point, where the tension is highest.

options.label: A
options.text: The captain leaves the watch in the morning.

options.label: B
options.text: Khalid finds the spring and the watch ticks as the horn sounds.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This comes after the turning point.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is part of the rising action.

items.stem: Which event causes Khalid to knock the box of screws to the floor?

explanation.whyCorrect: After the spring vanishes, Khalid sweeps his hands across the bench in panic.
explanation.tip: Events in a plot are often connected by cause and effect.

options.label: A
options.text: His uncle calls him from the other room.
options.rationale: His uncle is ill and does not call him.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The horn sounds at the very end.

options.label: C
options.text: He panics after the spring disappears.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The captain does not return until the dock.

items.stem: How does the flashback fit into the structure of the plot?

explanation.whyCorrect: Remembering his uncle’s lesson leads Khalid to slow down and find the spring.
explanation.tip: Ask how each part of a story helps the plot move forward.

options.label: A
options.text: It has no connection to the main events.
options.rationale: It leads directly to Khalid calming down.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the resolution of the story.
options.rationale: The resolution is the repaired watch.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the opening event of the story.
options.rationale: The story opens in 1955 in the shop.

options.label: D
options.text: It interrupts the rising action and gives Khalid the idea that solves the problem.

items.stem: Which TWO events are part of the rising action in “The Two Wells”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rising action is the series of events that build tension before the climax.
explanation.tip: Rising action comes after the conflict begins and before the turning point.

options.label: A
options.text: Hamdan charges a coin for each bucket.

options.label: B
options.text: The children dig for seven days.

options.label: C
options.text: The villagers name the Children’s Well.
options.rationale: This is part of the resolution.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the falling action or resolution.

items.stem: Why does the author end “The Two Wells” with Hamdan’s words?

explanation.whyCorrect: Hamdan’s final line states the theme of sharing, closing the story.
explanation.tip: The final event of a folktale often states its lesson.

options.label: A
options.text: To show the lesson of the story through the character who learned it.

options.label: B
options.text: To explain where Hamdan’s money came from.

options.label: C
options.text: To introduce a new problem for the village.

options.label: D
options.text: To describe how the new well was dug.

items.stem: Which paragraph of “The Last Repair” is a flashback?

explanation.whyCorrect: The story goes back to “the first day his uncle had let him touch a watch,” when he was eight.
explanation.tip: A flashback moves back in time to an earlier event.

options.label: A
options.text: The one about the captain leaving the watch
options.rationale: That happens on the same day.

options.label: B
options.text: The one about Khalid at age eight and the sand timer

options.label: C
options.text: The one about the ship’s horn

options.label: D
options.text: The one about the spring flying away

items.stem: Which words signal the start of the flashback?

explanation.whyCorrect: The verb “remembered” tells the reader the story is going back in time.
explanation.tip: Look for words like remembered, years ago, or had + verb.

items.stem: What does the flashback reveal about Uncle Faris?

explanation.whyCorrect: He gently teaches that a watchmaker’s hands must be slower than the sand.
explanation.tip: Flashbacks often reveal character traits through past events.

options.label: A
options.text: He wanted Khalid to become a sailor.
options.rationale: Nothing in the flashback says this.

options.label: B
options.text: He does not trust Khalid with watches.
options.rationale: He let Khalid touch a watch at eight.

options.label: C
options.text: He is strict and often angry.
options.rationale: He calmly turns over a sand timer.

options.label: D
options.text: He is a patient teacher who helped Khalid stay calm.

items.stem: The flashback in “The Last Repair” happens before the captain leaves his watch.

explanation.whyCorrect: The flashback is from when Khalid was eight, years before the day of the story.
explanation.tip: Compare the time of the flashback with the time of the main story.

items.stem: How would the story change if the author removed the flashback?

explanation.whyCorrect: The memory of the sand timer explains why Khalid counts slowly and searches calmly.
explanation.tip: Ask what a flashback explains that the reader would otherwise miss.

options.label: A
options.text: Readers would not understand why Khalid suddenly calms down.

options.label: B
options.text: The captain would not need his watch.
options.rationale: The flashback does not affect the captain.

options.label: C
options.text: The story would happen in a different city.
options.rationale: The setting does not depend on the flashback.

options.label: D
options.text: Khalid would not have a problem.
options.rationale: The problem still happens without the flashback.

items.stem: The sand timer in the flashback and the ship’s horn at the end are both connected to time. Why does the author include both?

explanation.whyCorrect: The timer teaches patience; the horn shows the deadline. Together they show Khalid using patience against time.
explanation.tip: Look for how details in a flashback connect to the main story.

options.label: A
options.text: To prove that sand timers are more accurate than watches
options.rationale: The story makes no comparison of accuracy.

options.label: B
options.text: To show Khalid learning to work calmly even under time pressure

options.label: C
options.text: To show that ships always leave late
options.rationale: The ship leaves at sunset as planned.

options.label: D
options.text: To explain how sand timers are made
options.rationale: The story does not explain this.

items.stem: Where and when does “The Two Wells” take place?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first sentence gives both the time (long ago) and the place (a desert village).
explanation.tip: Folktales often begin with a time and place like “Long ago, in…”

options.label: A
options.rationale: The story says “Long ago” and describes a village.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The story happens in a desert village.

options.label: C
options.text: Long ago, in a village at the edge of a desert

options.label: D
options.rationale: The story describes desert and palm trees.

items.stem: Why is the desert setting important to the conflict?

explanation.whyCorrect: Because water is rare in a desert, owning the only well lets Hamdan charge for it.
explanation.tip: Ask how the place creates or shapes the problem.

options.label: A
options.text: Deserts have many wells, so water is cheap.
options.rationale: The village has only one well.

options.label: B
options.text: The desert is too hot for the children to play.
options.rationale: Play is not part of the conflict.

options.label: C
options.text: The desert makes the merchant rich from gold.
options.rationale: His power comes from water, not gold.

options.label: D
options.text: In a desert, water is scarce, so controlling the only well gives Hamdan power.

items.stem: Which detail about the setting helps Salma solve the problem?

explanation.whyCorrect: Salma reasons that green trees in the heat mean water is close to the surface.
explanation.tip: Setting details can be clues that characters use.

options.label: A
options.text: One grove of palm trees stays green in the hottest month.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is part of the conflict.

options.label: C
options.text: The village is at the edge of a desert.
options.rationale: This explains the problem, not the solution.

options.label: D
options.text: Every child knows the way to the well in the dark.

items.stem: Which details show the time period of “The Last Repair”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The story names 1955, and a captain depending on a pocket watch fits that time.
explanation.tip: Look for dates and objects from a particular period.

options.label: A
options.rationale: These could happen at any time.

options.label: B
options.text: The year 1955 and the ship’s captain who needs a pocket watch

options.label: C
options.rationale: These are not tied to a time period.

options.label: D
options.text: The magnifying glass and the tweezers

items.stem: The smells of sea salt and cardamom help show that “The Last Repair” is set in a port city.

explanation.whyCorrect: Sea salt suggests the sea, and the story mentions a harbor and a ship.
explanation.tip: Sensory details can show the setting without naming it directly.

items.stem: How does the setting of the harbor add to the tension at the end of “The Last Repair”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The horn is a sound from the setting that signals the deadline, adding urgency.
explanation.tip: Setting can add tension through sounds, weather or time.

options.label: A
options.text: The harbor is far away, so the captain cannot be found.
options.rationale: Khalid reaches the dock in time.

options.label: B
options.text: The harbor is noisy, so Khalid cannot work.
options.rationale: He finishes the repair before the horn.

options.label: C
options.text: The ship’s horn across the harbor shows that time has run out.

items.stem: After Salma notices the green grove, what will she most likely do?

explanation.whyCorrect: She says, “Water must be close to the surface there.”
explanation.tip: A character’s observations often lead to their next action.

options.label: A
options.rationale: She values the trees as a clue.

options.label: B
options.rationale: She thinks there is water near the trees.

options.label: D
options.text: Look for water near the green trees.

items.stem: When Hamdan laughs at the children digging, what can readers predict?

explanation.whyCorrect: In folktales, a character who mocks hard work is often proven wrong.
explanation.tip: Use what you know about how folktales usually go.

options.label: B
options.rationale: His laughter shows he does not support them.

options.label: C
options.text: The children will buy Hamdan’s water.
options.rationale: They are digging to avoid buying it.

options.label: D
options.text: The children will stop digging that day.
options.rationale: They dig for seven days and keep going.

items.stem: After Khalid counts slowly to ten, a reader could predict that he will search more carefully.

explanation.whyCorrect: He has just calmed down, so a careful search is likely, and the story shows it.
explanation.tip: Predictions use the character’s change in behavior.

items.stem: In the drama, when Yusuf asks, “Where did you put the baking soda?”, what can the audience predict?

explanation.whyCorrect: Vinegar alone does not react; Yusuf’s question points to the missing ingredient.
explanation.tip: Use clues in the dialogue and what you know about science.

options.label: A
options.text: The judges will cancel the science fair.

options.label: B
options.text: The missing baking soda is why the volcano did not erupt.

options.label: C
options.text: Ms. Dawood will build a new volcano.
options.rationale: The students fix their own project.

options.label: D
options.rationale: She stays and solves the problem.

items.stem: Read: “Noor had practiced her speech every night, but when she saw the crowded hall, her mouth went dry.” What is the BEST prediction?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her nerves suggest a challenge, but her practice suggests she can succeed.
explanation.tip: Strong predictions weigh all the clues, not just one.

options.label: A
options.text: Noor will not need to speak at all.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the speech is canceled.

options.label: B
options.text: Noor will forget everything and run away.

options.label: C
options.text: Noor will feel nervous at first but use her practice to get through the speech.

options.label: D
options.text: The hall will be empty when she speaks.

items.stem: Which clue in “The Two Wells” BEST helped you predict that the children would find water?

explanation.whyCorrect: Trees stay green only with water, so this clue made finding water likely.
explanation.tip: The best clue is the one with the strongest link to the outcome.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This shows effort, not whether water is there.

options.label: C
options.text: Every child knew the way to the well.
options.rationale: This is about the old well.

options.label: D
options.text: The grove stayed green while the other trees turned brown.

items.stem: What is the purpose of the CAST list at the top of the play?

explanation.whyCorrect: A cast list (or cast of characters) introduces who appears in the play.
explanation.tip: Plays begin with a cast list, then scenes and dialogue.

options.label: A
options.text: It names the characters in the play.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The cast list names people, not props.

options.label: C
options.text: It tells where the play takes place.
options.rationale: That is the setting in the stage directions.

options.label: D
options.text: It gives the lesson of the play.
options.rationale: The cast list does not state a lesson.

items.stem: Which line is a stage direction?

explanation.whyCorrect: Stage directions in brackets tell actors what to do; they are not spoken.
explanation.tip: Stage directions are usually in brackets or italics.

options.label: C
options.text: MS. DAWOOD: Show me what you have learned.

options.label: D
options.text: LAYLA: The judges come at ten o’clock.

items.stem: The words in brackets in a play are spoken aloud by the actors.

explanation.whyCorrect: Words in brackets are stage directions; actors follow them but do not say them.
explanation.tip: Only the words after a character’s name are spoken.

items.stem: Why does the play have two scenes?

explanation.whyCorrect: Scene 2 begins “Ten minutes later,” showing a jump in time.
explanation.tip: A new scene often signals a change in time or place.

options.label: A
options.text: A new character is the narrator.
options.rationale: There is no narrator in this play.

options.label: B
options.text: Scene 2 tells the story from the beginning again.

options.label: C
options.text: The time changes: Scene 2 happens ten minutes later.

options.label: D
options.text: The setting moves to a different school.
options.rationale: Both scenes are in the classroom.

items.stem: What does the stage direction [covering her face] tell the audience about Layla?

explanation.whyCorrect: Covering your face is a common sign of embarrassment or despair.
explanation.tip: Stage directions show feelings through actions and gestures.

options.label: A
options.text: She is tired and wants to sleep.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Covering her face shows distress, not laughter.

options.label: C
options.text: She is hiding from the judges.
options.rationale: The judges have not arrived yet.

items.stem: Match each part of the play with its example.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each part of a drama has a different job in telling the story.
explanation.tip: Look at the format: names, brackets, spoken lines and headings.

pairs.right: We tested it three times last night.

items.stem: How does Yusuf feel at the beginning of Scene 1?

explanation.whyCorrect: The stage direction says he speaks “calmly,” and he says, “It will work.”
explanation.tip: Stage directions and dialogue both show a character’s feelings.

options.label: C
options.rationale: He speaks calmly and helps her.

options.label: D
options.rationale: He is ready to pour the vinegar.

items.stem: How is Layla’s perspective different from Yusuf’s at the start of the play?

explanation.whyCorrect: Layla paces and wrings her hands; Yusuf calmly points to their three tests.
explanation.tip: Compare how two characters see the same situation.

options.label: A
options.text: Both are bored by the science fair.

options.label: B
options.text: Layla worries the volcano will fail; Yusuf trusts their testing.

options.label: C
options.text: Layla is confident; Yusuf is worried.
options.rationale: It is the other way around.

options.label: D
options.text: Both think the volcano will fail.

items.stem: How does Layla’s perspective change by the end of the play?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her last line is, “You check every step, and you never panic.”
explanation.tip: A character’s last words often show how their perspective changed.

options.label: A
options.text: She thinks the judges were unfair.
options.rationale: The judges have not judged unfairly.

options.label: B
options.text: She decides science is too stressful.
options.rationale: She laughs and gives a positive lesson.

options.label: C
options.text: She learns to stay calm and check each step.

options.label: D
options.text: She blames Yusuf for the problem.
options.rationale: She forgot the baking soda herself.

items.stem: From whose point of view is “The Two Wells” told?

explanation.whyCorrect: The narrator uses “she,” “he” and “they,” so it is third person.
explanation.tip: First person uses I/we; third person uses he/she/they.

options.label: C
