options.rationale: The story uses “she” for Salma, not “I.”

options.label: D
options.text: A third-person narrator who is not a character

items.stem: How would “The Two Wells” be different if Hamdan told it?

explanation.whyCorrect: A first-person narrator shares their own thoughts, so we would hear Hamdan’s side.
explanation.tip: Changing the narrator changes whose thoughts and feelings the reader sees.

options.label: A
options.text: Readers would learn his reasons for building the wall and how he felt when no one came.

options.label: C
options.text: The villagers would not find the new well.

options.label: D
options.text: The story would take place in a city.
options.rationale: The narrator does not change the setting.

items.stem: At the end of “The Last Repair,” the captain’s smile shows that he is pleased.

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says, “the captain’s smile told him everything,” meaning he was happy with the repair.
explanation.tip: Characters’ expressions can show their perspective without words.

items.stem: What is the author’s main claim in “Every School Needs a Garden”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first sentence states the claim directly.
explanation.tip: A claim is the main point an author wants you to agree with.

options.label: B
options.text: Every school should have a garden where students grow food.

options.label: C
options.text: Gardens are too expensive for schools.
options.rationale: The author argues against this view.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The author calls the garden an outdoor classroom.

items.stem: Which reason supports the claim that gardens make lessons real?

explanation.whyCorrect: Measuring growth is a real math activity, which supports the first reason.
explanation.tip: Match each piece of evidence to the reason it supports.

options.label: B
options.text: Children are more willing to taste vegetables.

options.label: C
options.text: Students practice math by measuring plant growth.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is not a reason about lessons.

items.stem: Match each reason in the article with its supporting detail.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each paragraph gives one reason followed by a detail that supports it.
explanation.tip: In an argument, reasons are supported by evidence or examples.

items.stem: How does the author respond to people who say gardens cost too much?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author presents the counterclaim and then answers it with a low-cost solution.
explanation.tip: Strong arguments respond to the opposing side (a counterclaim).

options.label: B
options.text: By agreeing that gardens should be canceled

options.label: C
options.text: By saying money does not matter at all
options.rationale: The author gives a practical answer about cost.

options.label: D
options.text: By explaining that gardens can start small with containers and donated seeds

items.stem: Which piece of evidence is the WEAKEST support for the claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: Saying a tomato is “more interesting” is an opinion, not evidence that can be checked.
explanation.tip: Evidence is stronger when it can be checked; opinions are weaker support.

options.label: A
options.text: “A tomato you have watered for weeks is much more interesting than one from a store shelf.”

options.label: B
options.text: “When students measure plant growth, they practice math.”
options.rationale: This is a clear, specific example.

options.label: C
options.text: “Teachers… often report that students remember these lessons longer.”
options.rationale: This is evidence from teachers’ reports.

options.label: D
options.text: “Older students can teach younger ones how to plant seeds.”
options.rationale: This is a specific example of cooperation.

items.stem: The author of “Every School Needs a Garden” includes an opposing view.

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph beginning “Some people argue…” presents the opposing view.
explanation.tip: Look for signal words like “some people argue” or “however.”

items.stem: How does the author of “Every School Needs a Garden” feel about school gardens?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author says every school “should” have a garden and gives three reasons.
explanation.tip: An author’s perspective is their attitude or point of view about a topic.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The author argues for gardens throughout.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The author makes a confident claim.

items.stem: Which phrase BEST shows the author’s positive perspective?

explanation.whyCorrect: Calling garden lessons “some of the best” shows strong approval.
explanation.tip: Look for words that show the author’s feelings.

options.label: C
options.text: “some of the best lessons grow from the ground up”

options.label: D
options.text: “Some people argue that gardens cost too much”

items.stem: How is the perspective in “Every School Needs a Garden” different from “Sea Turtles of the Red Sea”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The garden text makes a claim with reasons; the turtle text explains facts with headings.
explanation.tip: Compare the author’s purpose and attitude in each text.

options.label: A
options.text: Both articles are told by a character.

options.label: B
options.text: The turtle article argues against gardens.

options.label: C
options.text: Both articles try to persuade readers.
options.rationale: The turtle article mainly gives facts.

options.label: D
options.text: The garden article tries to persuade; the turtle article mainly informs.

items.stem: Why does the author compare spending on books and computers with spending on a garden?

explanation.whyCorrect: The final paragraph places gardens alongside books and computers as worth paying for.
explanation.tip: Authors use comparisons to strengthen their perspective.

options.label: A
options.text: To suggest that a garden is as worthy an investment as other school materials

options.label: B
options.text: To argue that schools should stop buying books
options.rationale: The author does not oppose books.

options.label: C
options.text: To show that computers are better than gardens
options.rationale: The author says schools should ALSO invest in gardens.

options.label: D
options.text: To explain how much a garden costs

items.stem: An author’s perspective can be found in the words the author chooses.

explanation.whyCorrect: Word choice, such as “best” or “should,” reveals how an author feels.
explanation.tip: Notice strong or emotional words.

items.stem: Which sentence would an author with the OPPOSITE perspective most likely write?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence argues against gardens, so it shows an opposing perspective.
explanation.tip: An opposing perspective disagrees with the author’s claim.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This agrees with the original author.

options.label: B
options.text: School time is limited, so it should be spent on core subjects indoors.

options.label: C
options.text: Even a sunny corner can become a place to learn.
options.rationale: This is from the original argument.

options.label: D
options.text: Families enjoy volunteering in school gardens.

items.stem: Which heading would help you find out how hatchlings reach the sea?

explanation.whyCorrect: “From Egg to Ocean” describes the eggs hatching and the hatchlings leaving the nest.
explanation.tip: Headings tell you what each section is about.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This section is about nesting beaches.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This sidebar is about sand temperature.

items.stem: Where can you find the meaning of “hatchling”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The glossary at the end gives the meaning of “hatchling.”
explanation.tip: A glossary defines important words from the text.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The sidebar gives an extra fact.

options.label: B
options.text: In the heading “Dangers on the Beach”

items.stem: What does the caption add to the article?

explanation.whyCorrect: A caption is a short description next to a picture.
explanation.tip: Captions connect pictures to the text.

options.label: A
options.text: It explains what the photograph shows.

options.label: B
options.text: It lists the dangers turtles face.
options.rationale: That is in the section “Dangers on the Beach.”

options.label: D
options.text: It tells how many eggs turtles lay.
options.rationale: That is in the main text.

items.stem: The “Did You Know?” sidebar gives information that is NOT in the main sections.

explanation.whyCorrect: The fact about sand temperature appears only in the sidebar.
explanation.tip: Sidebars add interesting extra facts.

items.stem: How does the caption connect to the section “Dangers on the Beach”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The section explains that hatchlings move toward the brightest horizon, which the photograph shows.
explanation.tip: Text features work together with the main text.

options.label: A
options.text: It shows a mother turtle laying eggs.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows a hatchling moving toward the bright horizon, which explains how hatchlings find the sea.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows a beach covered in buildings.
options.rationale: The caption describes a hatchling and the sea.

items.stem: Match each text feature with its purpose.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each feature helps readers find or understand information in a different way.
explanation.tip: Ask: What job does this feature do for the reader?

pairs.right: Tells what a section is about

items.stem: How is “Every School Needs a Garden” organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article states a claim, gives first, second and third reasons, answers a counterclaim, and concludes.
explanation.tip: Argumentative texts use a claim-and-reasons structure.

options.label: A
options.rationale: It argues for gardens rather than solving one problem.

options.label: B
options.text: Sections with headings about one animal

options.label: C
options.text: A claim, followed by reasons with evidence and a response to the other side

options.label: D
options.text: Events in the order they happened
options.rationale: It is an argument, not a story in time order.

items.stem: How is the structure of “Sea Turtles of the Red Sea” different from “Every School Needs a Garden”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The turtle text is organized by topic headings; the garden text by claim and reasons.
explanation.tip: Compare how each author organizes information.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The turtle article informs, it does not persuade.

options.label: B
options.text: Both tell a story with characters.

options.label: C
options.text: The garden article uses headings; the turtle article does not.
options.rationale: It is the other way around.

options.label: D
options.text: The turtle article uses headings to describe facts; the garden article uses reasons to persuade.

items.stem: The section “From Egg to Ocean” is mostly organized in time order.

explanation.whyCorrect: It moves from laying eggs, to two months in the sand, to hatchlings digging out.
explanation.tip: Different sections of one text can use different structures.

items.stem: Which structure does the section “Dangers on the Beach” use?

explanation.whyCorrect: Bright lights (cause) confuse hatchlings so they crawl the wrong way (effect).
explanation.tip: Signal words such as “can confuse” and “may” show causes and effects.

options.label: B
options.rationale: It does not follow events over time.

options.label: C
options.rationale: It explains a danger but gives no solution.

options.label: D
options.rationale: It does not compare two things.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about both articles are true?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both are nonfiction texts organized into paragraphs, but only one has text features and only one argues.
explanation.tip: Find what the texts share before listing differences.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Only the garden article does this.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Only the turtle article has a sidebar.

options.label: C
options.text: Both give information about a real-world topic.

options.label: D
options.text: Both use paragraphs to group related ideas.

items.stem: Why did the author of the turtle article choose headings instead of a claim and reasons?

explanation.whyCorrect: Headings let readers find information about nesting, hatching and dangers quickly.
explanation.tip: An author’s purpose shapes the structure of a text.

options.label: A
options.text: Because the author wanted to persuade readers to buy turtles

options.label: B
options.text: Because the purpose is to inform readers about different parts of the topic

options.label: C
options.rationale: Structure is chosen for purpose, not length.

options.label: D
options.text: Because turtles cannot be argued about
options.rationale: Any topic can be argued; the purpose here is to inform.

items.stem: Which sense does “the bread oven breathes, warm and red” appeal to most?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Warm” appeals to touch, and “red” appeals to sight.
explanation.tip: Imagery uses details that appeal to the five senses.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Bread is mentioned, but the line describes warmth and color.

options.label: B
options.rationale: There is no sound in this line.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The line focuses on warmth and redness.

items.stem: Which line from “Harbor at Dawn” appeals to the sense of smell?

explanation.whyCorrect: You can smell salt and diesel fuel carried on the wind.
explanation.tip: Ask which sense each image uses.

options.label: A
options.text: “the last stars folding up the night”

options.label: B
options.text: “Gulls stitch the sky with silver thread”

items.stem: What does “Gulls stitch the sky with silver thread” help you picture?

explanation.whyCorrect: Like a needle going in and out, the gulls dart across the sky, catching silver light.
explanation.tip: Imagery often uses figurative language to create a picture.

options.label: A
options.text: Birds flying back and forth, flashing silver in the light

options.label: B
options.rationale: The image is a metaphor, not literal sewing.

items.stem: “Ropes creak like old men’s knees” appeals to the sense of hearing.

explanation.whyCorrect: A creak is a sound, and the comparison helps you hear it.
explanation.tip: Sound words such as creak, buzz and hiss create hearing images.

items.stem: Match each image from the poem with the sense it appeals to most.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each image uses a different sense to bring the harbor to life.
explanation.tip: Read each image and ask: Do I see, hear, smell, taste or feel this?

pairs.left: salt and diesel ride the breeze

items.stem: What overall mood does the imagery in “Harbor at Dawn” create?

explanation.whyCorrect: Words like “yawns,” “sleep” and “pearl-gray light” suggest a quiet morning waking up.
explanation.tip: The images together create the mood of a poem.

options.label: B
options.text: A calm, sleepy morning slowly waking up

options.label: C
options.rationale: The poem describes dawn and gentle sounds.

options.label: D
options.rationale: It is dawn and things are just waking.

items.stem: Which stage direction helps you picture Layla’s nervousness?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pacing back and forth is a picture of someone who is nervous.
explanation.tip: Stage directions help readers visualize characters’ actions.

options.label: A
options.text: [MS. DAWOOD walks in with a clipboard.]

options.label: B
options.text: [A clay volcano sits on a table.]

items.stem: What should you picture when you read “Red foam bubbles up and spills down the sides”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The verbs “bubbles up” and “spills down” show the foam moving.
explanation.tip: Strong verbs help you create a moving picture in your mind.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The text describes foam, not smoke.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The foam comes from the volcano.

options.label: D
options.text: Foam rising from the volcano and running down it

items.stem: In “The Last Repair,” the description “a silver curl no bigger than a fingernail” helps you picture the spring’s size.

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing it to a fingernail shows how tiny it is.
explanation.tip: Comparisons to familiar objects help you visualize size.

items.stem: Which detail helps you visualize Khalid’s panic?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sweeping hands and screws scattering show rushed, panicked movement.
explanation.tip: Look for actions that show feelings.

options.label: A
options.text: He swept his hands across the bench, knocking a box of screws to the floor.

options.label: B
options.text: He had opened the watch and cleaned every gear.
options.rationale: This shows careful work, not panic.

options.label: C
options.text: He closed the case and wound the crown.

options.label: D
options.text: He picked up the magnifying glass.

items.stem: Reading the play aloud, how should the actor playing Layla say “The baking soda… is still in my backpack”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The ellipsis (…) and the direction “slowly lowering her hands” suggest a slow, embarrassed realization.
explanation.tip: Visualizing a scene includes imagining how lines are spoken.

options.label: B
options.text: Slowly and with embarrassment, pausing at the dots

options.label: C
options.rationale: The ellipsis shows a slow, hesitant pause.

options.label: D
options.rationale: She realizes her own mistake, so anger does not fit.

items.stem: How does visualizing the two scenes help you understand the play?

explanation.whyCorrect: Picturing the actions in each scene shows Layla’s growth from Scene 1 to Scene 2.
explanation.tip: Picture how characters look and move at different points in the story.

options.label: A
options.text: You can see that Yusuf leaves the room.

options.label: B
options.text: You can see that the volcano never works.

options.label: C
options.text: You can see Layla change from panicked pacing to proudly standing beside the volcano.

options.label: D
options.text: You can see that Ms. Dawood is the main character.

items.stem: Which is the BEST summary of “The Two Wells”?

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary includes the problem, the key events and the resolution.
explanation.tip: Include the main character, the problem and the outcome.

options.label: A
options.text: The village had palm trees and a well.
options.rationale: This leaves out the conflict and resolution.

options.label: B
options.text: Salma’s hands blistered after seven days.
options.rationale: This is a detail, not a summary.

options.label: C
options.text: Hamdan was rich and had a gate.

options.label: D
options.text: When a merchant charges for the only well, Salma finds a new well, and the merchant learns to share.

items.stem: Which sentence BEST summarizes “Sea Turtles of the Red Sea”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The summary covers each main section: nesting, hatching and dangers.
explanation.tip: Use the headings to identify the main ideas to summarize.

options.label: A
options.text: Red Sea turtles nest on beaches, their hatchlings head to the sea, and bright lights can confuse them.

options.label: C
options.text: A hatchling is a young animal just out of its egg.

items.stem: A summary of “The Last Repair” should include what kind of fabric Khalid’s apron is made of.

explanation.whyCorrect: The fabric is not important and is not even mentioned; the apron matters only because the spring is found there.
explanation.tip: Summaries leave out small details.

items.stem: Which detail should be LEFT OUT of a summary of “Every School Needs a Garden”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The tomato line is a vivid example, not one of the main reasons.
explanation.tip: Keep the claim and main reasons; drop examples and descriptions.

options.label: B
options.text: A tomato you have watered for weeks is more interesting.

options.label: C
options.text: Gardens can start small to save money.

items.stem: Put these sentences in order to summarize “The Last Repair.”

explanation.whyCorrect: These four sentences give the beginning, problem, turning point and resolution.
explanation.tip: A story summary follows the plot from beginning to end.

sequence: Khalid must fix a captain’s watch before sunset.
He loses a tiny spring and panics.
He remembers his uncle’s lesson about patience.
He finds the spring and finishes just in time.

items.stem: A student summarized the garden article as “Gardens are great and everyone loves them.” What is the main problem with this summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary should state the author’s claim and main reasons, not a general opinion.
explanation.tip: Summaries are objective and include the main ideas.

options.label: A
options.text: It uses the author’s exact words.
options.rationale: It does not quote the author.

options.label: C
options.text: It adds an opinion and leaves out the author’s actual reasons.

items.stem: You are unsure why hatchlings crawl the wrong way. Which section should you reread?

explanation.whyCorrect: This section explains that bright lights confuse hatchlings.
explanation.tip: Use headings to choose which part to reread.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The title does not explain the danger.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This section is about nesting beaches.

items.stem: Rereading can help you notice how one paragraph connects to another.

explanation.whyCorrect: A second reading often reveals connections you missed the first time.
explanation.tip: Reread slowly and look for links between ideas.

items.stem: After rereading “Every School Needs a Garden,” a student understands why the author mentions “donated seeds.” What did rereading help the student see?

options.text: The detail answers the claim that gardens cost too much.

options.label: B
options.text: The author wants students to sell seeds.

options.label: D
options.text: Gardens need no seeds at all.
options.rationale: The text mentions seeds as a cheap way to start.

items.stem: Which question would rereading the first section of the turtle article help you answer?

explanation.tip: Know which section answers which question.

options.label: A
options.text: How long do eggs stay in the sand?

options.label: B
options.text: Which kinds of turtles swim in the Red Sea?

options.text: Why do bright lights confuse hatchlings?
options.rationale: That is in “Dangers on the Beach.”

items.stem: A reader thinks the turtle article says lights help hatchlings. What should the reader do?

items.stem: Which TWO details would a careful reread of “From Egg to Ocean” reveal?

options.text: The eggs stay in the sand for about two months.

options.label: B
options.text: Hatchlings usually dig out at night.

options.label: C
options.text: Hatchlings follow their mother to the water.

options.label: D
options.text: The mother turtle stays to protect the nest.

items.stem: Which question is answered in the sidebar of the turtle article?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sidebar says the temperature of the sand affects this.
explanation.tip: Match questions to the part of the text that answers them.

options.label: A
options.text: How many eggs does a turtle lay?
options.rationale: That is answered in “From Egg to Ocean.”

options.label: B
options.rationale: The article does not define caption.

options.label: C
options.rationale: That is answered in the first section.

options.label: D
options.text: What affects whether hatchlings become males or females?

items.stem: Which question can be answered by quoting the garden article directly?

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says gardens can start “with a few containers and donated seeds.”
explanation.tip: Ask questions that the text can answer with evidence.

options.text: What does the author suggest for schools with little money?

options.label: B
options.text: What does the author’s school garden look like?
options.rationale: The author does not describe a specific garden.

items.stem: The turtle article explains exactly how many hatchlings survive to adulthood.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article does not give survival numbers; you would need another source.
explanation.tip: Notice when a text does NOT answer your question.

items.stem: A reader asks, “Why do hatchlings move toward the horizon?” Which sentence answers this?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence explains that the bright horizon leads them to the sea.
explanation.tip: Use the question’s key words to find the answer.

options.text: Hatchlings find the sea by moving toward the brightest horizon, which is normally the moonlit water.

options.text: She covers the nest and returns to the sea.

options.label: D

items.stem: Which question shows the DEEPEST thinking about the garden article?

explanation.whyCorrect: This question applies the author’s ideas to a new situation.
explanation.tip: Strong readers ask questions that go beyond recall.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is a simple recall question.

options.label: C
options.text: Would the author’s reasons work for a school in a very dry climate?

options.label: D
options.text: Who argues that gardens cost too much?

items.stem: Which inference is BEST supported by the turtle article?

explanation.tip: Combine details from the text to answer a question it does not state directly.

options.label: A
options.text: Hawksbill turtles do not lay eggs.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The article says warmer sand produces more females, not that turtles prefer cold.

options.label: D
options.text: Keeping beaches dark at night could help more hatchlings reach the sea.

items.stem: Which group of words is a complete sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: It has a subject (The new library) and a predicate (opens on Sunday) and expresses a complete thought.
explanation.tip: A sentence needs a subject, a verb and a complete thought.

options.label: A
options.text: The new library opens on Sunday.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This dependent clause is not a complete thought.

items.stem: Choose the end mark: “Have you ever seen a shooting star____”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Have you ever…” asks a question, so it ends with a question mark.
explanation.tip: Statements end with periods; questions end with question marks.

options.label: A
options.rationale: A semicolon cannot end a sentence.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A comma cannot end a sentence.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This sentence asks something, so it needs a question mark.

items.stem: Which interrogative word best begins this question? “____ did the museum close early today?”

explanation.whyCorrect: The question asks for a reason, so “Why” fits.
explanation.tip: Interrogatives: who (person), what (thing), when (time), where (place), why (reason), how (manner).

options.label: A
options.rationale: “Who” asks about a person, not a reason.

options.label: D
options.rationale: “Which” needs a noun after it here.

items.stem: Which sentence uses an appositive correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: An appositive that renames a noun in the middle of a sentence is set off by commas on both sides.
explanation.tip: Appositives explain a nearby noun and are usually set off with commas.

options.label: A
options.text: Our librarian Ms. Rahma, ordered, new atlases.
options.rationale: The commas are in the wrong places.

options.label: B
options.text: Ms. Rahma our librarian, ordered new atlases.
options.rationale: The appositive needs a comma on both sides.

options.label: C
options.text: Ms. Rahma, our librarian, ordered new atlases.

options.label: D
options.text: Ms. Rahma, our librarian ordered new atlases.
options.rationale: The appositive needs a closing comma.

items.stem: Choose the correct form: “Of all the players, Majed had the ____ score.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Best” is the superlative of “good,” used when comparing more than two.
explanation.tip: good → better → best; bad → worse → worst.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Never add -est to an irregular superlative.

options.label: C
options.rationale: “Better” compares two; this compares all the players.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Worse” is already the comparative form of “bad,” so “more” must be removed.
explanation.tip: Never add more or most to an irregular comparative form.

items.stem: What is the complete predicate? “The friendly dog waited patiently for her owner.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The complete predicate includes the verb and all the words that tell about it.
explanation.tip: Complete predicate = everything that tells what the subject did or is.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is part of the predicate only.

items.stem: What is the simple subject? “Several excited volunteers from the museum cleaned the beach.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Remove describing words and phrases; the main noun is “volunteers.”
explanation.tip: The simple subject is never inside a prepositional phrase.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is part of a prepositional phrase.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is part of the predicate.

items.stem: In “Under the old bridge lived a family of ducks,” the subject comes after the verb.

explanation.whyCorrect: The verb is “lived”; the subject “a family of ducks” comes after it.
explanation.tip: In inverted sentences, ask “Who or what lived?” to find the subject.

items.stem: Which sentence has BOTH a compound subject and a compound predicate?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two subjects (Reem, Dana) share two predicates (wrote…, directed…).
explanation.tip: Find the subjects first, then the verbs.

options.label: A
options.text: Reem wrote the script, and Dana directed the play.

options.label: B
options.text: Reem and Dana wrote the script and directed the play.

options.label: C
options.text: Reem and Dana wrote the script.
options.rationale: This has a compound subject only.

options.label: D
options.text: Reem wrote the script and directed the play.
options.rationale: This has a compound predicate only.

items.stem: What is the simple predicate? “The students have been practicing their lines all week.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The simple predicate is the whole verb phrase: have been practicing.
explanation.tip: Include helping verbs in the simple predicate.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the object of the verb.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The simple predicate includes the helping verbs.

items.stem: Add a simple subject that makes sense: “At dawn, the hungry ____ chirped loudly in the nest.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Something in a nest that chirps, such as “birds,” is a logical subject.
explanation.tip: The subject is who or what does the action.

items.stem: Which is a run-on sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two complete sentences are joined with no conjunction or punctuation.
explanation.tip: A run-on joins sentences without the proper conjunction and punctuation.

options.label: A
options.text: I went to the store, but it was closed.
options.rationale: This is a correct compound sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: When I went to the store.
options.rationale: This is a fragment, not a run-on.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is a correct simple sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: I went to the store it was closed.

items.stem: Which is a sentence fragment?

explanation.whyCorrect: It has no subject and verb that complete a thought.
explanation.tip: A fragment leaves the reader asking, “What happened?”

options.label: C
options.text: It rained, so we played games.

options.label: D
options.text: The weekend was long and rainy.

items.stem: Which is the best way to correct this run-on? “The museum was crowded we waited an hour.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma plus the conjunction “so” correctly joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.tip: Fix run-ons with a period, or a comma plus and/but/or/so.

options.label: A
options.text: The museum was crowded, we waited an hour.
options.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two sentences (comma splice).

options.label: B
options.text: The museum was crowded, so we waited an hour.

options.label: C
options.text: The museum was crowded we, waited an hour.
options.rationale: The comma is in the wrong place.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This removes words and is still a run-on.

items.stem: “Running down the hallway with a heavy backpack” is a complete sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: It has no subject and no complete verb; it is a fragment.
explanation.tip: Ask: Who is running? A complete sentence would tell you.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences; add a conjunction such as “and.”
explanation.tip: Two independent clauses need a comma AND a conjunction, or a period.

items.stem: Which revision fixes BOTH problems? “Because the bus was late. We missed the start of the play we were upset.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Attaching the fragment to the next clause and splitting the run-on fixes both errors.
explanation.tip: Fix fragments by joining them to a sentence; fix run-ons by separating or properly joining clauses.

options.label: A
options.text: The bus was late we missed the start. Of the play we were upset.
options.rationale: This creates new run-ons and fragments.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the bus was late. We missed the start of the play, we were upset.
options.rationale: The fragment and a comma splice remain.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the bus was late, we missed the start of the play. We were upset.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the bus was late, we missed the start of the play we were upset.
options.rationale: The run-on at the end remains.

items.stem: Choose the correct plural: “We packed our ____ for the trip.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Add -es to nouns ending in s, sh, ch or x: lunch → lunches.
explanation.tip: Words ending in s, sh, ch or x add -es.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is not a correct spelling.

options.label: D
options.rationale: An apostrophe shows possession, not a plural.

items.stem: Choose the correct plural: “The library has three ____ of that book.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Copy ends in a consonant + y, so change y to i and add -es: copies.
explanation.tip: Vowel + y → add s (keys). Consonant + y → ies (copies).

options.label: A
options.rationale: Consonant + y: change y to i and add -es.

options.label: C
options.rationale: An apostrophe does not form a plural.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Change the y to i first.

items.stem: Choose the correct plural: “Autumn ____ covered the path.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Some nouns ending in f change the f to v and add -es: leaf → leaves.
explanation.tip: Watch for f/fe words: leaf/leaves, knife/knives, half/halves.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Leaf changes f to v and adds -es.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The f must change to v.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is a verb, not the plural of leaf.

items.stem: Which sentence uses an irregular plural correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Deer” is the same in singular and plural.
explanation.tip: Learn irregular plurals: deer, sheep, fish; tooth/teeth; child/children.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The plural of tooth is teeth.

options.label: B
options.text: Three deers drank from the stream.
options.rationale: “Deer” stays the same in the plural.

options.label: C
options.text: The childs played in the yard.
options.rationale: The plural of child is children.

options.label: D
options.text: Three deer drank from the stream.

items.stem: Match each singular noun with its plural.

explanation.whyCorrect: Some -o words add s, others add es; vowel + y adds s; woman is irregular.
explanation.tip: Check the letter before the final y or o.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a collective noun with the correct verb?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Orchestra” names one group acting together, so it takes the singular verb “plays.”
explanation.tip: Collective nouns (team, class, family) usually take singular verbs.

options.label: A
options.text: The orchestra plays every Thursday evening.

options.label: B
options.text: The orchestra play every Thursday evening.
options.rationale: A collective noun acting as one group takes a singular verb.

options.label: C
options.text: The orchestras plays every Thursday evening.

options.label: D
options.text: The orchestra are playing every Thursday evening.
options.rationale: When the group acts as a whole, use a singular verb.

items.stem: Choose the correct possessive: “____ bicycle has a flat tire.”

explanation.whyCorrect: In your Wonders book, a name ending in s takes an apostrophe and s: Lucas’s.
explanation.tip: Names and singular nouns ending in s: add ’s (Lucas’s, the class’s).

options.label: A
options.rationale: The name needs to show ownership.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is a plural, not a possessive.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The name is Lucas, not Luca.

items.stem: Choose the correct possessive: “The ____ final project won first prize.”

explanation.whyCorrect: One class owns the project; a singular noun ending in s adds ’s.
explanation.tip: Decide whether there is one owner or more than one.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This shows more than one class.

items.stem: Choose the correct possessive: “The ____ uniforms were washed after the match.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A plural noun ending in s adds only an apostrophe: athletes’.
explanation.tip: Plural ending in s → add only ’.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This shows one athlete, but the uniforms belong to many.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Plural nouns ending in s add only an apostrophe.

items.stem: Which phrase is written correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Plural nouns that do not end in s add ’s: people’s.
explanation.tip: Irregular plurals (people, women, children, oxen) add ’s.

options.label: C
options.rationale: “People” is already plural and does not end in s.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The books belong to two authors, so the plural possessive is “authors’.”
explanation.tip: If a plural noun shows ownership, it needs an apostrophe.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses both a plural noun and a possessive noun?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Atlas’s” is a singular possessive; “islands” is a plain plural.
explanation.tip: Do not confuse plurals with possessives.

options.label: A
options.text: The atlases index lists all the island’s.

options.label: B
options.text: The atlas index list’s all the islands.
options.rationale: “Lists” is a verb and needs no apostrophe.

options.label: C
options.text: The atlas’s index lists all the islands.

options.label: D
options.text: The atla’s index lists all the islands.
options.rationale: The word is “atlas,” so the possessive is “atlas’s.”

items.stem: Choose the contraction for “are not”: “The shops ____ open on Fridays.”

explanation.whyCorrect: are + not → aren’t; the apostrophe replaces the o.
explanation.tip: The apostrophe goes where letters are left out.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The apostrophe replaces the o in “not.”

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “____ going to love this museum!”

explanation.whyCorrect: You are → you’re. Test it: “You are going to love this museum.”
explanation.tip: Your = belongs to you; you’re = you are.

options.label: B
options.rationale: “Your” shows ownership; the sentence needs “you are.”

items.stem: Which word is a modal helping verb in “You should wear a helmet”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Modals such as can, could, may, might, must, should and would express possibility or obligation.
explanation.tip: A modal comes before the main verb and changes its meaning.

items.stem: Which modal shows that something is REQUIRED? “Visitors ____ show a ticket at the gate.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Must” expresses obligation.
explanation.tip: must = required; may/might = possible; can/could = able.

items.stem: Choose the correct pronoun: “The twins built the model by ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Plural reflexive pronouns end in -selves: themselves.
explanation.tip: -self for one, -selves for more than one.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is not a standard word.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The customer belongs to the company, so the possessive “its” (no apostrophe) is needed.
explanation.tip: Possessive pronouns (its, yours, theirs) never use apostrophes.

items.stem: Which word is an adjective? “The tiny kitten slept on the rug.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Tiny” describes the kitten (what kind).
explanation.tip: Adjectives tell what kind, how many or how much.

items.stem: Which sentence capitalizes the proper adjective correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Lebanese” comes from the proper noun Lebanon, so it is capitalized.
explanation.tip: Proper adjectives come from proper nouns.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Proper adjectives from place names are capitalized.

items.stem: Choose the article: “She ate ____ orange after lunch.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Orange” begins with a vowel sound, so use “an.”
explanation.tip: a + consonant sound; an + vowel sound.

options.label: C
options.rationale: “The” points to a specific orange; any orange is meant here.

options.label: D
options.rationale: “This” is a demonstrative adjective, not an article.

items.stem: Choose the demonstrative adjective: “____ books right here on my desk are new.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Plural and near → “these.”
explanation.tip: this/these = near; that/those = far.

options.label: B
options.rationale: “Those” points to things far away; “right here” shows they are near.

items.stem: Which phrase lists the adjectives in the correct order?

explanation.whyCorrect: The order is number, opinion, size, age, color: two (number) beautiful (opinion) old (age).
explanation.tip: Number → opinion → size → age → color.

items.stem: Which sentence uses commas with adjectives correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two adjectives that equally describe the noun are separated by a comma.
explanation.tip: Test: if you can put “and” between the adjectives, use a comma.

options.label: A
options.text: Jorge played a quiet, gentle song on the oud.

options.label: B
options.text: Jorge played a quiet gentle, song on the oud.
options.rationale: A comma never goes between the last adjective and the noun.

options.label: C
options.text: Jorge played a, quiet gentle song on the oud.

options.label: D
options.text: Jorge played three, quiet songs on the oud.
options.rationale: A comma does not follow a number.

items.stem: Choose the past tense: “Yesterday, Amal ____ the ball.”

explanation.whyCorrect: catch → caught.
explanation.tip: Irregular verbs do not add -ed in the past tense.

options.label: B
options.rationale: “Catch” is irregular and does not add -ed.

items.stem: Choose the past tense: “Last week, we ____ a new route to school.”

explanation.whyCorrect: choose → chose (past) → have chosen (past participle).
explanation.tip: Learn the three forms of irregular verbs.

items.stem: Match each verb with its past tense.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each of these verbs forms its past tense irregularly.
explanation.tip: Say “Yesterday I…” to test the past tense.

items.stem: Choose the correct form: “By noon, the guests had ____ all the dates.”

explanation.whyCorrect: had + past participle: had eaten.
explanation.tip: Past tense stands alone (ate); the past participle follows have/has/had (eaten).

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Fall” is irregular: the past tense is “fell.”
explanation.tip: If a past tense sounds strange with -ed, check whether the verb is irregular.

items.stem: Which sentence uses irregular verbs correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: knew (past of know) and had read (past participle of read) are both correct.
explanation.tip: Some irregular verbs, like read, keep the same spelling but change pronunciation.

options.label: A
options.text: She knew the answer because she had red the chapter twice.
options.rationale: “Red” is a color; the past of read is spelled “read.”

options.label: B
options.text: She knew the answer because she had read the chapter twice.

options.label: C
options.text: She knowed the answer because she had readed the chapter twice.

options.label: D
options.text: She known the answer because she had read the chapter twice.

items.stem: Which sentence uses negatives correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Use only one negative per clause: “didn’t” + the positive word “anything.”
explanation.tip: Do not use two negatives in the same clause.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This has two negatives and wrong word order.

options.label: D
options.text: I didn’t never do anything wrong.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “Nobody ____ where the key is.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Nobody knows” has one negative, which is correct.
explanation.tip: Negative words include no, not, nobody, nothing, never, no one and nowhere.

options.label: A
options.rationale: “Nobody” is already negative, so this makes a double negative.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is a double negative and does not agree with “Nobody.”

items.stem: “We don’t want to go nowhere today” is correct.

explanation.whyCorrect: It is a double negative. Correct: “We don’t want to go anywhere today.”
explanation.tip: Replace one negative with its positive form.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “There isn’t ____ milk left in the fridge.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Isn’t” is already negative, so use the positive word “any.”
explanation.tip: After a negative verb, use any, anything, anyone, ever or anywhere.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Hasn’t” is negative, so the second word must be positive: “anybody.”
explanation.tip: Check each clause for more than one negative word.

items.stem: Which pair of revisions BOTH correct “She never says nothing in class”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Remove one negative (says nothing) or change one to a positive (never says anything).
explanation.tip: A double negative can be fixed two ways: remove one negative, or make it positive.

options.label: A
options.text: “She always says nothing” or “She never says nothing”
options.rationale: The second one still has a double negative.

options.label: B
options.text: “She doesn’t never say anything” or “She never says nothing”

options.label: C
options.text: “She never doesn’t say anything in class” or “She says nothing never”

options.label: D
options.text: “She never says anything in class” or “She says nothing in class”

items.stem: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Cities, months and the first word of a sentence are capitalized.
explanation.tip: Capitalize names of places, days, months and holidays.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The first word of a sentence is capitalized.

items.stem: Which group of words is capitalized correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Geographical names, historical events and holidays are all proper nouns.
explanation.tip: Capitalize each important word in a multi-word proper noun.

options.label: A
options.text: the Red Sea, the Battle of Badr, saudi national day

options.label: B
options.text: the Red Sea, the Battle of Badr, Saudi National Day

options.label: C
options.text: the red sea, the Battle of Badr, Saudi National Day

options.label: D
options.text: the Red Sea, the battle of badr, Saudi National Day

items.stem: Which abbreviation is written correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Titles and initials are capitalized and end with a period.
explanation.tip: Initial = first letter of a name, capitalized with a period.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Titles and initials end with periods.

items.stem: Acronyms such as NASA and the UN are usually written in all capital letters without periods.

explanation.whyCorrect: This matches the rule for acronyms in your grammar book.
explanation.tip: Acronyms are formed from the first letters of words in a name.

items.stem: Which closing for a letter is capitalized correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: In a closing, capitalize only the first word.
explanation.tip: Greeting: capitalize the first word and names. Closing: first word only.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Capitalize only the first word of a closing.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Only the first word is capitalized.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The first word must be capitalized.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Abbreviations of days are capitalized: Thurs.
explanation.tip: Abbreviations of proper nouns keep their capital letters.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Quotation marks go around the speaker’s words, with the comma inside.
explanation.tip: Commas and periods go inside closing quotation marks.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A comma is needed before the closing quotation mark.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The comma goes inside the closing quotation marks.

options.label: D
options.text: I finished my project, said Nouf.
options.rationale: Quotation marks are needed around her words.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma separates the speaker tag from the quotation; the period goes inside.
explanation.tip: Speaker tag + comma + “Quotation.”

options.label: C
options.rationale: The first word of a quotation is capitalized.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The period goes inside the quotation marks.

items.stem: There should be a space between an opening quotation mark and the first word of the quotation.

explanation.whyCorrect: There is no space after an opening quotation mark or before a closing one.
explanation.tip: Quotation marks sit right next to the words they enclose.

items.stem: Where do the commas belong? “If we hurry” said Omar “we can catch the bus.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Correct: “If we hurry,” said Omar, “we can catch the bus.”
explanation.tip: When a speaker tag interrupts a sentence, use commas on both sides of it.

options.label: A
options.rationale: A comma is also needed inside the first quotation.

options.label: C
options.text: After “hurry” (inside the quotation mark) and after “Omar”

options.label: D
options.rationale: Commas go where the quotation is interrupted.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark.
explanation.tip: Commas and periods always go inside closing quotation marks.

segments: “Mom, I had so much fun at the party”
items.correction: “Mom, I had so much fun at the party,”

items.stem: Put the pieces in order to make a correctly punctuated sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: The quotation is interrupted by the speaker tag, with commas on both sides.
explanation.tip: An interrupted quotation: “Part one,” speaker tag, “part two.”

sequence: “When the bell rings,”
said the teacher,
“please line up quietly.”

items.stem: What makes this a pun? “The baker quit because he couldn’t make enough dough.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A pun plays on a word with two meanings; “dough” can mean bread mixture or money.
explanation.tip: A pun is a joke that uses a word’s double meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: It repeats the same sound at the start.

options.label: B
options.text: It compares a baker to money using “like.”

options.label: D
options.text: “Dough” means both bread mixture and, informally, money.

items.stem: Which sentence is a pun?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Interest” means both money a bank pays and curiosity.
explanation.tip: Look for one word that makes sense in two ways.

options.label: A
options.text: I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.

options.label: C
options.text: I worked at the bank for ten years.
options.rationale: There is no double meaning here.

options.label: D
options.text: My bank is next to the bakery.

items.stem: “The math book looked sad because it had too many problems” is a pun.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Problems” means both math exercises and troubles.
explanation.tip: Ask whether one word works with two different meanings.

items.stem: Which word creates the pun? “Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Flies” is a verb (moves quickly) in the first part and a noun (insects) in the second.
explanation.tip: Puns can switch a word between two parts of speech.

items.stem: Match each pun with the word that has the double meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each pun depends on a word or phrase that sounds like or means two things.
explanation.tip: Find the phrase that makes the reader smile.

pairs.left: The tailor won because he was always on pins and needles.
The bicycle couldn’t stand up because it was two-tired.
The scarecrow got an award for being outstanding in his field.

items.stem: Why might an author use a pun in a historical story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Puns reveal a playful or witty character and give readers a moment of humor.
explanation.tip: Think about the effect of wordplay on the reader.

options.label: A
options.text: To give exact dates and facts

options.label: B
options.rationale: Puns are often part of dialogue.

options.label: C
options.text: To show a character’s cleverness or add humor

options.label: D
options.text: To make the story sound more serious

items.stem: You want to know whether “record” in your sentence is a noun or a verb. Which part of the dictionary entry should you check?

explanation.whyCorrect: Dictionary entries label each meaning with its part of speech, such as noun or verb.
explanation.tip: Look for small labels like n., v., adj. after the entry word.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Syllables do not tell the part of speech.

options.label: B
options.text: The guide words at the top of the page
options.rationale: Guide words help you find the page, not the word’s use.

options.label: C
options.text: The first letter of the entry word
options.rationale: The first letter only helps with alphabetical order.

options.label: D
options.text: The part-of-speech label, such as (n.) or (v.)

items.stem: A digital thesaurus lists “glance, peek, scan, gaze” for “look.” Which word means to look for a long time?

explanation.whyCorrect: To gaze is to look steadily for a long time, often with wonder.
explanation.tip: Synonyms have shades of meaning; check the dictionary to choose precisely.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A peek is a quick, secret look.

options.label: C
options.rationale: A glance is a quick look.

options.label: D
options.rationale: To scan is to look quickly over something.

items.stem: The dictionary shows “con·duct (noun) KON-dukt; (verb) kuhn-DUKT.” How should you say “conduct” in “The students will conduct an experiment”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Will conduct” is a verb, so the stress is on the second syllable.
explanation.tip: Some words change stress depending on their part of speech.

options.label: A
options.text: KON-dukt, because it is a noun
options.rationale: Here it is a verb (an action).

options.label: B
options.text: kuhn-DUKT, because it is a verb

options.label: C
options.text: Either way, because the meaning is the same
options.rationale: Stress changes with the part of speech.

items.stem: A glossary is found at the back of a book and defines words used in that book.

explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike a dictionary, a glossary only covers words from that book.
explanation.tip: Glossary = mini-dictionary for one book.

items.stem: Which source should you use to check whether “principal” or “principle” fits your sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: A dictionary gives each word’s meaning so you can choose correctly.
explanation.tip: Use a dictionary for meaning and spelling; a thesaurus for synonyms.

options.label: A
options.rationale: An almanac gives yearly facts and data.

options.label: C
options.text: A dictionary, to compare the meanings

items.stem: Put these words in dictionary order.

explanation.whyCorrect: Compare letter by letter: harb-i, harb-o, hard, harm, harv.
explanation.tip: When words begin the same way, keep comparing until a letter differs.

sequence: harbinger
harbor
hardship
harmony
harvest

items.stem: What does the suffix -less mean in “spotless”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Spotless means without spots, completely clean.
explanation.tip: -less = without; -ful = full of.

options.label: B
options.rationale: That is the meaning of -er or -or.

options.label: C
options.rationale: That is the meaning of the prefix re-.

items.stem: What does “washable” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The suffix -able means able to be: washable = able to be washed.
explanation.tip: Add the meaning of the suffix to the base word.

options.label: B
options.rationale: -able means able to be, not already done.

items.stem: Choose the word that means “the state of being kind”: “Her ____ made everyone feel welcome.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The suffix -ness turns an adjective into a noun meaning “the state of being.”
explanation.tip: -ness = state or quality of.

options.label: B
options.rationale: -ly makes an adverb, not a noun.

items.stem: Match each suffix with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: Knowing suffix meanings helps you figure out new words.
explanation.tip: Think of a word you know with each suffix.

items.stem: Which word means “in a careful way”?

explanation.whyCorrect: care + -ful (full of) + -ly (in a … way) = in a careful way.
explanation.tip: Some words have two suffixes; build the meaning step by step.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is an adjective; it does not describe how something is done.

items.stem: In “The government announced a new agreement,” how do the suffixes help you understand “government” and “agreement”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Govern → government; agree → agreement. Both become nouns naming a thing or result.
explanation.tip: Suffixes can change a word’s part of speech.

options.label: C
options.text: -ment turns the verbs “govern” and “agree” into nouns.

items.stem: Choose the verb: “The scientist ____ through the microscope.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Scientist” is singular, so the verb adds -s: looks.
explanation.tip: Singular subject → verb + s. Plural subject → no -s.

options.label: A
options.rationale: A singular subject takes a verb ending in -s in the present tense.

options.label: D
options.rationale: “Are” does not agree with the singular subject.

items.stem: Choose the verb: “Audrey and her sister ____ catch in the field.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Two people joined by “and” make a plural subject, so the verb has no -s.
explanation.tip: Subject + and + subject = plural.

options.label: A
options.rationale: “Has” does not agree with a plural subject.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A compound subject joined by “and” is plural.

options.label: D
options.rationale: “Is” does not agree with a plural subject.

items.stem: Choose the verb: “The box of old toys ____ dust in the attic.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The prepositional phrase “of old toys” does not change the subject; “box” is singular.
explanation.tip: Cross out prepositional phrases to find the real subject.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The subject is “box,” which is singular.

items.stem: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Flock” is a collective noun referring to the group as a whole, so it takes a singular verb.
explanation.tip: Collective nouns (flock, team, class) usually take singular verbs.

options.label: A
options.text: A flock of birds fly over the river every evening.

options.label: B
options.text: A flocks of birds flies over the river every evening.

options.label: C
options.text: A flock of birds flying over the river every evening.
options.rationale: This is a fragment with no main verb.

options.label: D
options.text: A flock of birds flies over the river every evening.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: In a compound sentence, each subject agrees with its own verb: “brother” is singular, so “watches.”
explanation.tip: Check the verb in each clause of a compound sentence separately.

items.stem: Which sentence is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: The subject is “Each,” which is singular, so the verb is “has.”
explanation.tip: Words like each, every and either are singular subjects.

options.label: A
options.text: Each of the students has a locker.

options.label: B
options.text: Each of the students having a locker.

options.label: C
options.text: Each of the student have a locker.
options.rationale: “Student” should be plural and the verb singular.

options.label: D
options.text: Each of the students have a locker.
options.rationale: “Each” is singular; “of the students” does not change it.

items.stem: What is the role of the NARRATOR in “The Interview”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The narrator explains when and where the play takes place and why Sara is there.
explanation.tip: A narrator in a play speaks to the audience to provide background.

options.label: B
options.text: To introduce the setting and situation before the action begins

options.label: C
options.text: To play a character in the interview
options.rationale: The narrator does not take part in the scenes.

options.label: D
options.text: To give stage directions to actors

items.stem: What is an aside, as used by Sara in Scene 1?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sara’s aside reveals her frustration to the audience without Mr. Aziz hearing it.
explanation.tip: Asides let the audience know a character’s private thoughts.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Scene changes are marked with scene headings.

options.label: B
options.text: A long speech to another character

options.label: C
options.text: A comment spoken to the audience that other characters do not hear

options.label: D
options.text: A stage direction about where to stand
options.rationale: An aside is spoken, not a direction.

items.stem: In “The Interview,” Scene 2 takes place two hours after Scene 1.

explanation.whyCorrect: The stage directions for Scene 2 say “Two hours later.”
explanation.tip: Scene headings and stage directions show changes in time and place.

items.stem: How does the stage direction [stopping, then smiling for the first time] contribute to the plot?

explanation.whyCorrect: After this moment his short answers change into a long story, which shifts the interview.
explanation.tip: Stage directions can mark important changes in a character or in the plot.

options.label: A
options.text: It explains why the gym flooded.
options.rationale: The flood is explained in his dialogue.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows that Mr. Aziz is finished working for the day.
options.rationale: He continues to talk, not to leave.

options.label: D
options.text: It marks the turning point when Mr. Aziz begins to open up.

items.stem: Why did the playwright divide the play into two short scenes instead of one?

explanation.whyCorrect: Jumping two hours ahead lets the audience see how much the interview changed things.
explanation.tip: A scene break can compress time and highlight a change.

options.label: A
options.text: To skip the long interview and show its result: Sara’s full notebook and changed attitude

options.label: B
options.text: To show a different character’s point of view
options.rationale: Both scenes focus on Sara and Mr. Aziz.

options.label: C
options.text: To give the narrator more lines
options.rationale: The narrator speaks only at the start.

options.label: D
options.text: To introduce a second setting far from the school
options.rationale: Both scenes are in the storage room.

items.stem: Match each element of “The Interview” with how it contributes to the play.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each element plays a specific role in the structure and meaning of the drama.
explanation.tip: Ask what each part of a play does for the audience.

pairs.right: Sets the time, place and purpose
Reveals her private frustration to the audience
Expresses the play’s message about care

items.stem: What can you infer about Mr. Aziz at the start of Scene 1?

explanation.whyCorrect: He says, “There is not much to tell,” which suggests he undervalues his own story.
explanation.tip: An inference combines text evidence with what you already know.

options.label: A
options.text: He wants to stop working immediately.

options.label: B
options.text: He does not think his own work is interesting.

options.label: D
options.text: He has forgotten his years at the school.

items.stem: Why does Sara ask about the radio?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her aside shows she needs longer answers, so she tries a new question about an object in the room.
explanation.tip: Use a character’s goal to infer the reason for their actions.

options.label: A
options.text: She thinks the radio is broken and wants to fix it.
options.rationale: She is a writer, not fixing things.

options.label: B
options.text: She wants to listen to the news.

options.label: C
options.text: She is looking for a way to get Mr. Aziz talking.

options.label: D
options.text: She wants to buy the radio.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests she wants to buy it.

items.stem: What does Mr. Aziz’s final line suggest about how he sees his job?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Some things last if you look after them” reflects pride in thirty years of care.
explanation.tip: Characters’ final lines often reveal their deeper values.

options.label: A
options.text: He wants Sara to become a custodian.
options.rationale: He is giving her a keepsake, not career advice.

options.label: B
options.text: He thinks doorknobs are worth a lot of money.
options.rationale: The value he means is not money.

options.label: C
options.text: He regrets working at the school.
options.rationale: His tone is proud and gentle.

options.label: D
options.text: He believes caring for things over time gives them lasting value.

items.stem: Which inference about the letter writer is BEST supported by the text?

explanation.whyCorrect: She mentions her grandfather’s spice stall and her first school bag bought there.
explanation.tip: Cite specific details that support your inference.

options.label: A
options.text: She feels a personal connection to the souq through her family.

options.label: B
options.text: She dislikes visitors to the city.
options.rationale: She suggests ways to welcome visitors.

options.label: C
options.text: She has never visited the souq.
options.rationale: She describes walking under its arches.

options.label: D
options.text: She works for the city council.

items.stem: The letter suggests that Huda believes old buildings and tourism can work together.

explanation.whyCorrect: She proposes repairs and signs in several languages to “protect our heritage and welcome visitors at the same time.”
explanation.tip: Inferences must be supported by evidence in the text.

items.stem: Which TWO details support the inference that Mr. Aziz has hidden depths?

explanation.whyCorrect: The vivid flood story and the full notebook show how much he had to share.
explanation.tip: Look for evidence that contrasts with first impressions.

options.label: A
options.text: Sara’s notebook is full after two hours.

options.label: B
options.text: He shrugs at the first question.
options.rationale: This shows his reserve, not depth.

options.label: C
options.text: He tells a detailed story about carrying two hundred chairs during a flood.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This shows his work, not hidden depths.

items.stem: What is Huda’s main purpose in writing her letter?

explanation.whyCorrect: She writes, “I urge the council to change its plan.”
explanation.tip: Persuasive writing tries to convince readers to think or act in a certain way.

options.label: A
options.text: To entertain readers with a funny story
options.rationale: The letter is serious and persuasive.

options.label: B
options.text: To persuade the council to save the old souq

options.label: C
options.text: To explain how shopping centers are built
options.rationale: She argues against one; she does not explain construction.

options.label: D
options.text: To describe how spices are grown
options.rationale: Spices are mentioned only as part of family history.

items.stem: Why does Huda include the story of her grandfather’s stall?

explanation.whyCorrect: Personal history makes her argument about heritage feel real and emotional.
explanation.tip: Ask how each detail serves the author’s purpose.

options.label: B
options.text: To give directions to the souq

options.label: C
options.text: To show that the souq is part of real families’ history

options.label: D
options.text: To prove that spices are expensive

items.stem: How does Huda respond to the council’s argument about visitors?

explanation.whyCorrect: She turns the council’s own goal into a reason to keep the souq.
explanation.tip: Strong persuasive writers answer opposing arguments.

options.label: A
options.text: She agrees that a mall would bring more visitors.

options.label: C
options.text: She says visitors are not important.

options.label: D
options.text: She argues that visitors come for what is unique, which the souq offers and a mall does not.

items.stem: The closing image “disappear behind a glass wall” is meant to create an emotional reaction.

explanation.whyCorrect: The image of history vanishing behind glass appeals to readers’ feelings.
explanation.tip: Word choice can convey an author’s point of view.

items.stem: Which phrase BEST shows Huda’s point of view about the shopping center?

explanation.whyCorrect: The phrase suggests a mall is ordinary and replaceable, unlike the souq.
explanation.tip: Look for phrases that reveal what the author values.

options.label: A
options.text: “They can visit a shopping center in any city in the world”

options.label: B
options.text: “The city council plans to replace our old covered souq”
options.rationale: This states a fact about the plan.

items.stem: How does Huda make her letter persuasive WITHOUT being rude to the council?

explanation.whyCorrect: Suggesting repairs, lighting and signs shows a constructive attitude, and “Respectfully” keeps a polite tone.
explanation.tip: An author’s purpose shapes tone as well as content.

options.label: A
options.text: She threatens the council with consequences.

options.label: B
options.text: She offers practical alternatives and closes respectfully.

options.label: C
options.text: She uses insults to show strong feeling.

options.label: D
options.text: She refuses to mention the council’s view.

items.stem: What theme do “The New Field” and “Transplant” share?

explanation.whyCorrect: Yasmin learns the new field; the lemon tree grows new buds after a hard period.
explanation.tip: Compare how different genres approach the same theme.

options.label: A
options.text: Football is more important than gardening.
options.rationale: The poem is not about football.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Both the tree and Yasmin change.

options.label: C
options.text: Adjusting to a new place takes time but can lead to growth.

options.label: D
options.text: Moving is always a terrible experience.

items.stem: How is the lemon tree’s experience similar to Yasmin’s?

explanation.whyCorrect: Yasmin sits on the bench and misses home; the tree drops its leaves. Both later thrive.
explanation.tip: Look for parallel stages in each text.

options.label: A
options.text: Both are moved by a coach.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Yasmin moves away from the sea.

options.label: D
options.text: Both struggle at first after being moved, then adapt.

items.stem: How does the poem’s form change the way the theme is presented compared with the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The poem compresses the idea into images; the story develops it through a character’s actions over time.
explanation.tip: Genre affects how an author develops a theme.

options.label: A
options.text: The poem uses a single image and rhyme to suggest the theme; the story shows it through events and dialogue.

options.label: B
options.text: The story uses rhyme and stanzas.

options.label: C
options.text: The poem gives more details about football practice.
options.rationale: The poem does not mention football.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The poem has a tree, not Yasmin.

items.stem: In both texts, a turning point shows the main subject beginning to thrive.

explanation.whyCorrect: Yasmin scores her first goal; the tree breaks out in new buds.
explanation.tip: Compare the structure as well as the theme.

items.stem: Match each detail from the story with a similar detail from the poem.

explanation.whyCorrect: The texts follow parallel stages: leaving, struggling, thriving.
explanation.tip: Pair details that play the same role in each text.

pairs.left: Yasmin leaves her team by the sea
pairs.right: The tree is lifted from its courtyard

pairs.left: Yasmin sits on the bench missing home
pairs.right: The tree drops its yellow light

items.stem: Which statement BEST explains a DIFFERENCE between the texts?

explanation.whyCorrect: Yasmin practices every morning; the tree simply recovers “one morning.”
explanation.tip: Compare not only what happens but why it happens in each text.

options.label: A
options.text: The poem explains how to care for lemon trees.

options.label: B
options.text: The story credits effort and practice for the change, while the poem presents growth as something that comes with time.

options.label: C
options.text: The story is sad, but the poem is happy throughout.
options.rationale: Both move from hardship to hope.

options.label: D
options.text: Only the poem has a hopeful ending.

items.stem: Which line from “Desert Night” appeals mainly to the sense of taste?

explanation.whyCorrect: The speaker tastes smoke and spice from the coffee.
explanation.tip: Sensory language appeals to sight, sound, smell, taste and touch.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This appeals to touch and sight.

options.label: C
options.text: “and taste the smoke, the spice, the vast and silent dark”

items.stem: What does the simile “like a coin into a pocket” suggest about the sunset?

explanation.whyCorrect: A coin slips out of sight smoothly and fast, like the sun sinking.
explanation.tip: A simile compares two things using like or as.

options.label: A
options.text: The sun is made of metal.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The image is playful, not about theft.

options.label: C
options.rationale: A coin slipping into a pocket is quick.

options.label: D
options.text: The sun disappears quickly and neatly below the dunes.

items.stem: “The coffee pot hisses on the coals” appeals to the sense of hearing.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Hisses” is a sound word.
explanation.tip: Sound words create auditory imagery.

items.stem: What does the metaphor “the sky unrolls its black carpet, scattered with salt” describe?

explanation.whyCorrect: The black carpet is the dark sky, and the scattered salt is the stars.
explanation.tip: A metaphor describes one thing as if it were another.

options.label: A
options.text: The night sky spreading out, full of white stars

options.label: B
options.rationale: The image is calm and dark, not stormy.

options.label: C
options.text: Salt being spilled on a rug

items.stem: Match each image from “Desert Night” with the sense it appeals to most.

explanation.whyCorrect: The poet uses every sense to place the reader in the desert.
explanation.tip: Identify the sense each detail relies on.

pairs.left: the sand gives back the day’s heat
a camel groans, low as a cello string
the sky unrolls its black carpet

items.stem: How does the imagery in the last two lines shift the poem’s focus?

explanation.whyCorrect: “I hold the small cup with both hands” brings the reader close to the speaker’s senses.
explanation.tip: Notice when a poem moves from wide images to close-up ones.

options.label: A
options.rationale: It is still night at the end.

options.label: B
options.text: From the wide desert landscape to the speaker’s close, personal experience

options.label: D
options.text: From the speaker to the camel
options.rationale: The focus moves to the speaker, not away.

items.stem: What is the subject of the command “Close the window, please”?

explanation.whyCorrect: In an imperative sentence, the subject “you” is understood.
explanation.tip: Commands have an understood subject.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Commands have an understood subject: you.

options.label: D
options.rationale: “Please” is a polite word, not the subject.

items.stem: What is the simple subject? “Neither of the answers on the board was correct.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Remove “of the answers on the board”; the subject is “Neither.”
explanation.tip: The subject is never inside a prepositional phrase.

options.label: A
options.rationale: “Answers” is part of the prepositional phrase “of the answers.”

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is part of a prepositional phrase.

items.stem: Find the subject: “Here are the results of the survey.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Rearranged: “The results of the survey are here.” The subject is “results.”
explanation.tip: In sentences beginning with here or there, the subject follows the verb.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the object of the preposition “of.”

options.label: C
options.rationale: “Here” is an adverb, not the subject.

items.stem: In “The team and its coach celebrated and posed for photos,” the sentence has a compound subject and a compound predicate.

explanation.whyCorrect: Subjects: team, coach. Predicates: celebrated, posed.
explanation.tip: Find all subjects, then all verbs.

items.stem: What is the complete predicate? “During the storm, the old fishing boat drifted slowly toward the rocks.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The complete predicate is the verb and everything that tells about it.
explanation.tip: Introductory phrases are not part of the subject.

options.label: C
options.text: During the storm, the old fishing boat
options.rationale: This includes an introductory phrase and the subject.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is only part of the predicate.

items.stem: Write the simple predicate (main verb phrase): “By next June, the new library will have opened its doors.” ____

explanation.whyCorrect: The simple predicate includes all helping verbs: will have opened.
explanation.tip: Include every helping verb in the simple predicate.

items.stem: Which compound sentence is punctuated correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses.
explanation.tip: FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

options.label: A
options.text: The museum closed early but, the café stayed open.
options.rationale: The comma goes before the conjunction.

options.label: B
options.text: The museum closed early, the café stayed open.
options.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

options.label: C
options.text: The museum closed early, but the café stayed open.

options.label: D
options.text: The museum, closed early but the café stayed open.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon?

explanation.whyCorrect: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.
