explanation.tip: Each side of a semicolon should be a complete sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: The rain stopped the; players returned.
options.rationale: The semicolon is in the wrong place.

options.label: B
options.text: The rain; stopped the players returned.
options.rationale: The semicolon must separate two complete clauses.

options.label: C
options.text: The rain stopped; and the players returned.
options.rationale: Do not use a semicolon with a coordinating conjunction this way.

options.label: D
options.text: The rain stopped; the players returned to the field.

items.stem: Choose the conjunction: “He was exhausted, ____ he finished the race.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Yet” shows a surprising contrast.
explanation.tip: yet/but = contrast; so = result; for = reason; or = choice.

options.label: C
options.rationale: “So” shows a result, but finishing despite exhaustion is a contrast.

items.stem: Choose the conjunction: “Neither the coach was ready, ____ were the players.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Neither … nor” is a correlative pair.
explanation.tip: Pairs: either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This does not complete the negative pair.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Two independent clauses joined only by a comma create a comma splice; use a semicolon (or add a conjunction).
explanation.tip: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences.

items.stem: Which revision best combines the ideas to show cause and effect? “The bridge was closed. Traffic moved slowly all morning.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “So” shows that the closed bridge caused the slow traffic.
explanation.tip: Choose the conjunction that matches the logical relationship.

options.label: A
options.text: The bridge was closed, so traffic moved slowly all morning.

options.label: B
options.text: The bridge was closed, but traffic moved slowly all morning.

options.label: C
options.text: The bridge was closed, traffic moved slowly all morning.

options.label: D
options.text: The bridge was closed, or traffic moved slowly all morning.

items.stem: Which word is an adverb? “The choir sang beautifully at the ceremony.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Beautifully” tells how the choir sang.
explanation.tip: Adverbs tell how, when, where or to what extent.

items.stem: What question does the adverb answer? “We will leave tomorrow.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Tomorrow” tells when we will leave.
explanation.tip: Adverbs of time: today, soon, later, tomorrow.

options.label: B
options.rationale: It does not name a place.

items.stem: Choose the relative adverb: “I still remember the day ____ we moved to a new city.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “When” introduces a clause that tells about a time: the day.
explanation.tip: Relative adverbs: where (place), when (time), why (reason).

options.label: A
options.rationale: “Where” refers to a place, not a time.

items.stem: Choose the correct form: “Of all the runners, Nasser finished ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Use “most” + adverb to compare three or more.
explanation.tip: -ly adverbs: more/most + adverb.

options.label: A
options.rationale: “More” compares two; this compares all the runners.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Well” is the adverb that describes how she did; “good” is an adjective.
explanation.tip: Use well (adverb) to describe actions; good (adjective) to describe nouns.

items.stem: Which word does the adverb “extremely” modify? “The extremely tired hikers rested by the stream.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Extremely” modifies the adjective “tired,” telling to what extent.
explanation.tip: Adverbs can modify verbs, adjectives or other adverbs.

options.label: C
options.rationale: “Extremely” describes how tired, not how they rested.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “____ turn is it to present?”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Whose” shows ownership: whose turn.
explanation.tip: Who’s = who is/who has; whose = belonging to whom.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “The students said ____ ready to present their project.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “They are ready to present” makes sense, so the contraction “they’re” is correct.
explanation.tip: Expand the contraction to check if it fits.

items.stem: Which sentence uses its and it’s correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: It’s = it is; its = belonging to it.
explanation.tip: Possessive pronouns never use apostrophes.

options.label: A
options.text: It’s clear that the team lost its focus.

options.label: B
options.text: It’s clear that the team lost it’s focus.

options.label: C
options.text: Its clear that the team lost its focus.

options.label: D
options.text: Its clear that the team lost it’s focus.

items.stem: Match each word with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: Contractions contain apostrophes; possessive pronouns do not.
explanation.tip: Replace the word with its expanded form to test it.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “You’re” (you are) is needed: “If you are finished.” The second “your” is correct.
explanation.tip: Check each your/you’re in the sentence separately.

items.stem: Which sentence is completely correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: There (existence), they’re (they are), their (possession), its (possession) are all used correctly.
explanation.tip: Test every homophone in a long sentence one at a time.

options.label: A
options.text: There are two reasons why their late: there bus broke down, and its replacement was delayed.

options.label: B
options.text: There are two reasons why they’re late: their bus broke down, and its replacement was delayed.

options.label: C
options.text: There are two reasons why they’re late: there bus broke down, and it’s replacement was delayed.

options.label: D
options.text: Their are two reasons why there late: they’re bus broke down, and it’s replacement was delayed.

items.stem: What does the prefix mis- mean in “misunderstand”?

explanation.whyCorrect: To misunderstand is to understand wrongly.
explanation.tip: mis- = wrongly or badly.

items.stem: Using the prefix inter- (between), what does “international” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: inter- + national = between nations.
explanation.tip: inter- = between; intra- = within.

options.label: A
options.rationale: That would be intra- or domestic.

items.stem: Match each prefix with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: These Greek and Latin prefixes appear in many academic words.
explanation.tip: Think of an example: submarine, transport, antibiotic, autograph.

items.stem: Choose the word that means “heat before”: “Please ____ the oven before you put the bread inside.”

explanation.whyCorrect: pre- means before: preheat = heat before.
explanation.tip: Combine the prefix meaning with the base word.

items.stem: If “bi-” means two and “tri-” means three, what is a “tripod”?

explanation.whyCorrect: tri- (three) + pod (foot) = three-footed stand.
explanation.tip: Use both the prefix and the root to find the meaning.

options.label: B
options.rationale: That is a tricycle; “pod” refers to feet or legs.

items.stem: In “The scientist’s findings were later proven to be a misinterpretation,” what does the prefix help you understand?

explanation.whyCorrect: mis- (wrongly) + interpretation = a wrong explanation.
explanation.tip: Prefixes change meaning even in long academic words.

options.label: A
options.text: The findings were explained before the study.

options.label: B
options.text: The findings had been explained incorrectly.

options.label: D
options.text: The findings were explained across many countries.
options.rationale: That would need trans- or inter-.

items.stem: Which word is an adjective? “A shiny bike leaned against the wall.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Shiny” describes the bike.
explanation.tip: Adjectives describe nouns: what kind, how many, which one.

items.stem: Choose the adjective that tells HOW MANY: “We saw ____ camels near the road.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Seven” tells how many camels.
explanation.tip: Number words are adjectives that tell how many.

options.label: C
options.rationale: “Brown” tells what kind, not how many.

items.stem: Which sentence uses “a” and “an” correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: “An” comes before vowel sounds; “a” comes before consonant sounds.
explanation.tip: Say the next word aloud to hear its first sound.

options.label: A
options.text: I ate a apple and an banana.

options.label: B
options.text: I ate an apple and an banana.
options.rationale: Use “a” before a consonant sound: a banana.

options.label: C
options.text: I ate a apple and a banana.
options.rationale: Use “an” before a vowel sound: an apple.

options.label: D
options.text: I ate an apple and a banana.

items.stem: Choose the adjective: “That was the ____ storm we have had all year.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing more than two, the superlative of “bad” is “worst.”
explanation.tip: good–better–best; bad–worse–worst.

items.stem: Which sentence uses an adjective correctly after the verb “smells”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Smells” links the bread to a describing word, so the adjective “wonderful” is correct.
explanation.tip: After linking verbs (is, seems, smells, tastes), use adjectives.

options.label: B
options.rationale: After a linking verb like “smells,” use an adjective, not an adverb.

options.label: C
options.rationale: “Freshly” is an adverb; a noun needs the adjective “fresh.”

options.label: D
options.rationale: “Bread” is singular, so the verb is “smells.”

items.stem: Which word tells HOW the turtle moved? “The turtle moved slowly across the sand.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Slowly” is an adverb that tells how.
explanation.tip: Many adverbs end in -ly.

items.stem: Choose the adverb that tells WHEN: “We will visit the museum ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Tomorrow” tells when.
explanation.tip: Adverbs answer how, when or where.

items.stem: Which word is an adverb that tells WHERE? “The children played outside after lunch.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Outside” tells where they played.
explanation.tip: Where-adverbs: here, there, outside, inside, upstairs.

items.stem: Choose the relative adverb: “Nobody knows the reason ____ the bell rang early.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Why” goes with “the reason.”
explanation.tip: Relative adverbs: where (place), when (time), why (reason).

options.label: A
options.rationale: “Who” is a relative pronoun for people.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Quickly” is the adverb that tells how he ran; “quick” is an adjective.
explanation.tip: Use an adverb to describe a verb.

items.stem: Choose the word: “A whale is ____ than a dolphin.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing two animals uses -er: bigger.
explanation.tip: Two things: -er. Three or more: -est.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Use -est to compare three or more.

items.stem: Choose the word: “Of the three puppies, Coco is the ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing three puppies uses -est.
explanation.tip: “Of the three” signals a superlative.

items.stem: Which sentence compares two things correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Long adjectives use “more” to compare two things.
explanation.tip: Long words: more/most. Short words: -er/-est.

options.label: A
options.text: This puzzle is more difficulter than that one.

options.label: B
options.text: This puzzle is most difficult than that one.

options.label: C
options.text: This puzzle is difficulter than that one.

options.label: D
options.text: This puzzle is more difficult than that one.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Use -est OR most, never both: “the hottest.”
explanation.tip: Never double up comparing words.

items.stem: Which sentence uses comparing words correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: good → better → best.
explanation.tip: Irregular comparatives must be memorized.

options.label: A
options.text: Huda’s drawing is good, Rami’s is better, and Sami’s is the best.

options.label: B
options.text: Huda’s drawing is good, Rami’s is more better, and Sami’s is the best.

options.label: C
options.text: Huda’s drawing is good, Rami’s is gooder, and Sami’s is the goodest.

options.label: D
options.text: Huda’s drawing is good, Rami’s is better, and Sami’s is the bestest.

items.stem: “Ran to the gate” is a complete sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: It has no subject: who ran? It is a fragment.
explanation.tip: A sentence needs a subject and a verb.

items.stem: Which group of words is a fragment?

explanation.whyCorrect: There is a subject but no verb, so it is not a complete thought.
explanation.tip: Ask: What did the girl do?

options.label: B
options.text: The girl with the red umbrella.

options.label: C
options.text: The girl opened her red umbrella.
options.rationale: This has a subject and a verb.

items.stem: Which is a correct way to fix this run-on? “The power went out we lit candles.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Splitting the run-on into two sentences fixes it.
explanation.tip: Fix run-ons with a period, or a comma and a conjunction.

options.label: A
options.text: The power went out and, we lit candles.

options.label: B
options.text: The power went out, we lit candles.
options.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two sentences.

options.label: C
options.text: The power went out. We lit candles.

options.label: D
options.text: The power went out we, lit candles.
options.rationale: The comma is in the wrong place.

items.stem: Which revision fixes the fragment? “When the bell rang. We lined up.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Join the dependent clause to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.tip: A clause starting with “When” needs a main clause.

options.label: A
options.text: The bell. When we lined up.

options.label: B
options.text: When the bell rang we. Lined up.

options.label: C
options.text: When the bell rang. we lined up.

options.label: D
options.text: When the bell rang, we lined up.

items.stem: Choose the past tense: “Yesterday I ____ to the market.”

explanation.whyCorrect: go → went.
explanation.tip: Irregular verbs change their spelling in the past.

items.stem: Choose the past tense: “Last night Mama ____ a story.”

explanation.whyCorrect: tell → told.
explanation.tip: Say “Yesterday she…” to test.

items.stem: Match each verb with its past tense.

explanation.whyCorrect: These verbs change their vowel in the past tense.
explanation.tip: Many irregular verbs change a vowel.

items.stem: Choose the correct form: “Have you ever ____ a camel?”

explanation.whyCorrect: have + past participle: have ridden.
explanation.tip: ride → rode → (have) ridden.

items.stem: Which sentence uses irregular verbs correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: rang and began are correct past-tense forms.
explanation.tip: Past tense stands alone; past participles need has/have/had.

options.label: A
options.text: The bell rang, and the students began to write.

options.label: B
options.text: The bell rang, and the students begun to write.

options.label: C
options.text: The bell ringed, and the students began to write.

options.label: D
options.text: The bell rung, and the students began to write.

items.stem: Which word is a negative?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Never” means “not ever.”
explanation.tip: Negatives: no, not, never, nobody, nothing, nowhere.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “I don’t have ____ homework tonight.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Use only one negative: “don’t” + “any.”
explanation.tip: One negative per sentence.

items.stem: “Nobody never cleans the board” is correct.

explanation.whyCorrect: It has two negatives. Correct: “Nobody ever cleans the board.”
explanation.tip: Change one negative to a positive word.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “There wasn’t ____ in the box.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Wasn’t” is negative, so use the positive “anything.”
explanation.tip: After n’t, use any-words.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Couldn’t” is already negative, so “nowhere” must become “anywhere.”
explanation.tip: Look for n’t plus another negative.

items.stem: Which word names a SPECIFIC river and is a proper noun?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Nile” names one particular river, so it is capitalized.
explanation.tip: Proper nouns name specific people, places and things.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is a common noun for any river.

items.stem: Which TWO words are nouns? “The farmer fed the hungry goats.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea.
explanation.tip: Test: can you put “the” before it?

items.stem: Which word is an abstract noun (an idea or feeling)?

explanation.whyCorrect: Courage is a quality you cannot see or touch.
explanation.tip: Abstract nouns name ideas and feelings.

items.stem: Which word is a collective noun?

explanation.whyCorrect: A collective noun names a group: a flock of birds.
explanation.tip: Collective nouns: team, class, family, flock, herd.

items.stem: In “Her kindness surprised the whole class,” which words are nouns?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Kindness” is an abstract noun; “class” is a collective noun.
explanation.tip: Nouns can be people, places, things or ideas.

items.stem: Choose the plural: “I have two ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Most nouns add -s to make plurals.
explanation.tip: Add -s to most nouns.

items.stem: Choose the plural: “The ____ played in the yard.”

explanation.whyCorrect: puppy → puppies.
explanation.tip: Consonant + y → -ies.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Consonant + y: change y to i and add -es.

items.stem: Which sentence uses plural nouns correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: women, children, knives are irregular plurals.
explanation.tip: Learn irregular plurals by heart.

options.label: A
options.text: The women gave the childrens some knives and forks.

options.label: B
options.text: The women gave the children some knifes and forks.

options.label: C
options.text: The women gave the children some knives and forks.

options.label: D
options.text: The womans gave the childs some knifes and forks.

items.stem: Match each singular noun with its plural.

explanation.whyCorrect: These plurals do not just add -s.
explanation.tip: Some plurals change vowels or stay the same.

items.stem: Which word is a preposition? “The ball rolled under the car.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Under” shows where the ball rolled.
explanation.tip: Prepositions show position or direction.

items.stem: Choose the preposition: “Put the books ____ the shelf.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “On” shows where to put the books.
explanation.tip: Common prepositions: on, in, under, over, between, behind.

items.stem: What is the object of the preposition? “We walked along the narrow path.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The object is the noun after the preposition: path.
explanation.tip: Preposition + (describing words) + noun = phrase.

items.stem: Which TWO are prepositional phrases? “After school, the cat slept beside the window.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Each phrase starts with a preposition and ends with a noun.
explanation.tip: Find the preposition, then its noun.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is a verb and preposition only.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the subject and verb.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Between” is the preposition; “of” is not needed.
explanation.tip: Use one preposition before the object.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “Is this ____ backpack?”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Your” shows ownership.
explanation.tip: your = belongs to you; you’re = you are.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The coats belong to them, so use “their.”
explanation.tip: their = belonging to them.

items.stem: Which sentence is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: They’re = they are; their = belonging to them; there = a place.
explanation.tip: Test each word separately.

options.label: A
options.text: They’re bringing there kites over their.
options.rationale: The second and last are wrong.

options.label: B
options.text: They’re bringing their kites over there.

options.label: C
options.text: There bringing their kites over they’re.
options.rationale: The first and last are wrong.

options.label: D
options.text: Their bringing there kites over they’re.

items.stem: Which pronoun can replace “Sara” in “Sara likes art”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sara is one girl, so “she.”
explanation.tip: Pronouns take the place of nouns.

options.label: D
options.rationale: “He” is for a boy or man.

items.stem: Choose the pronoun: “Mom gave the gift to ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: After “to,” use the object pronoun “me.”
explanation.tip: I is a subject; me is an object.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Use “me” after a verb or preposition.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Use only when the subject is also “I.”

items.stem: Choose the relative pronoun: “The book ____ I borrowed was exciting.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “That” refers to things like the book.
explanation.tip: who = people; which/that = things.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: As part of the subject, use “I.” Test: “I finished,” not “me finished.”
explanation.tip: Remove the other person to test.

items.stem: Which sentence is a command?

explanation.whyCorrect: A command tells someone to do something.
explanation.tip: Commands often begin with a verb.

items.stem: Choose the end mark: “What a beautiful sunset____”

explanation.whyCorrect: Exclamations show strong feeling.
explanation.tip: ! = strong feeling.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This shows strong feeling, so it needs an exclamation mark.

options.label: C
options.rationale: A comma cannot end a sentence.

items.stem: Match each sentence with its type.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each type has a purpose and an end mark.
explanation.tip: Look at the end mark and the purpose.

items.stem: Which sentence is a statement that ends correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: A statement tells something and ends with a period.
explanation.tip: Capital letter at the start, period at the end.

options.label: B
options.text: Does the train leave at noon.
options.rationale: A question ends with a question mark.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Sentences begin with a capital letter.

options.label: D
options.rationale: A statement ends with a period.

items.stem: Change the statement into a question: “Laila can speak three languages.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Move the helping verb “can” to the front to form a question.
explanation.tip: Questions often start with a helping verb.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Moving the helping verb makes a clearer question.

items.stem: Choose the verb: “The dog ____ at the mail carrier.”

explanation.whyCorrect: One dog → barks.
explanation.tip: Singular subject → verb with -s.

options.label: D
options.rationale: “Are” does not agree with one dog.

items.stem: Choose the verb: “My brothers ____ football every Friday.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Plural subject → no -s: play.
explanation.tip: Plural subject → verb without -s.

items.stem: Choose the verb: “The plates on the shelf ____ clean.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “On the shelf” does not change the subject; “plates” is plural, so “are.”
explanation.tip: Cover the prepositional phrase to find the real subject.

items.stem: Which sentence has correct agreement?

explanation.whyCorrect: With “either … or,” the verb agrees with the nearer subject: uncle drives.
explanation.tip: or/nor: match the closest subject.

options.label: A
options.text: Either my aunt or my uncle drive us to school.
options.rationale: With “or,” the verb agrees with the nearer subject (uncle).

options.label: B
options.text: Either my aunt or my uncle have driven us.

options.label: C
options.text: Either my aunt or my uncle drives us to school.

options.label: D
options.text: Either my aunt or my uncle are driving us to school.

items.stem: Choose the FUTURE tense: “Tomorrow we ____ the zoo.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Will” + verb shows the future.
explanation.tip: Future = will + verb.

items.stem: Which sentence is in the PAST tense?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Painted” and “yesterday” show the past.
explanation.tip: Time words help show tense.

options.label: B
options.text: We are painting the fence now.

options.label: C
options.text: We will paint the fence tomorrow.

items.stem: Choose the verb (present progressive): “Look! The bus ____ right now.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Right now” shows an action happening now: is leaving.
explanation.tip: Present progressive = am/is/are + -ing.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Yesterday” and “fed” show the past, so “walk” must be “walked.”
explanation.tip: Keep verb tenses consistent.

items.stem: Which word is an action verb? “The baby giggled at the clown.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Giggled” shows an action.
explanation.tip: Action verbs show what someone does.

items.stem: Which word is a linking verb? “The soup is hot.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Is” links the soup to the word that describes it.
explanation.tip: Linking verbs: am, is, are, was, were, seem, become.

items.stem: Choose the helping verb: “The students ____ finished their projects.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Have finished” is a verb phrase with a helping verb.
explanation.tip: Helping verbs: have, has, had, is, are, will, can.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is not a complete verb.

items.stem: Which modal verb shows possibility? “It ____ rain this afternoon.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Might” shows something possible but not certain.
explanation.tip: might/may = possible; must = required.

options.label: B
options.rationale: “Shall” is used for offers and plans.

items.stem: Which TWO words are verbs? “Huda seemed tired, so she rested.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Seemed” is a linking verb; “rested” is an action verb.
explanation.tip: Find every word that shows action or links.

items.stem: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Capitalize days, names of places and the first word.
explanation.tip: Proper nouns get capitals.

options.label: A
options.text: on Friday, we visited the Red Sea Museum.

options.label: B
options.text: On friday, we visited the Red Sea Museum.

options.label: C
options.text: On Friday, we visited the red sea museum.

options.label: D
options.text: On Friday, we visited the Red Sea Museum.

items.stem: Which title is capitalized correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Capitalize the first word and the important words in a title.
explanation.tip: Short words like “a” and “of” stay lowercase unless first.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The first word is always capitalized.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Important words in a title are capitalized.

items.stem: Which sentence capitalizes a family title correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Family titles used as names are capitalized; after “my” they are not.
explanation.tip: Test: can you replace it with a name?

options.label: A
options.text: Yesterday my Grandma told us a story.
options.rationale: After “my,” it is not a name, so it stays lowercase.

options.label: B
options.text: Yesterday Grandma told us a story.

options.label: C
options.text: yesterday Grandma told us a story.

options.label: D
options.text: Yesterday grandma told us a story.
options.rationale: Used as a name, “Grandma” is capitalized.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: City names are proper nouns and need capital letters.
explanation.tip: Capitalize the names of cities and countries.

items.stem: Which sentence uses commas in a list correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Commas separate three or more items in a series.
explanation.tip: Use commas between items in a list.

options.label: A
options.text: We bought dates, figs, and, grapes.

options.label: B
options.text: We bought, dates, figs, and grapes.

options.label: C
options.text: We bought dates, figs, and grapes.

options.label: D
options.text: We bought dates figs and grapes.
options.rationale: Commas separate items in a list.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a comma after an introductory word correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Use a comma after an introductory word such as yes, no or well.
explanation.tip: Pause words at the start get a comma.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes I would like some tea
options.rationale: A comma and a period are needed.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes I, would like some tea.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes I would like, some tea.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, I would like some tea.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a comma in direct address correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Use a comma to set off the name of the person being spoken to.
explanation.tip: Name + comma when you speak to someone.

options.label: A
options.text: Fatima, please hand me the ruler.

options.label: B
options.text: Fatima please, hand me the ruler.
options.rationale: The comma goes right after the name.

options.label: C
options.text: Fatima, please hand, me the ruler.

options.label: D
options.text: Fatima please hand me the ruler.
options.rationale: A comma is needed after the name.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma goes between the day and the year in a date.
explanation.tip: Dates: month day, year.

items.stem: Which sentence uses ALL commas correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Commas follow the introductory word, set off the name, separate list items and separate the day from the date.
explanation.tip: Check each comma rule one at a time.

options.label: A
options.text: Well Rania, we need flour, eggs, and milk before Tuesday March 12.

options.label: B
options.text: Well, Rania, we need flour, eggs, and milk before Tuesday, March 12.

options.label: C
options.text: Well, Rania, we need, flour, eggs, and milk before Tuesday, March 12.

options.label: D
options.text: Well, Rania we need flour eggs, and milk before Tuesday, March 12.

items.stem: Which words should be inside quotation marks? Majed said I love reading.

explanation.whyCorrect: Quotation marks go around the exact words someone says.
explanation.tip: Put only the spoken words inside.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Only the spoken words go in quotation marks.

options.label: B
options.rationale: These words tell who is speaking.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: The comma goes inside the closing quotation marks.
explanation.tip: Comma, then closing quotation mark.

options.label: A
options.text: “Let’s go to the beach” said Hessa.
options.rationale: A comma is needed before the closing quotation mark.

options.label: B
options.text: Let’s go to the beach, said Hessa.

options.label: C
options.text: “Let’s go to the beach”, said Hessa.
options.rationale: The comma belongs inside the quotation marks.

options.label: D
options.text: “Let’s go to the beach,” said Hessa.

items.stem: Which question is punctuated correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: A question mark that belongs to the quotation goes inside the quotation marks.
explanation.tip: The end mark stays with the spoken words.

options.label: B
options.text: Where is my notebook? asked Saad.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The quotation is a question, so it needs a question mark.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The first word of a quotation that is a complete sentence is capitalized.
explanation.tip: Start quotations with a capital letter.

items.stem: Put the pieces in order to make a correctly punctuated sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: The speaker tag interrupts the quotation and is set off by commas.
explanation.tip: Interrupted quotation: “part one,” tag, “part two.”

sequence: “After lunch,”
said Coach,
“we will practice passing.”

items.stem: Which sentence from “Our School Needs a Garden” states the author’s claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first sentence tells exactly what the author wants the school to do.
explanation.tip: The claim is often in the first sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: “The empty lot is wasted space right now.”
options.rationale: This is a supporting point in the conclusion.

options.label: B
options.text: “Our school should turn the empty lot behind the library into a vegetable garden.”

options.label: C
options.rationale: This supports a reason; it is not the main claim.

options.label: D
options.text: “Each class could care for its own bed.”
options.rationale: This is a detail about teamwork.

items.stem: Which piece of evidence would make the garden argument STRONGER?

explanation.whyCorrect: Real data that matches one of the author’s reasons strengthens the claim.
explanation.tip: Facts and data are stronger than opinions.

options.label: A
options.text: A sentence saying gardens are pretty
options.rationale: This is an opinion, not evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: A list of all the classes in the school
options.rationale: This does not support any reason.

options.label: C
options.text: A survey showing students ate more vegetables after a nearby school started a garden

options.label: D
options.text: A picture of the author’s favorite flower
options.rationale: This is personal and does not prove a reason.

items.stem: How does the author of “Our School Needs a Garden” feel about the empty lot?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author calls it “wasted space right now.”
explanation.tip: Look for words that show feelings.

options.label: A
options.text: It is too small for anything.
options.rationale: The author plans a garden there.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The author wants to change it.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the best part of the school.

items.stem: Which word in “The Dripping Taps” shows how the author first viewed the problem?

explanation.whyCorrect: The students “noticed something worrying,” which shows concern.
explanation.tip: Authors reveal their view through word choice.

items.stem: The author of “Nature’s Engineers” thinks beavers only cause problems.

explanation.whyCorrect: The author admits dams can flood roads but says many scientists think benefits are greater.
explanation.tip: Check whether the author presents more than one side.

items.stem: How does the author of “Nature’s Engineers” show a balanced point of view?

explanation.whyCorrect: The last paragraph admits problems and weighs them against benefits.
explanation.tip: Balanced writing presents more than one side.

options.label: A
options.text: By describing only how beavers build lodges
options.rationale: That would show only one side.

options.label: B
options.text: By mentioning that dams can flood roads, then explaining why scientists still value beavers

options.label: C
options.text: By telling a story about one beaver
options.rationale: The article is not a story.

options.label: D
options.text: By saying beavers are dangerous to people
options.rationale: The text does not say this.

items.stem: How does the author of “The Dripping Taps” show the students’ success instead of just giving an opinion?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author points to evidence collected “a month later,” which shows a reporting point of view.
explanation.tip: Notice whether an author proves a point with facts or with opinions.

options.label: A
options.text: By saying the students were the best class in the school
options.rationale: This is an opinion the text does not state.

options.label: B
options.text: By telling the reader to save water at home
options.rationale: The author reports events rather than giving commands.

options.label: C
options.text: By reporting results that were checked: the taps stopped dripping and the water bill was lower.

options.label: D
options.text: By describing the colors of the signs
options.rationale: Sign colors do not show success.

items.stem: What is the author’s main purpose in “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article walks through the steps of baking.
explanation.tip: Ask: Is the author informing, persuading or entertaining?

options.label: A
options.text: To persuade readers to buy bread
options.rationale: The text explains; it does not persuade.

options.label: B
options.text: To tell a funny story about a baker
options.rationale: There is no story or humor.

options.label: C
options.text: To compare clay ovens with metal ones

options.label: D
options.text: To explain how bread is baked in a clay oven

items.stem: Why did the author write “Our School Needs a Garden”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author gives reasons why the school “should” build a garden.
explanation.tip: “Should” often signals persuasion.

options.label: A
options.text: To persuade the school to build a garden

options.label: B
options.text: To entertain with a garden adventure

options.label: C
options.text: To describe a garden that already exists
options.rationale: The garden does not exist yet.

options.label: D
options.text: To teach readers how to grow tomatoes

items.stem: Why does the author of “How Honeybees Share Directions” explain how scientists studied bees?

explanation.whyCorrect: The last paragraph explains the source of the information.
explanation.tip: Authors include details for a reason.

options.label: A
options.text: To explain how honey is sold

options.label: B
options.text: To show readers how we know about the bee dances

options.label: C
options.text: To describe the colors of glass

options.label: D
options.text: To convince readers to become scientists

items.stem: Why does the author of “Nature’s Engineers” use headings?

explanation.whyCorrect: Headings like “Building a Dam” divide the article into topics.
explanation.tip: Text features support the author’s purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: To show the beaver’s point of view

options.label: B
options.text: To tell the reader what to believe

options.label: C
options.text: To organize information so readers can find each part easily

options.label: D
options.rationale: Headings organize; they do not add length for its own sake.

items.stem: The author of “The Dripping Taps” ends with: “a small problem, noticed and measured, can lead to a big change.” What purpose does this ending serve?

explanation.whyCorrect: The final sentence turns the event into a general lesson.
explanation.tip: Endings often show the author’s deeper purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: To list the steps the students took

options.label: B
options.rationale: The plumber is not the focus.

options.label: D
options.text: To share a lesson readers can use in their own lives

items.stem: In “The Dripping Taps,” what CAUSED the cup to fill?

explanation.whyCorrect: The dripping tap slowly filled the cup.
explanation.tip: A cause is why something happens.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The plumber fixed the taps later.

items.stem: What was one EFFECT of the class’s signs?

explanation.whyCorrect: Teachers noticed more students turning off the water.
explanation.tip: An effect is what happens because of a cause.

options.label: B
options.text: More students turned off the water while soaping.

options.label: C
options.text: The cup was placed under the tap.

items.stem: Match each cause with its effect.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each effect in the article is caused by something beavers build.
explanation.tip: Look for signal words: because, so, as a result.

pairs.left: The beaver dam slows the stream

pairs.right: Predators cannot easily reach the family

pairs.left: A pond is the only water for miles
pairs.right: Deer and birds travel to drink there

items.stem: In “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven,” why must the oven walls be very hot before the dough is added?

explanation.whyCorrect: The bread is pressed onto the wall and puffs up after a few minutes, which needs a very hot surface.
explanation.tip: Connect a step to its result.

options.label: A
options.text: Hot walls keep insects away from the bread.

options.label: B
options.text: Hot walls make the clay oven stronger.
options.rationale: The text does not say this.

options.label: C
options.text: The bread bakes on the hot wall in only a few minutes.

options.label: D
options.text: Hot walls help the dough rise under the cloth.
options.rationale: The dough rises before it goes in the oven.

items.stem: What is the main idea of “Keeping Bees in the Mountains”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Every paragraph tells about how the families keep bees and make honey.
explanation.tip: The main idea covers the whole text.

options.label: D
options.text: Mountain families carefully keep bees and collect honey.

items.stem: Which detail BEST supports the main idea of “How Honeybees Share Directions”?

explanation.whyCorrect: This detail directly explains how bees share directions.
explanation.tip: Supporting details explain the main idea.

options.label: A
options.text: The direction of the waggle tells bees which way to fly.

items.stem: What is the central idea of “The Dripping Taps”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The text follows the problem, the actions and the result.
explanation.tip: Ask: What is the whole article mostly about?

options.label: B
options.text: Students noticed water being wasted and took steps that saved water.

items.stem: Which TWO details support the main idea of “Nature’s Engineers”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The main idea is that beavers change the land and help other living things.
explanation.tip: Supporting details connect to the main idea.

options.label: A
options.text: Beavers pile sticks, rocks and mud to build dams.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is a detail about wolves, not beavers’ engineering.

options.label: C
options.text: Beaver ponds give frogs, ducks and fish a home.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is a problem, not the main idea.

items.stem: Which sentence would BEST end a summary of the central idea of “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?

explanation.whyCorrect: It captures the whole process from ingredients to finished bread.
explanation.tip: A central idea ties all the steps together.

options.label: A
options.text: Clay ovens are found only in villages.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is a detail, not the central idea.

options.label: C
options.text: Each careful step turns simple ingredients into warm, golden bread.

options.label: D
options.text: The basket is the most important tool.
options.rationale: The basket is a small detail.

items.stem: Which word BEST describes Omar in “The Stick Bridge”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Omar points out the crack and suggests triangles.
explanation.tip: Use actions to describe a character.

items.stem: How does Noura change from the flashback to the present in “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter”?

explanation.whyCorrect: At five the waves frightened her; at ten she fears “the empty months without him.”
explanation.tip: Compare a character at two times.

options.label: A
options.text: She stops fearing the sea but starts fearing time without her father.

options.label: D
options.text: She becomes afraid of the stars.
options.rationale: She plans to count the stars.

items.stem: What does the grandmother’s way of helping in “The Kite Repair” show about her?

explanation.whyCorrect: She brings tape and tissue paper, shares a memory, and they patch the kite “together.”
explanation.tip: A character’s methods reveal their values.

options.label: A
options.text: She prefers new kites to old ones.
options.rationale: She says fixed kites fly better.

options.label: B
options.text: She teaches by working alongside Omar instead of simply fixing it for him.

options.label: C
options.text: She thinks Omar is too young to help.

options.label: D
options.text: She does not care about the festival.
options.rationale: She helps him get ready for it.

items.stem: Which signal words show compare and contrast?

explanation.whyCorrect: Compare-contrast texts use words that show likenesses and differences.
explanation.tip: Learn the signal words for each structure.

items.stem: In “How Honeybees Share Directions,” how are the waggle dance and the round dance DIFFERENT?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article contrasts when each dance is used.
explanation.tip: Contrast = how things are different.

options.label: A
options.text: Both dances are for food that is very far away.
options.rationale: The round dance is for nearby food.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the round dance happens inside the hive.

options.label: C
options.text: The waggle dance is done by scientists.

options.label: D
options.text: The waggle dance is for far food; the round dance is for nearby food.

items.stem: The last paragraph of “Nature’s Engineers” contrasts the problems beavers cause with their benefits.

explanation.whyCorrect: It says dams can flood roads, but scientists argue the benefits are greater.
explanation.tip: “However” often signals a contrast.

items.stem: Match each description of a text with the structure it would use.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each structure fits a different kind of information.
explanation.tip: Ask how the information would best be organized.

pairs.left: Steps for baking bread, from mixing to serving
Students find wasted water and fix it
How two kinds of dances are alike and different

items.stem: Why might an author use a compare-and-contrast structure to write about beaver dams?

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing benefits and problems helps readers weigh both sides.
explanation.tip: Structure should match the author’s purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: To show the benefits of dams alongside the problems they cause

options.label: B
options.text: To tell a story about one beaver family

options.label: C
options.text: To list the steps for building a dam in order

options.label: D
options.text: To describe only what a lodge looks like

items.stem: In a play, what is the list of characters called?

explanation.whyCorrect: Plays begin with a cast list (CHARACTERS).
explanation.tip: Drama words: cast, scene, dialogue, stage directions.

items.stem: What does the stage direction “(KARIM paces back and forth)” show?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pacing back and forth often shows worry.
explanation.tip: Stage directions show feelings through actions.

options.label: A
options.text: Karim is looking for the ranger.
options.rationale: He is waiting while Layla thinks.

options.label: B
options.text: Karim is lost in the dark.

items.stem: How is “The Missing Map” different from a story about the same events?

explanation.whyCorrect: Plays show events through what characters say and do on stage.
explanation.tip: Drama: dialogue + stage directions.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The missing map is the problem.

options.label: D
options.text: It is told through dialogue and stage directions instead of a narrator.

items.stem: Why does Ms. Hassan enter near the END of the play?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her late entrance lets her praise Layla’s “calm head.”
explanation.tip: Think about why a character enters at a certain moment.

options.label: A
options.text: To show that Layla solved the problem before any adult arrived

options.label: B
options.text: To find the map for them
options.rationale: She does not find the map.

options.label: D
options.text: To tell them they took the wrong trail

items.stem: Which words from “Night Rain” help you HEAR the rain?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tapping is a sound.
explanation.tip: Imagery can appeal to hearing.

items.stem: In “Night Rain,” what are the “blurry moons”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “The lamps are blurry moons” compares the lamps to moons.
explanation.tip: Read the whole line to see what is being compared.

options.label: B
options.rationale: There is only one moon; the lamps are being described.

options.label: C
options.text: The street lamps seen through the rain

items.stem: “The bread puffs up and turns golden brown” helps the reader picture the bread baking.

explanation.whyCorrect: You can see the bread rising and changing color.
explanation.tip: Imagery helps you see changes.

items.stem: Which sense does “I pull my blanket to my chin” appeal to?

explanation.whyCorrect: You can feel the blanket being pulled up.
explanation.tip: Ask which sense the words use.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This line is about feeling the blanket.

items.stem: How does the imagery in the last stanza of “Night Rain” change the feeling of the poem?

explanation.whyCorrect: Images like “singing me to sleep” and “soft and silver feet” create a cozy, peaceful feeling.
explanation.tip: Notice how images in the final stanza shape the mood.

options.label: A
options.text: It makes the rain feel gentle and comforting as the speaker falls asleep.

options.label: B
options.text: It makes the rain feel loud and frightening.
options.rationale: The rain is “singing me to sleep.”

options.label: C
options.text: It shows that the rain has stopped.
options.rationale: The speaker still listens to the beat.

items.stem: Why does Omar kick a stone in “The Kite Repair”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Kicking a stone right after saying “It’s ruined” shows frustration.
explanation.tip: Actions show feelings.

options.label: A
options.text: He is happy about the festival.

options.label: B
options.text: He is upset that his kite is ruined.

items.stem: What can you infer about Layla in “The Missing Map”?

explanation.whyCorrect: She sits on a rock, studies the sign, and uses the sun and the lake.
explanation.tip: Combine clues to understand a character.

options.label: A
options.text: She is afraid of the forest.
options.rationale: She sits and studies the sign calmly.

options.label: B
options.text: She knows the trail by heart.
options.rationale: She has to figure it out.

options.label: C
options.text: She stays calm and thinks carefully under pressure.

options.label: D
options.text: She doesn’t care about getting lost.
options.rationale: She works hard to find the way.

items.stem: In “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter,” the white shell will help Noura feel close to her father.

explanation.whyCorrect: He says she will “hear the sea that is carrying me home.”
explanation.tip: Use what characters say to make inferences.

items.stem: Based on “The Dripping Taps,” what can you infer about Mrs. Hassan?

explanation.whyCorrect: After the letter, “the school asked a plumber to fix the leaking taps.”
explanation.tip: Inferences use text evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: She was angry with the class.

options.label: C
options.rationale: A plumber came to fix the taps.

options.label: D
options.text: She took the students’ letter seriously.

items.stem: In “The Kite Repair,” why does Omar know “the patch was the strongest part of all”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The kite flew steadily in strong wind, proving his grandmother’s idea about fixing things.
explanation.tip: Connect the ending to earlier dialogue.

options.label: A
options.text: Because fixing it taught him how the kite works, just as his grandmother said

options.label: B
options.rationale: It held during the gusty wind.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the patch was made of metal
options.rationale: It was made of tissue paper and bamboo.

options.label: D
options.text: Because his grandmother told him the color was best

items.stem: What happens FIRST in “The Missing Map”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The play opens with Layla turning her backpack upside down.
explanation.tip: Track events from beginning to end.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This happens after the map is missing.

options.label: B
options.text: Layla finds that the map is gone.

items.stem: What is the turning point in “The Kite Repair”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Fixing the kite changes the direction of the story.
explanation.tip: The turning point changes things for the better or worse.

options.label: A
options.text: The festival is in two days.

options.label: C
options.text: Omar and his grandmother patch the kite and lengthen its tail.

options.label: D
options.text: The wind pushes the kite into the tree.

items.stem: Put these events from “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter” in the order they are TOLD.

explanation.whyCorrect: The flashback is told in the middle of the story.
explanation.tip: Order of telling can differ from order of happening.

sequence: Noura walks down to the shore.
Her father asks about her first trip to the shore.
Noura remembers being five.
Her father gives her a white shell.
The dhow sails away.

items.stem: Why does the author have the bridge break on Tuesday night instead of during the contest?

explanation.whyCorrect: A break before the contest creates a problem that can still be solved in time.
explanation.tip: Authors place events in an order that builds the plot.

options.label: A
options.text: So the teacher can build a new bridge

options.label: B
options.text: So the contest can be canceled

options.label: C
options.text: So Maya can quit the contest

options.label: D
options.text: So Maya and Omar have time to fix it, which leads to a successful ending.

items.stem: How many lines are in each stanza of “Rain on the Roof”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The poem has two stanzas of four lines each.
explanation.tip: A stanza is a group of lines; count one group.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Count the lines in one group.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Eight is the total for the whole poem.

items.stem: Which lines in “Rain on the Roof” rhyme?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Begins” and “pins” end with the same sound.
explanation.tip: Rhyming words often end lines.

items.stem: What is the rhyme pattern of the first stanza of “Night Rain”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Slow” (line 2) and “below” (line 4) rhyme.
explanation.tip: Mark the last word of each line to find the pattern.

items.stem: How is “Night Rain” organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: Poems are organized in lines and stanzas, often with rhyme.
explanation.tip: Notice the shape of a text on the page.

options.label: A
options.text: as a numbered list of steps

options.label: C
options.text: as a play with a cast list

options.label: D
options.text: in short lines grouped into stanzas, with some rhyming line endings

items.stem: Which sentence is written in FIRST person?

explanation.whyCorrect: First person uses I, me, my, we.
explanation.tip: First person: I/we. Third person: he/she/they.

items.stem: From what point of view is “Night Rain” told?

explanation.whyCorrect: “I pull my blanket to my chin” shows first person.
explanation.tip: Look for pronouns.

options.label: A
options.text: Third person: a narrator describes others.
options.rationale: The speaker says “I pull my blanket.”

options.label: B
options.text: First person: the speaker uses “I” and “my.”

options.label: C
options.text: From the rain’s point of view.
options.rationale: The rain is described, not speaking.

items.stem: “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter” is told in third person.

explanation.whyCorrect: The narrator uses “she” and “her” for Noura.
explanation.tip: Third person uses he, she and they.

items.stem: If “The Kite Repair” were told by the grandmother in first person, what would readers learn?

explanation.whyCorrect: A first-person narrator shares their own thoughts and memories.
explanation.tip: Narrator choice changes what we know.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The narrator change would not explain the wind.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A first-person grandmother would not know them for sure.

options.label: C
options.text: Her own memories and thoughts about fixing kites

items.stem: How would “The Missing Map” feel different if it were told by Karim as a first-person story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Karim paces nervously; as narrator he could tell his feelings directly.
explanation.tip: Imagine the story through another character’s eyes.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Changing narrator does not change form.

options.label: B
options.text: The map would be found in the backpack.

options.label: C
options.text: Layla would no longer be in the story.
options.rationale: She would still be in it.

options.label: D
options.text: Readers would hear how worried Karim felt while Layla was thinking.

items.stem: Which sentence from “The Stick Bridge” shows that the bridge succeeded?

explanation.whyCorrect: Not wobbling under the dictionary shows success.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that directly proves the point.

options.label: C
options.text: “At twelve seconds, there was a sharp snap.”

options.label: D
options.text: “By Tuesday night the bridge looked perfect.”

items.stem: Which detail is evidence that beaver ponds help other animals?

explanation.whyCorrect: This detail names animals that benefit from ponds.
explanation.tip: Evidence must match the idea you are supporting.

options.label: B
options.text: “Frogs lay eggs in the still water, ducks find food.”

options.label: D
options.text: “A beaver family begins by piling sticks.”

items.stem: Which TWO quotations support the idea that Omar’s grandmother is patient?

explanation.whyCorrect: She waits quietly, then works alongside him.
explanation.tip: Find quotations about the right character.

options.label: D
options.text: “She did not say anything at first.”

items.stem: A student says, “The beekeepers care about their bees.” Which quotation is the STRONGEST evidence?

explanation.whyCorrect: Leaving honey for the bees shows concern for their survival.
explanation.tip: The best evidence clearly proves the claim.

options.label: B
options.text: “Honey from these mountains is famous for its rich taste.”

options.label: C
options.text: “They always leave enough honey in the hive for the bees to eat.”

options.label: D
options.text: “Some families have kept honeybees for generations.”

items.stem: Which text feature in “Nature’s Engineers” tells what each section is about?

explanation.whyCorrect: Headings such as “Building a Dam” name each section.
explanation.tip: Headings work like signposts.

options.label: A
options.rationale: There are no captions in this article.

items.stem: Where would you look to find the page about beaver lodges in a long book?

explanation.whyCorrect: The index lists topics alphabetically with page numbers.
explanation.tip: Index = at the back; table of contents = at the front.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This shows the title and author.

items.stem: A diagram of a beaver lodge would MOST help readers understand what?

explanation.whyCorrect: Diagrams show parts and how they fit together.
explanation.tip: Choose the feature that fits the information.

options.label: B
options.text: how the underwater entrances lead into the lodge

options.label: C
options.text: how many frogs live in the pond

options.label: D
options.rationale: A diagram shows parts, not opinions.

items.stem: Match each text feature with what it shows.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each feature presents a different kind of information.
explanation.tip: Ask what each feature is best at showing.

pairs.right: numbers or facts in rows and columns

items.stem: Which heading would BEST fit the last paragraph of “Nature’s Engineers”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph discusses flooding problems and the benefits scientists see.
explanation.tip: A good heading names the paragraph’s main topic.

options.label: A
options.rationale: That heading is already used for the dam section.

items.stem: What lesson does Maya learn in “The Stick Bridge”?

explanation.whyCorrect: She says, “Next time, I’ll listen when you find a crack.”
explanation.tip: A theme is a lesson the character learns.

options.label: D
options.text: Listen when someone points out a problem.

items.stem: Which theme does “The Dripping Taps” suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: The students’ care for the school’s water saved water for everyone.
explanation.tip: A theme is a message the text suggests.

options.label: A
options.text: Taking care of shared resources helps everyone.

options.label: B
options.text: Water is too expensive to use.
options.rationale: The text is about wasting, not cost alone.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The text does not say this.

items.stem: Read: “The desert was so arid that no plants grew for miles.” What does arid mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The clue “no plants grew” shows the land had no water.
explanation.tip: Look for clues that explain the word.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The clue is that no plants grew.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Deserts in the sentence are dry, not cold.

items.stem: The root “tele” means far. What is a telescope?

explanation.tip: Combine root meanings.
