options.text: a tool for seeing things that are far away

items.stem: Match each root with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: These roots appear in many science words.
explanation.tip: Think of examples: biology, geography, aquarium, phone.

items.stem: The Latin root “spect” means look or watch. Which word means “a person who watches an event”?

explanation.whyCorrect: spect (watch) + -ator (one who) = one who watches.
explanation.tip: Find the root, then the suffix.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A translator changes words into another language.

options.label: C
options.rationale: A sculptor shapes art; it has no “spect.”

items.stem: Using roots, what does “geothermal energy” most likely mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: geo (earth) + therm (heat) = heat from the earth.
explanation.tip: Break long words into roots.

options.label: A
options.text: heat energy that comes from inside the earth

options.label: C
options.text: energy from water in the ocean

items.stem: What does “it’s raining cats and dogs” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: This idiom describes very heavy rain.
explanation.tip: Idioms mean something different from their words.

options.label: A
options.text: Pets are playing in the rain.
options.rationale: The words are not about pets.

options.label: D
options.text: Animals are falling from the sky.
options.rationale: An idiom is not meant literally.

items.stem: Kareem was “all ears” when the coach announced the team. What does this mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: “All ears” means paying close attention.
explanation.tip: Use the situation to understand an idiom.

items.stem: What does the adage “The early bird catches the worm” teach?

explanation.whyCorrect: The saying encourages getting a head start.
explanation.tip: Adages are short sayings with life lessons.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Adages are lessons, not facts about birds.

options.label: D
options.text: People who start early often succeed.

items.stem: Match each saying with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: The first two are idioms; the last two are adages.
explanation.tip: Think about when people use each saying.

pairs.right: what you do matters more than what you say
doing something often makes you better

items.stem: In “The bat flew out of the cave,” what does bat mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: Something that flies out of a cave is an animal.
explanation.tip: Use the rest of the sentence to pick the meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: a stick for hitting a ball
options.rationale: A stick does not fly out of a cave.

items.stem: Which sentence uses “light” to mean NOT HEAVY?

explanation.whyCorrect: An empty box that is easy to carry is not heavy.
explanation.tip: Test each meaning in the sentence.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Here it means to set on fire.

options.label: B
options.text: The empty box was light enough to carry.

options.label: D
options.text: The room was full of light.

items.stem: Read: “The coach told the team to stick together.” What does stick mean here?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Stick together” means stay together as a group.
explanation.tip: Notice whether the word is a noun or a verb.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This sentence uses stick as a verb.

items.stem: In which TWO sentences does “ring” mean a sound?

explanation.whyCorrect: Phones and bells make sounds.
explanation.tip: Group sentences by the meaning used.

options.label: C
options.text: The boxers stepped into the ring.
options.rationale: Here it is a place for boxing.

items.stem: Choose the word that means “not tidy”: “Clothes all over the floor made the room ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: un- means not: untidy = not tidy, messy.
explanation.tip: un- = not.

options.label: A
options.rationale: “Tidy” means neat, the opposite of the meaning needed.

items.stem: Choose the word that means “not agree”: “The two friends ____ about the best game.”

explanation.whyCorrect: dis- means not or opposite: disagree.
explanation.tip: dis- = not, opposite of.

items.stem: What does “overcooked” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: over- means too much.
explanation.tip: over- = too much.

items.stem: Which word means “not able to be seen”?

explanation.whyCorrect: in- means not: invisible = not able to be seen.
explanation.tip: Some prefixes mean “not”: un-, in-, im-, dis-, non-.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Visible means able to be seen.

items.stem: What does “teacher” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: -er can mean “one who.”
explanation.tip: -er/-or = one who.

items.stem: What does “joyful” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: -ful means full of.
explanation.tip: -ful = full of.

items.stem: Choose the word that means “in a quiet way”: “The baby slept ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: -ly means “in a … way.”
explanation.tip: -ly often makes an adverb.

items.stem: How does the suffix change the word in “The movement of the ship made me dizzy”?

explanation.whyCorrect: move (verb) + -ment = movement (noun).
explanation.tip: Suffixes can change a word’s part of speech.

options.label: D
options.text: -ment turns the verb “move” into a noun.

items.stem: Which word is a synonym for “brave”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Courageous and brave mean almost the same.
explanation.tip: Synonyms have similar meanings.

items.stem: Which word is an antonym for “ancient”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Ancient means very old; modern means new.
explanation.tip: Antonyms have opposite meanings.

items.stem: Match each word with its ANTONYM.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each pair has opposite meanings.
explanation.tip: Think of the opposite meaning first.

items.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: because: b-e-c-a-u-s-e.
explanation.tip: Say each part slowly: be-cause.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The letters a and u are swapped.

items.stem: Add -ed to the word stop: “The bus ____ at the corner.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Double the final consonant before adding -ed: stopped.
explanation.tip: Short vowel + one consonant: double it before -ed.

items.stem: Which sentence has every word spelled correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: surprised, beautiful and weather are spelled correctly.
explanation.tip: Check tricky words letter by letter.

options.label: A
options.text: We were surprised by the beatiful weather.

options.label: B
options.text: We were surprised by the beautiful wether.

options.label: C
options.text: We were suprised by the beautiful weather.

options.label: D
options.text: We were surprised by the beautiful weather.

items.stem: Add -ing to the word make: “I am ____ a card for my mother.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Drop the silent e before adding -ing: making.
explanation.tip: Silent e + -ing: drop the e.

items.stem: Which word is more precise than “said” in: “‘Help!’ he ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Shouted” shows how he spoke.
explanation.tip: Precise words give clearer pictures.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is not a speaking word.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the most precise language?

explanation.whyCorrect: Specific nouns and details create a clear picture.
explanation.tip: Replace general words with specific ones.

options.label: B
options.text: The golden retriever chewed the red sneaker.

options.label: C
options.text: The animal did something to the thing.

items.stem: Which sentence is the most precise for a science report?

explanation.whyCorrect: Reports use exact numbers and terms.
explanation.tip: Use measurements and specific vocabulary in reports.

options.label: B
options.text: The water did a cool thing.

options.label: C
options.text: The water boiled at 100 degrees Celsius after eight minutes.

options.label: D
options.text: The water got really hot after a while.

items.stem: Which revision of “The big storm made a lot of damage” is MOST precise?

explanation.whyCorrect: Specific words (fierce sandstorm, three palm trees, tore) show exactly what happened.
explanation.tip: Precise language names exact things, numbers and actions.

options.label: B
options.text: The storm was really big and bad.

options.label: C
options.text: The large storm made much damage.

options.label: D
options.text: The fierce sandstorm tore three palm trees from the ground.

items.stem: Which word is an adverb? “The fox crept silently through the grass.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Silently” tells how the fox crept.
explanation.tip: Adverbs tell how, when, where or how often.

items.stem: Choose the adverb that tells HOW OFTEN: “Our family ____ eats dinner together.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Always” tells how often.
explanation.tip: Frequency adverbs: always, usually, often, sometimes, never.

items.stem: Which word does the adverb “almost” describe in “The jar was almost empty”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Almost” tells to what extent the jar was empty.
explanation.tip: Adverbs can describe adjectives.

options.label: A
options.rationale: “Almost” tells how empty, not how it was.

items.stem: Choose the correct form: “Of everyone in the choir, Reem sings ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing many people uses “most” + adverb.
explanation.tip: Two → more; three or more → most.

options.label: B
options.rationale: An adverb form is needed to describe how she sings.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Really” is the adverb that describes “well”; “real” is an adjective.
explanation.tip: Use an adverb to describe another adverb.

items.stem: Which group of words is a dependent clause?

explanation.whyCorrect: It has a subject and verb but begins with “until,” so it cannot stand alone.
explanation.tip: Subordinating conjunctions make clauses dependent.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This has no verb, so it is not a clause.

items.stem: What is the independent clause? “Although the test was long, Salma finished early.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Salma finished early” can stand alone.
explanation.tip: Remove the clause that starts with although/because/when.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is part of the dependent clause.

items.stem: Choose the subordinating conjunction: “Please wait here ____ I get the tickets.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “While” makes a dependent clause about time.
explanation.tip: Subordinating: while, because, although, unless, until.

items.stem: Which revision turns two choppy sentences into ONE complex sentence with the clearest meaning? “The museum was closed. We visited the park.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Because” shows that the closed museum caused the change of plan.
explanation.tip: Choose the conjunction that matches the relationship.

options.label: A
options.text: Because the museum was closed, we visited the park.

options.label: B
options.text: The museum was closed and we visited the park.
options.rationale: This is compound and does not show why.

options.label: C
options.text: Although we visited the park, the museum was closed.

options.label: D
options.text: The museum was closed, we visited the park.

items.stem: Combine: “Hala likes chess. Hala likes painting.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Join the two objects with “and” and remove repeated words.
explanation.tip: Combine words that repeat.

options.label: C
options.text: Hala likes chess Hala likes painting.

items.stem: Combine using an appositive: “Dr. Noor is a dentist. Dr. Noor lives next door.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The appositive “a dentist” renames Dr. Noor and is set off by commas.
explanation.tip: Place the appositive right after the noun.

options.label: A
options.text: Dr. Noor lives next door a dentist.

options.label: B
options.text: Dr. Noor a dentist lives next door.

options.label: C
options.text: Dr. Noor, a dentist, lives next door.

options.label: D
options.text: A dentist lives next door Dr. Noor.

items.stem: Which is the BEST combined sentence? “The cat jumped. The cat landed on the table. The table was wooden.”

explanation.whyCorrect: One clear sentence keeps all the information without repeating.
explanation.tip: Cut repeated words and combine actions.

options.label: A
options.text: The cat jumped and the cat landed and the table was wooden.

options.label: C
options.text: The cat jumped, it landed, the table was wooden.

options.label: D
options.text: The cat jumped onto the wooden table.

items.stem: Combine with a participial phrase: “Ali opened the box. He found a letter.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The -ing phrase describes Ali, the subject that follows it.
explanation.tip: An introductory phrase must describe the subject right after the comma.

options.label: A
options.text: Opening the box, Ali found a letter.

options.label: B
options.text: Opening the box, a letter was found by Ali.
options.rationale: The phrase must describe the subject (Ali).

options.label: C
options.text: Ali opened the box, found a letter.

options.label: D
options.text: Ali opening the box found a letter.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The phrase “Walking to school” must describe the person walking, not the rain (dangling modifier).
explanation.tip: Check who is doing the action in an introductory phrase.

items.correction: I got soaked by the rain, including

items.stem: Choose: “A cheetah is ____ than a horse.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Two animals → -er: faster.
explanation.tip: Two things: -er; many: -est.

items.stem: Choose: “Mount Everest is the ____ mountain in the world.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing with all mountains → highest.
explanation.tip: “In the world” signals a superlative.

items.stem: Which sentence uses “less” or “fewer” correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Apples can be counted, so “fewer.”
explanation.tip: fewer = countable; less = not countable.

options.label: B
options.text: This bag has fewer apples than that one.

options.label: C
options.text: This bag has fewer sugar than that one.
options.rationale: Use “less” with amounts you cannot count.

options.label: D
options.text: This bag has less apples than that one.
options.rationale: Use “fewer” with things you can count.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Use -er OR more, never both.
explanation.tip: Do not double comparatives.

items.stem: Which sentence is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: When comparing exactly two, use the comparative form.
explanation.tip: Two items → comparative, even with “the.”

options.label: A
options.text: Of the two essays, Hadi’s is the strongest.
options.rationale: With only two, use the comparative.

options.label: B
options.text: Of the two essays, Hadi’s is the more stronger.

options.label: C
options.text: Of the two essays, Hadi’s is the stronger.

options.label: D
options.text: Of the two essays, Hadi’s is the most strong.
options.rationale: Use -er for short words, and comparative for two.

items.stem: Which coordinating conjunction can mean “because”? “We hurried home, ____ a storm was coming.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “For” gives a reason, like “because.”
explanation.tip: FANBOYS: for = reason; so = result.

options.label: B
options.rationale: “So” shows a result, not a reason.

items.stem: Which compound sentence is punctuated correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Comma + coordinating conjunction joins two independent clauses.
explanation.tip: Comma before FANBOYS.

options.label: A
options.text: The phone rang, so Majed answered it.

options.label: B
options.text: The phone rang so, Majed answered it.

options.label: C
options.text: The phone rang, Majed answered it.

options.label: D
options.text: The phone, rang so Majed answered it.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses “not only … but also”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Not only won … but also broke” joins two parallel verb phrases.
explanation.tip: Correlative pairs join matching parts.

options.label: A
options.text: Hessa not only won the race also broke the record.

options.label: B
options.text: Hessa not only won the race but also broke the record.

options.label: C
options.text: Hessa not only won the race but broke also the record.

options.label: D
options.text: Not only Hessa won the race but also broke the record.
options.rationale: The pair must sit next to parallel parts.

items.stem: Which TWO words are common nouns? “The scientist studied the volcano near Naples.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Common nouns name general people, places or things.
explanation.tip: Proper nouns are capitalized; common nouns are not.

items.stem: Which word is a concrete noun?

explanation.whyCorrect: You can see and touch a telescope.
explanation.tip: Concrete nouns can be sensed.

items.stem: In “My parents walked the dog around the park,” how is “dog” used?

explanation.whyCorrect: The dog receives the action of “walked.”
explanation.tip: A direct object answers “what?” or “whom?” after the verb.

options.label: C
options.text: as the object of a preposition

items.stem: Which word is the object of a preposition? “The kite drifted over the hills.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Hills” comes after the preposition “over.”
explanation.tip: Preposition + noun = object of the preposition.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a collective noun with a singular verb correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: A committee acting together is one unit, so the verb is singular.
explanation.tip: Collective nouns usually take singular verbs.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Acting as one group, it takes “meets.”

options.label: D
options.text: The committee are meeting every Monday.
options.rationale: Acting as one group, use a singular verb.

items.stem: Which word is a preposition? “The cat hid behind the sofa.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Behind” shows where the cat hid.
explanation.tip: Prepositions show position, direction or time.

items.stem: Choose the preposition of time: “The shop closes ____ midnight.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Use “at” with clock times.
explanation.tip: at + time; on + day; in + month/year.

items.stem: What is the prepositional phrase? “Students from every grade joined the parade.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The phrase begins with “from” and ends with the noun “grade.”
explanation.tip: Preposition → … → noun.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A phrase ends with a noun.

items.stem: Which TWO prepositional phrases tell WHERE? “During the trip, we camped beside a lake under the stars.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Beside” and “under” show location.
explanation.tip: Ask what each phrase answers: when or where?

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the subject and verb.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: After the preposition “to,” use the object pronoun “me.”
explanation.tip: Objects of prepositions use me, him, her, us, them.

items.stem: Choose: “The dog wagged ____ tail.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Its” shows the tail belongs to the dog.
explanation.tip: its = belonging to it.

items.stem: Choose: “Please put your shoes over ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “There” names a place.
explanation.tip: there contains “here”: it is about place.

items.stem: Choose: “____ been to the new science museum?”

explanation.whyCorrect: Who’s = who has.
explanation.tip: who’s = who is / who has.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This needs a verb: who has.

items.stem: Match each word with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: Contractions have apostrophes; possessive pronouns do not.
explanation.tip: Expand each word to test it.

items.stem: Which sentence is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: You’re = you are; your = belonging to you.
explanation.tip: Check each one by expanding it.

options.label: A
options.text: You’re welcome to borrow your cousin’s bike.

options.label: B
options.text: You’re welcome to borrow you’re cousin’s bike.

options.label: C
options.text: Your welcome to borrow your cousin’s bike.

options.label: D
options.text: Your welcome to borrow you’re cousin’s bike.

items.stem: Which word is a pronoun? “They planted three trees.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “They” replaces the names of people.
explanation.tip: Pronouns replace nouns.

items.stem: Choose the possessive pronoun: “The blue umbrella is ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Hers” shows ownership.
explanation.tip: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.

items.stem: Choose the reflexive pronoun: “I taught ____ to juggle.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject.
explanation.tip: -self / -selves.

options.label: B
options.rationale: When the subject is “I,” use myself.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Each” is singular, so the pronoun should be singular: his.
explanation.tip: Pronouns agree in number with their antecedents.

items.stem: Which sentence has a clear pronoun reference?

explanation.whyCorrect: Naming Lina again removes the confusion.
explanation.tip: Make sure each pronoun clearly points to one noun.

options.label: A
options.text: Lina told Sara that she won.

options.label: C
options.text: When Lina met Sara, Lina gave her a gift.

options.label: D
options.text: When Lina met Sara, she gave her a gift.

items.stem: Choose the past progressive: “At eight o’clock, we ____ dinner.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Past progressive = was/were + -ing.
explanation.tip: Progressive tenses show ongoing action.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the future perfect tense?

explanation.whyCorrect: will have + past participle = future perfect.
explanation.tip: Perfect tenses use has/have/had/will have.

options.label: C
options.text: I finished the book in June.

options.label: D
options.text: By June, I will have finished the book.

items.stem: Choose the LINKING verb: “After the long race, Omar ____ exhausted.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Felt” links Omar to the word that describes him, “exhausted.”
explanation.tip: Linking verbs: is, seem, feel, become, look, appear.

options.label: B
options.rationale: “Ran” is an action verb and does not link to “exhausted.”

items.stem: Choose the helping verb: “The guests ____ arriving soon.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Will be arriving” is a verb phrase showing the future.
explanation.tip: Helping verb + main verb = verb phrase.

items.stem: Which sentence has a transitive verb (an action done TO something)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Painted” acts on the object “a mural.”
explanation.tip: Transitive verbs have a direct object.

items.stem: Choose the modal that shows ability: “I ____ swim across the pool now.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Can” shows ability.
explanation.tip: can = able; must = required; should = advised.

items.stem: Which TWO sentences use a verb phrase with a helping verb?

explanation.whyCorrect: has practiced and are reading each contain a helping verb.
explanation.tip: Look for has/have/is/are/will before the main verb.

options.label: C
options.text: The team has practiced every day.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma follows the introductory word “Yes.” (The comma after the name is already correct.)
explanation.tip: Introductory words and direct address both need commas.

items.stem: Which is the abbreviation for “Street”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Street → St.
explanation.tip: Address abbreviations: St., Ave., Rd.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Use a capital S, lowercase t and a period.

items.stem: How should a song title be written?

explanation.whyCorrect: Short works (songs, poems, articles) use quotation marks.
explanation.tip: Short works → quotation marks.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Titles are not written in all caps.

items.stem: Which sentence writes a magazine title and an article title correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Article titles take quotation marks; magazine titles are italicized.
explanation.tip: Part → quotes; whole → italics.

options.label: A
options.text: I read Saving the Reefs in “Ocean World.”
options.rationale: Reversed: article in quotes, magazine in italics.

options.label: B
options.text: I read Saving The Reefs in ocean world.

options.label: C
options.text: I read “saving the reefs” in Ocean World.

options.label: D
options.text: I read “Saving the Reefs” in Ocean World.

items.stem: Which date uses abbreviations correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Abbreviated days and months keep a capital letter and take a period.
explanation.tip: Mon., Tues., Jan., Feb.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Only the first letter is capitalized.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Abbreviations of days and months are capitalized.

items.stem: Which sentence is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Title abbreviation with a period; book title italicized with capitals.
explanation.tip: Check abbreviation, marks and capitals.

options.label: A
options.text: Dr Hamid’s book, “The Desert Garden,” won an award.
options.rationale: Book titles are italicized; Dr. needs a period.

options.label: B
options.text: Dr. Hamid’s book, The Desert Garden, won an award.

options.label: C
options.text: Dr. Hamid’s book, the Desert Garden, won an award.
options.rationale: Capitalize the first word of a title.

options.label: D
options.text: dr. Hamid’s book, The desert garden, won an award.

items.stem: What is the main purpose of “Why the Moon Changes Shape”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article explains moon phases.
explanation.tip: Ask: inform, persuade or entertain?

options.label: A
options.text: to tell a story about astronauts

options.label: B
options.text: to describe how calendars are printed

options.label: C
options.text: to explain why the Moon looks different during the month

options.label: D
options.text: to persuade readers to visit space

items.stem: Why does the author of “Catching Water in the Desert” begin by describing rare rain?

explanation.whyCorrect: The opening sets up the problem of saving water.
explanation.tip: Openings often introduce the problem or topic.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: to show the problem that the solutions address

items.stem: How is the purpose of the news report different from Rania’s journal in “The Storm: Two Accounts”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The report lists wind speeds and outages; the journal says “I was scared.”
explanation.tip: Compare purpose through the details each writer chooses.

options.label: A
options.text: The report informs with facts; the journal shares personal feelings.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The report gives numbers and facts.

options.label: D
options.rationale: It reports real events in the scenario.

items.stem: Why does the turtle article include a glossary?

explanation.whyCorrect: The glossary defines “hatchling.”
explanation.tip: Text features support the author’s purpose.

options.label: B
options.text: to help readers understand a key word

options.label: D
options.text: to persuade readers to protect turtles

items.stem: The author of “Catching Water in the Desert” ends with engineers combining ancient ideas and modern materials. What point of view does this ending suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: The final sentence shows respect for ancient methods and hope for improvement.
explanation.tip: Endings often reveal the author’s attitude.

options.label: A
options.text: Modern materials make ancient ideas useless.
options.rationale: The author says they are combined.

options.label: C
options.text: Old solutions are still valuable and can be improved, not replaced.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The text shows it is possible.

items.stem: In “Catching Water in the Desert,” what causes rainwater to disappear quickly?

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says water “rushes over the hard, dry ground and disappears.”
explanation.tip: Find what makes something happen.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Check dams help it soak in.

options.label: D
options.text: It rushes over hard, dry ground.

items.stem: What is an effect of check dams?

explanation.whyCorrect: The walls slow the water, “giving it time to soak into the soil.”
explanation.tip: Signal words like “giving” can show effects.

options.label: A
options.text: Water soaks into the soil instead of running away.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Check dams do not change rainfall.

items.stem: In “The Storm: Two Accounts,” what was an effect of the 120 millimeters of rain?

explanation.whyCorrect: Heavy rain in six hours flooded streets.
explanation.tip: Connect each cause with its direct result.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Wind is not caused by rain.

options.label: C
options.rationale: That was the result of repairs.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Lightning is not caused by rain.

items.stem: Match each cause from the turtle article with its effect.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each effect in the article follows from a condition on the beach.
explanation.tip: Use “because” to test each pair.

pairs.left: Eggs stay warm for about two months

items.stem: What is the central idea of “Why the Moon Changes Shape”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Every paragraph explains our changing view of the lit half.
explanation.tip: The central idea connects all paragraphs.

options.label: C
options.text: The Moon’s shape seems to change because we see different amounts of its lit half.

options.label: D
options.text: The Moon makes its own light.

items.stem: Which detail BEST supports the central idea of the turtle article?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article is about how Red Sea turtles nest and the dangers hatchlings face.
explanation.tip: Supporting details develop the main idea.

options.label: A
options.text: Hatchling is defined in the glossary.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is a text feature, not a key detail.

options.label: D
options.text: Females lay about one hundred eggs on sandy beaches.

items.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “The Last Repair”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The story turns on Khalid calming himself and finding the spring.
explanation.tip: Ask what the whole story is mostly about.

options.label: A
options.text: Under pressure, Khalid succeeds by remembering to slow down.

options.label: C
options.text: Jeddah smells of sea salt and cardamom.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This explains why Khalid works alone.

items.stem: Which word BEST describes Dana in “The Second Try”?

explanation.whyCorrect: She whispers encouragement and gives advice.
explanation.tip: Use dialogue to describe a character.

items.stem: How does Salma solve the problem in “The Two Wells”?

explanation.whyCorrect: She notices the green grove and digs there.
explanation.tip: Characters’ actions show their traits.

options.label: C
options.text: She observes carefully and leads the children to dig a new well.

options.label: D
options.text: She asks the king for help.

items.stem: What does Yusuf’s question about the baking soda show about him?

explanation.whyCorrect: Instead of panicking, he checks the steps.
explanation.tip: Problem-solving shows character.

options.label: D
options.text: He thinks logically when something goes wrong.

items.stem: How does Khalid change between the moment the spring disappears and the end of “The Last Repair”?

explanation.whyCorrect: He knocks screws over in panic, then counts to ten and searches slowly.
explanation.tip: Track how a character’s behavior changes.

options.label: A
options.text: He moves from panic to calm, careful action.

options.label: B
options.text: He gives up and asks the captain for help.

options.label: C
options.text: He stays panicked until the end.

options.label: D
options.text: He moves from calm to anger.
options.rationale: He starts in panic and becomes calm.

items.stem: What topic do both accounts in “The Storm: Two Accounts” describe?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both are dated March 12 and describe the storm.
explanation.tip: Find the shared topic first.

options.label: C
options.rationale: A car is flooded but there is no accident.

items.stem: Which detail appears in BOTH accounts?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rania says the street was a river; the report says six streets flooded.
explanation.tip: Look for facts both writers mention.

options.label: A
options.text: Rania hid in her sister’s bed.

options.label: C
options.text: There was flooding in the streets.

items.stem: Using BOTH articles in the paired passage, which statement is true?

explanation.whyCorrect: The texts differ in purpose and structure.
explanation.tip: Compare purpose and structure across texts.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Only Text 2 is about turtles, and it informs.

options.label: D
options.text: One argues for gardens with reasons; the other explains facts about turtles with headings.

items.stem: A student writes a report about the storm’s effect on families. Why is using BOTH accounts better than using one?

explanation.whyCorrect: Combining facts and personal experience gives a fuller picture.
explanation.tip: Different sources add different kinds of information.

options.label: A
options.text: The report gives exact facts, and the journal shows how it felt to live through it.

options.label: C
options.rationale: They give different kinds of information.

items.stem: Why does the narrator of “The Second Try” leave the note cards in the desk?

explanation.whyCorrect: Dana advised, “Just talk like you’re telling me.”
explanation.tip: Link actions to earlier advice.

options.label: B
options.text: To speak naturally instead of reading

options.label: D
options.rationale: The narrator chose to leave them.

items.stem: What can you infer about Hamdan at the start of “The Two Wells”?

explanation.whyCorrect: He charges a silver coin even as poor families go thirsty.
explanation.tip: Actions reveal values.

options.label: C
options.text: He cares more about money than about his neighbors.

items.stem: In “The Last Repair,” the captain is pleased with Khalid’s work.

explanation.whyCorrect: “The captain’s smile told him everything.”
explanation.tip: Facial expressions support inferences.

items.stem: Why did the news report most likely include “No injuries were reported”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Reports often include safety information readers want.
explanation.tip: Think about what readers need to know.

options.label: A
options.text: To show the storm was weak

options.label: B
options.rationale: The report does not mention her.

options.label: D
options.text: To reassure readers that no one was hurt

items.stem: In “City Morning,” why does the speaker say “That minute, friend, is mine”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The last stanza contrasts the quiet golden sky with the loud day.
explanation.tip: Read the final lines in context.

options.label: A
options.text: The speaker treasures a quiet moment before the busy day.

options.label: B
options.text: The speaker is late for work.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The speaker addresses a friend warmly.

items.stem: How many stanzas are in “Harbor at Dawn”?

explanation.whyCorrect: There are two groups of four lines.
explanation.tip: Stanzas are separated by blank lines.

options.label: A
options.rationale: There is a break between two groups of lines.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Eight is the number of lines.

items.stem: Which pair of words rhymes in “Harbor at Dawn”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Light” and “night” end lines 1 and 2 and rhyme.
explanation.tip: Check line endings.

items.stem: What is the rhyme pattern of “Harbor at Dawn”?

explanation.whyCorrect: light/night, thread/red, knees/breeze, wet/net.
explanation.tip: Couplets: two rhyming lines in a row.

items.stem: In “City Morning,” how does the sentence run from stanza 2 into stanza 3?

explanation.whyCorrect: “don’t you miss / The quiet way…” carries the thought into stanza 3 (enjambment).
explanation.tip: Lines and stanzas can continue a sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: The question continues across the stanza break.

options.label: D
options.text: Each stanza is a separate sentence.

items.stem: How does the structure of “Harbor at Dawn” support its meaning?

explanation.whyCorrect: Stanza 1 shows sky and town; stanza 2 the harbor sounds and boats waking.
explanation.tip: Ask how form and meaning work together.

options.label: A
options.text: The stanzas are numbered steps in a process.
options.rationale: It is a description, not steps.

options.label: B
options.text: Two short rhyming stanzas move from the sky to the boats, like a scene slowly waking.

options.label: C
options.text: Each stanza tells a different character’s story.

items.stem: From what point of view is “The Two Wells” told?

explanation.whyCorrect: The narrator uses she, he and they.
explanation.tip: Pronouns reveal point of view.

items.stem: How does Rania’s first-person journal affect what readers learn?

explanation.whyCorrect: First person shares the narrator’s inner thoughts.
explanation.tip: Narrator choice shapes information.

options.label: D
options.text: Readers learn her personal feelings, like fear and amazement.

items.stem: If “The Volcano That Would Not Erupt” were told by Ms. Dawood, what might change?

explanation.whyCorrect: A different narrator knows and notices different things.
explanation.tip: Imagine the story through another character.

options.label: A
options.text: We would see the scene from the teacher’s view, perhaps without knowing about the missing baking soda.

options.label: B
options.text: The science fair would be canceled.

options.label: D
options.text: The volcano would be made of metal.

items.stem: What is the solution in “The Two Wells”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The new well gives free water.
explanation.tip: Solution = what fixes the problem.

options.label: B
options.text: The children dig a new well.

options.label: D
options.rationale: That is an effect of the problem.

items.stem: In the turtle article, the author gives a full solution for the problem of bright lights.

explanation.whyCorrect: The section explains the danger but does not describe a solution.
explanation.tip: Not every problem in a text is solved.

items.stem: How do cisterns and check dams solve the SAME problem in different ways?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both save scarce rainwater, using storage or soil.
explanation.tip: Compare how two solutions work.

options.label: C
options.text: Cisterns store water in tanks; check dams help water soak into the ground.

items.stem: Why does the author of the garden letter offer starting small with containers?

explanation.whyCorrect: This answers the cost objection with a practical solution.
explanation.tip: Persuasive texts can include solutions to objections.

options.label: D
options.text: To solve the problem that gardens may cost too much

items.stem: In “The Last Repair,” what happens right after the spring disappears?

explanation.whyCorrect: His panic follows immediately.
explanation.tip: Track time order.

options.label: A
options.text: Khalid knocks a box of screws to the floor.

items.stem: Put the steps of collecting rainwater in a cistern in order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article describes the path from roof to tank.
explanation.tip: Follow the path of the water.

sequence: Rain falls on the rooftop.
Gutters guide the water into pipes.
Pipes lead the water to the cistern.
The covered tank keeps the water cool.

items.stem: Put the events in the news report in time order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The report moves from the storm to the recovery.
explanation.tip: Use times as clues.

sequence: The storm strikes early Thursday morning.
Streets flood and power goes out.
City crews begin clearing drains at 7 a.m.
Electricity is restored by noon.

items.stem: After a full moon, what happens next in the cycle described in the article?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article says, “Then the pattern reverses until the next new moon.”
explanation.tip: Cycles return to their starting point.

options.label: B
options.text: The pattern reverses until the next new moon.

options.label: C
options.text: A full moon happens again the next night.

options.label: D
options.text: The Moon becomes a crescent immediately.

items.stem: Which line from “City Morning” uses onomatopoeia?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Hiss” imitates a sound.
explanation.tip: Onomatopoeia = sound words.

items.stem: Which words in “Harbor at Dawn” show alliteration?

explanation.whyCorrect: Many words repeat the s sound: stitch, sky, silver, salt.
explanation.tip: Listen for repeated beginning sounds.

options.label: A
options.rationale: These words begin with different sounds.

options.label: B
options.text: “the last stars folding up the night”

options.label: D
options.text: “salt and diesel… stitch the sky with silver”

items.stem: Which sound device appears in “Ropes creak”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Creak” imitates the sound of ropes.
explanation.tip: Sound words imitate real sounds.

options.label: D
options.rationale: There is no rhyme in these two words.

items.stem: Match each example from “City Morning” with its sound device.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each example uses sound in a different way.
explanation.tip: Say each aloud.

items.stem: Why does the poet use the alliteration “busy, bustling, buzzing throng”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The fast repeated b sounds echo the energy of the crowd.
explanation.tip: Sound devices support meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: The repeated b sounds create a noisy, rushing feeling like a crowd.

items.stem: Which sentence shows that the narrator of “The Second Try” was nervous at first?

explanation.whyCorrect: Shaking hands show nervousness.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that directly shows the idea.

items.stem: Which sentence supports the idea that cisterns are an old invention?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two-thousand-year-old cisterns prove they are ancient.
explanation.tip: Match evidence to the claim.

options.label: B
options.text: “Rain falls only a few times each year.”

options.label: D
options.text: “Archaeologists have found cisterns that are more than two thousand years old.”

items.stem: Which evidence shows that the villagers valued sharing?

explanation.whyCorrect: The villagers choose to share the new well freely.
explanation.tip: Quote words that prove the point.

options.label: A
options.text: “they shared it freely, as they always had.”

items.stem: Which TWO quotations support the idea that the storm was serious?

explanation.whyCorrect: High winds and many outages show a serious storm.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that fits the claim.

options.label: B
options.text: “winds of up to 90 kilometers per hour”

options.label: D
options.text: “electricity was restored to most homes by noon.”

items.stem: A student claims, “Layla learned from her mistake.” Which quotation is the STRONGEST evidence?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her final line states what she learned.
explanation.tip: The best evidence directly proves the claim.

options.label: B
options.text: “You check every step, and you never panic.”

options.label: D
options.text: “The baking soda… is still in my backpack.”
options.rationale: This shows the mistake, not the lesson.

items.stem: What is a theme of “The Two Wells”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Hamdan admits shared water is worth more than sold water.
explanation.tip: Theme = message about life.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is a fact, not a theme.

options.label: C
options.text: Sharing is worth more than profit.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Hamdan is not kind at first.

items.stem: Which detail BEST supports the theme of “The Last Repair”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The uncle’s lesson about patience is the message of the story.
explanation.tip: Find the line that states the lesson.

options.label: C
options.text: “The narrow lanes smelled of sea salt.”

options.label: D
options.text: “A watchmaker’s hands must be slower than the sand.”

items.stem: What theme does “The Volcano That Would Not Erupt” express?

explanation.whyCorrect: Layla’s last line states the lesson: check every step and never panic.
explanation.tip: A theme is a message about life.

options.label: A
options.text: Staying calm and checking your work helps you solve problems.

items.stem: How does the turtle memory in “The Second Try” help develop the theme?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Being knocked back… isn’t the same as being beaten.”
explanation.tip: Symbols and memories can carry themes.

options.label: A
options.text: It explains how to give a speech.

options.label: B
options.text: The turtles keep going after being knocked back, just as the narrator does.

options.label: D
options.rationale: It is central to the theme.

items.stem: Read: “The puppy was so lethargic after the long walk that it slept all afternoon.” What does lethargic mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The clue “slept all afternoon” shows tiredness.
explanation.tip: Use the effect described in the sentence.

items.stem: Read: “Unlike his loquacious cousin, who chatted for hours, Tamer rarely spoke more than a few words.” What does loquacious mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The contrast word “Unlike” and “chatted for hours” show the meaning.
explanation.tip: Contrast clues show the opposite of a nearby word.

items.stem: “The baker sings a sugared song.” What kind of figurative language describes the song as “sugared”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The song is described as if it were sweet like sugar.
explanation.tip: Metaphors compare without like or as.

options.label: A
options.text: a metaphor suggesting the song is sweet

options.label: C
options.rationale: Songs are not made of sugar.

items.stem: In “Harbor at Dawn,” what does “The harbor yawns” suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: Personification gives the harbor a human action at dawn.
explanation.tip: Personification gives human traits to things.

options.label: B
options.text: The harbor is just waking up, like a sleepy person.

options.label: C
options.text: The harbor is wide open and empty forever.

options.label: D
options.text: The harbor makes a loud noise.

items.stem: The Latin root “aqua” means water. Which word names a tank for fish?

explanation.whyCorrect: aqua (water) + -arium (place) = aquarium.
explanation.tip: Roots carry the core meaning.

items.stem: The Greek root “chron” means time. What is a chronological list?

explanation.whyCorrect: chron (time) → in the order things happened.
explanation.tip: Think of chronicle, chronometer.

items.stem: Using roots, what does “benevolent” most likely mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: bene (good) + vol (wish) = wishing good.
explanation.tip: Combine root meanings to define new words.

options.label: A
options.text: wishing to do good for others

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “The hikers walked for an ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Hour” means sixty minutes.
explanation.tip: Homophones sound alike but differ in meaning.

items.stem: In which sentence does “lead” rhyme with “bed”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Lead (the metal or pencil core) rhymes with bed.
explanation.tip: Homographs can have different pronunciations.

options.label: A
options.text: Please lead the line to lunch.

options.label: B
options.text: The pencil’s lead broke during the test.

options.label: D
options.text: The guide will lead us up the trail.

items.stem: “The farm was used to produce produce.” How do the two words differ?

explanation.whyCorrect: pro-DUCE (verb) vs. PRO-duce (noun).
explanation.tip: Stress can change with part of speech.

options.label: C
options.text: The first is a verb (make); the second is a noun (fruits and vegetables), with different stress.

options.label: D
options.rationale: One is an action and one is food.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A principal is the head of a school; a principle is a rule or belief.
explanation.tip: Principal = a pal who leads the school.

items.stem: What does “under the weather” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Under the weather” means feeling unwell.
explanation.tip: Idioms are not literal.

items.stem: Maryam “spilled the beans” about the surprise party. What did she do?

explanation.whyCorrect: To spill the beans is to reveal a secret.
explanation.tip: Use context to understand idioms.

items.stem: Match each proverb with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: Proverbs share advice about life.
explanation.tip: Think of a situation where each applies.

pairs.left: Don’t judge a book by its cover

pairs.right: doing something late is better than not doing it

items.stem: Choose the word that means “not possible”: “Climbing that cliff without ropes is ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: im- means not: impossible = not possible.
explanation.tip: Before p, b or m, “not” is often spelled im-.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is not a word; the prefix for “possible” is im-.

items.stem: Choose the word that means “to spell wrongly”: “Be careful not to ____ the new words.”

explanation.whyCorrect: mis- means wrongly.
explanation.tip: mis- = wrongly.

items.stem: What does “nonfiction” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: non- means not: not fiction.
explanation.tip: non- = not.

options.label: B
options.text: writing that is not made up

options.label: D
options.rationale: Poems can be fiction or not.

items.stem: Match each prefix with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: Prefixes change the meaning of base words.
explanation.tip: Use example words: preview, disagree, overflow, nonstop.

items.stem: Which word means “to judge someone before knowing them”?

explanation.whyCorrect: pre- (before) + judge = judge beforehand.
explanation.tip: Choose the prefix that matches the meaning.

items.stem: Which word is a synonym for “shout”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Shout and yell both mean to speak very loudly.
explanation.tip: Synonyms = similar meanings.

items.stem: Which word is an antonym for “visible”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Visible means able to be seen; hidden means not seen.
explanation.tip: Antonyms = opposites.

items.stem: Which word is the BEST synonym for “furious”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Furious and enraged both mean extremely angry.
explanation.tip: Match the strength of the feeling.

items.stem: Match each word with its SYNONYM.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each pair has a similar meaning.
explanation.tip: Synonyms can replace each other in a sentence.

items.stem: Which pair shows antonyms with the strongest contrast?

explanation.whyCorrect: Scorching and freezing are extreme opposites.
explanation.tip: Antonyms can show degrees of contrast.

items.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: neighbor: n-e-i-g-h-b-o-r.
explanation.tip: Weigh and neighbor: ei says long a.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is British spelling; use neighbor here.

items.stem: Add -ly to happy: “The children played ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Change y to i before adding -ly: happily.
explanation.tip: Consonant + y → i before a suffix.

items.stem: Which sentence has every word spelled correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: committee, definitely, receive, separate are tricky words spelled correctly.
explanation.tip: Check commonly misspelled words carefully.

options.label: A
options.text: Our committee will definitely receive the separate reports.

options.label: B
options.text: Our comittee will definitely receive the separate reports.
options.rationale: committee has double m and double t.

options.label: C
options.text: Our committee will definitely recieve the seperate reports.

options.label: D
options.text: Our committee will definately receive the separate reports.

items.stem: Which word is more precise than “walked” in: “The tired hiker ____ up the hill”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Trudged” shows slow, heavy walking.
explanation.tip: Choose verbs that show how.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the most precise language?

explanation.whyCorrect: Specific nouns (hawk, lizard) and verbs (swooped, snatched) create a clear picture.
explanation.tip: Replace general words with exact ones.

options.label: C
options.text: The hawk swooped down and snatched a lizard from the rock.

options.label: D
options.text: The bird went down and got something.

items.stem: Which domain-specific word fits a science report? “The water turned into vapor through ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Evaporation is the scientific term.
explanation.tip: Use subject-specific vocabulary in reports.

items.stem: Which revision is MOST precise for a report? “A lot of people came to the event.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Exact numbers and specific nouns make writing precise.
explanation.tip: Replace “a lot” with a number.

options.label: A
options.text: About 1,200 visitors attended the science fair.

options.label: D
options.text: Tons of people came to the event.

items.stem: Which sentence uses precise language to create a formal tone?

explanation.whyCorrect: Precise verbs (postponed) and nouns (sandstorm warning) suit formal writing.
explanation.tip: Formal writing avoids slang.

options.label: A
options.text: They put off the meeting ’cause of the storm thing.

options.label: B
options.text: The committee postponed the meeting because of the sandstorm warning.

options.label: C
options.text: The meeting got moved, like, later.

items.stem: Which word describes the noun “camel” in “The patient camel waited in the shade”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Patient” tells what kind of camel.
explanation.tip: Adjectives describe nouns.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a predicate adjective?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Cool” follows the linking verb “felt” and describes the subject.
explanation.tip: Predicate adjectives follow linking verbs.

options.label: A
options.text: The cool air arrived after sunset.

options.label: D
options.text: The desert air felt cool after sunset.

items.stem: Choose the correct form: “Of the two routes, the coastal road is ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing exactly two routes: more scenic.
explanation.tip: Two → comparative; three+ → superlative.

options.label: C
options.rationale: With two items, use the comparative.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: No comma between adjectives that are not coordinate (you would not say “new and wooden jewelry box” naturally), and never a comma before the noun.
explanation.tip: Use commas only between coordinate adjectives, and never before the noun.

items.stem: Which clause is dependent? “Unless the bus arrives soon, we will be late.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Unless” makes the clause dependent.
explanation.tip: Dependent clauses begin with subordinating conjunctions or relative pronouns.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is part of the dependent clause.

items.stem: Which sentence contains a relative clause?

explanation.whyCorrect: “who trained us” describes the coach.
explanation.tip: Relative clauses begin with who, which, that, whose.

options.label: A
options.text: The coach retired, and we were sad.

options.label: B
options.text: The coach who trained us retired this year.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the coach retired, we were sad.

items.stem: Choose the relative pronoun: “The book ____ cover is torn belongs to the library.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Whose” shows the cover belongs to the book.
explanation.tip: whose = possession.

items.stem: Which sentence is compound-complex?

explanation.whyCorrect: It has two independent clauses and one dependent clause.
explanation.tip: Compound-complex = 2+ independent + 1+ dependent.

options.label: B
options.text: We lit candles, and Mariam told stories.

options.label: C
options.text: When the power failed, we lit candles, and Mariam told stories.

options.label: D
options.text: When the power failed, we lit candles.

items.stem: Which revision places the relative clause correctly to avoid confusion?

explanation.whyCorrect: A relative clause should sit right after the noun it describes.
explanation.tip: Place modifiers next to what they modify.

options.label: A
options.text: That my aunt made, the vase sat on the shelf.

options.label: B
options.text: The vase sat that my aunt made on the shelf.

options.label: C
options.text: The vase sat on the shelf that my aunt made.
options.rationale: This suggests the aunt made the shelf.

options.label: D
options.text: The vase that my aunt made sat on the shelf.

items.stem: Which is a fragment?

explanation.whyCorrect: A dependent clause alone is a fragment.
explanation.tip: Ask: Because… what happened?

options.label: A
options.text: Because the robotics club stayed late.

items.stem: Which is a comma splice?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two independent clauses joined only by a comma form a comma splice.
explanation.tip: Comma alone ≠ enough to join sentences.

options.label: A
options.text: The reef is fragile, so it needs protection.

options.label: B
options.text: The reef is fragile, it needs protection.

options.label: D
options.text: The reef is fragile; it needs protection.

items.stem: Which revision fixes the run-on? “Scientists grow corals in nurseries they transplant them to reefs.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A semicolon correctly joins the two clauses.
explanation.tip: Use a period, semicolon, or comma + conjunction.

options.label: A
options.text: Scientists grow corals in nurseries, they transplant them to reefs.

options.label: B
options.text: Scientists grow corals. In nurseries they transplant them to reefs.

options.label: C
options.text: Scientists grow corals in nurseries; then they transplant them to reefs.

items.stem: What is the role of the first paragraph of the four-day week article?

explanation.whyCorrect: Introductions present the topic and claim.
explanation.tip: Ask what each paragraph does.

options.label: D
options.text: It introduces the issue and states the author’s cautious claim.

items.stem: How does paragraph 3 of the coral article fit into the whole text?

explanation.whyCorrect: Paragraph 2 sets up how the partnership works; paragraph 3 shows how it breaks down.
explanation.tip: Look at how ideas build.

options.label: A
options.text: It explains the main threat (bleaching) after paragraph 2 explains the partnership.

items.stem: Why does Huda place her solution paragraph near the end of her letter?

explanation.whyCorrect: Problem → value → counterargument → solution → appeal.
explanation.tip: Structure supports persuasion.

options.label: B
options.text: To offer a practical alternative after explaining the souq’s value and answering the council

items.stem: What does the sentence “However, visitors travel to see what is special about a place” do in the letter?

explanation.whyCorrect: “However” signals a rebuttal.
explanation.tip: Transition words show how parts connect.

options.label: C
options.text: It turns to a counterargument against the council’s claim.

items.stem: How do the second and third paragraphs of the four-day week article differ in focus?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each body paragraph tests one supporters’ claim.
explanation.tip: Compare how sections contribute differently.

options.label: D
options.text: Paragraph 2 examines learning and fatigue; paragraph 3 examines cost savings.

items.stem: What is the climax of “The Last Bus Home”?

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the turning point that changes his understanding.
explanation.tip: The climax is the turning point.

options.label: A
options.text: Yusuf finds Mariam waiting at the bakery and learns everyone was worried, not angry.

items.stem: How does the scene break in “The Interview” affect the plot?

explanation.whyCorrect: Scene 2 begins two hours later with a full notebook.
explanation.tip: Scene breaks shape pacing.

options.label: A
options.text: It changes the setting to a classroom.

options.label: B
options.text: It skips the long interview and shows its result, highlighting the change.

options.label: C
options.text: It ends the conflict before it starts.
options.rationale: The conflict is resolved across the scenes.

items.stem: Which event is the resolution of “The New Field”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The final paragraph resolves her struggle.
explanation.tip: Resolution follows the climax.

options.label: B
options.text: The coach tosses her a ball.

options.label: C
options.text: Her teammates cheer her first goal and she stops comparing fields.

items.stem: Why does the author reveal that Mariam is at the bakery only halfway through Yusuf’s walk?

explanation.whyCorrect: Delaying the reveal builds tension and contrast.
explanation.tip: Event order shapes the reader’s experience.

options.label: D
options.text: So Yusuf and the reader expect anger, making the surprise of worry and care stronger

items.stem: Which repeated word links the stanzas of “Ladder” together?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Each rung,” “each one,” “each step,” “each branch” repeat across the poem.
explanation.tip: Poets use repetition to connect stanzas.

options.label: B
options.rationale: It appears only in the first line.

options.label: D
options.rationale: It appears only in the last stanza.

items.stem: “Desert Night” does not rhyme regularly. What is this form called?

explanation.whyCorrect: Free verse has no regular rhyme or meter.
explanation.tip: Poems can be structured or free.

items.stem: In “Ladder,” what does each rung represent?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Each one a year he gave to me.”
explanation.tip: Look for the poem’s central metaphor.

options.label: B
options.text: a branch of the apple tree

options.label: C
options.text: a year of the speaker’s life with the grandfather

options.label: D
options.rationale: The tree fell in a storm.

items.stem: How does the final stanza of “Ladder” change the poem’s time frame?

explanation.whyCorrect: “I climb it now” shifts to the present.
explanation.tip: Watch for time words.

options.label: D
options.text: It moves from past memories to the speaker climbing in the present.

items.stem: How does the structure of “Transplant” mirror its meaning?

explanation.whyCorrect: The turn between stanzas matches the turn from struggle to growth.
explanation.tip: Form can echo meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: Stanza 1 shows the move and struggle; stanza 2 turns to new growth.

options.label: C
options.text: Each stanza is about a different tree.

items.stem: Which line from “Ladder” shows that the poem is told in the first person?

explanation.whyCorrect: “My” shows the speaker is telling about their own life.
explanation.tip: First person uses I, me, my, we.

options.label: A
options.text: “from the branches of a storm-felled tree”

items.stem: What does Sara’s aside reveal that Mr. Aziz does not know?

explanation.whyCorrect: Asides show a character’s private view to the audience.
explanation.tip: Dramatic irony: the audience knows more.

options.label: C
options.text: She is frustrated because she needs much longer answers.

items.stem: How does the narration of “The New Field” shape what readers know?

explanation.whyCorrect: “She missed the flat green field” shows her inner view.
explanation.tip: Third-person limited follows one character.

options.label: A
options.text: It is told in first person by Yasmin.

options.label: C
options.text: It is told by the coach.

options.label: D
options.text: It follows Yasmin’s feelings closely while telling the story in third person.

items.stem: How would “The Last Bus Home” change if told from Mariam’s point of view?

explanation.whyCorrect: Point of view controls what information is revealed and when.
explanation.tip: Consider what each narrator knows.

options.label: A
options.text: Readers would know from the start that the family is worried, not angry, which removes the surprise.

items.stem: Why might the playwright let Sara speak directly to the audience in an aside?

explanation.whyCorrect: The aside builds connection and humor with the audience.
explanation.tip: Consider the effect of narrative choices.

options.label: B
options.text: To create humor and let the audience share her private struggle

items.stem: Which is the best summary of “The Last Bus Home”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Includes problem, turning point and insight.
explanation.tip: Summaries cover beginning, middle and end.

options.label: C
options.text: After missing the last bus, Yusuf walks home expecting trouble but discovers his family was only worried and his sister had been looking out for him.

items.stem: Which detail should be LEFT OUT of a summary of the four-day week article?

explanation.whyCorrect: Specific examples are less essential than the main points.
explanation.tip: Keep main points; drop examples.

options.label: A
options.text: Families need childcare on the fifth day.

options.label: D
options.text: Buses and heating are examples of savings.

items.stem: Which is the most objective summary of the souq letter?

explanation.whyCorrect: Objective summaries avoid judgments.
explanation.tip: Report, don’t evaluate.

options.label: A
options.text: A student urges the council to repair the souq instead of replacing it, citing history and tourism.

options.label: C
options.text: The council is wrong and foolish.

options.label: D
options.text: A wise student bravely saves the best market ever.

items.stem: Which summary of “The Interview” keeps the important events in order?

explanation.whyCorrect: Correct sequence of key events.
explanation.tip: Keep events in order.

options.label: A
options.text: Sara writes for the school newspaper.

options.label: B
options.text: A student interviews a reserved custodian, a question about a radio unlocks his stories, and he gives her a doorknob as a keepsake.

options.label: C
options.text: A radio plays music in a storage room.

options.label: D
options.text: A custodian gives a student a doorknob, then she asks about the radio.

items.stem: Which sentence summarizes BOTH texts in the paired passage without adding opinions?

explanation.whyCorrect: It captures the shared pattern objectively.
explanation.tip: Summaries of paired texts note what both share.

options.label: A
options.text: Yasmin practices against a stone wall.

options.label: B
options.text: Moving is the worst thing that can happen.

options.label: C
options.text: A girl and a transplanted tree each struggle after moving and eventually thrive.

options.label: D
options.text: Lemon trees and football are both fun.

items.stem: Which sentence supports the claim that reefs protect coastlines?

explanation.whyCorrect: This states the protective function directly.
explanation.tip: Match evidence to the exact claim.

options.label: B
options.text: “A reef is built by tiny animals called coral polyps.”

options.label: D
options.text: “Coastlines are protected because reefs break the force of storm waves.”

items.stem: Which quotation supports the claim that four-day weeks may harm learning?

explanation.whyCorrect: Slower score growth is evidence about learning.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that matches the claim’s topic.

options.label: A
options.text: “students’ math scores grew more slowly than in similar five-day schools.”

options.label: D
options.text: “More schools are considering a four-day week.”

items.stem: Which detail shows that Yusuf expected to be in trouble?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rehearsing excuses shows he feared blame.
explanation.tip: Inner thoughts are strong evidence of feelings.

items.stem: Which TWO quotations support the inference that Mr. Aziz takes pride in his work?

explanation.whyCorrect: His careful effort and his belief in looking after things show pride.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that clearly supports the inference.

options.label: B
options.text: “Some things last if you look after them.”

options.label: C
options.text: “I carried two hundred chairs to the library, one by one.”

options.label: D
options.rationale: This begins the story but does not show pride.

items.stem: A reader claims Huda respects the council even while disagreeing. Which quotation is the STRONGEST evidence?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her respectful closing and constructive tone support the claim; the closing states it directly.
explanation.tip: The best evidence most directly proves the claim.

options.label: A
options.text: “Please do not let our history disappear behind a glass wall.”

options.label: B
options.text: “The city council plans to replace our old covered souq.”

options.label: D
options.text: “I urge the council to change its plan.”

items.stem: Which theme does “Ladder” express?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each rung holds a year he gave; the speaker now reaches what he planted.
explanation.tip: Themes are messages about life.

options.label: D
options.text: The love and lessons of family stay with us as we grow.

items.stem: Which detail best develops the theme of “The Interview”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The gift connects to “Some things last if you look after them.”
explanation.tip: Find details tied to the message.

options.label: A
options.text: Mr. Aziz gives Sara the doorknob from the first door he fixed.

options.label: D
options.text: It is the last week of school.

items.stem: What theme do “The New Field” and “Transplant” share?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both show struggle after moving, then success.
explanation.tip: Shared themes can appear in different genres.

options.label: B
options.text: Adapting to change takes time, but growth follows.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Both texts show growth after moving.

items.stem: How does the setting of “Desert Night” support its theme of peace and wonder?

explanation.whyCorrect: Quiet sounds, warm sand and a starry sky create calm wonder.
explanation.tip: Setting can help develop theme.

options.label: C
options.text: The vast, silent desert under the stars creates a feeling of calm awe.

options.label: D
options.text: The busy city noise creates excitement.
